###### **EDITORS’ BIOGRAPHIES** 

**Jorge M. Menacho** received his B.Sc. in Chemistry from the University of Chile in 1974 and his D.Sc. in Metallurgical Engineering from the University of Concepciуn in 1985. He then joined the Pennsylvania State University in 1985 – 1986 working in the field of mathematical modelling of comminution processes. Since 1973 to 1994, he worked for the Mining and Metallurgical Research Centre CIMM in Chile and thereafter he founded De Re Metallica Engineering, a consulting company in extractive metallurgy where he currently holds the General Manager position. He has been involved in academic activities at the University of Concepciуn, the University of Santiago, The Chilean Catholic University and the National Council for Science and Technology CONYCIT in Chile. ### **PREFACE** 

Copper 2013 International Conference is the 8<sup>th</sup> version of the most important global meeting that brings together leading scientists, researchers, academics, and executives from different companies and organizations devoted to the areas of economy, copper processing, metallurgical extraction techniques; environmental compatibility; copper applications, copper recovery, and waste management and recycling techniques. At the same time, the challenges faced by different mining projects will be addressed. We appreciate the work and collaboration from colleagues coming from over 30 countries and representing more than 300 companies and institutions. 

Copper 2013 Conferences find their origin in the joint work conducted between the Chilean Institute of Mining Engineers (IIMCh) and the Metallurgical Society of the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum (METSOC). Since 2007, when the Copper Conference was held in Toronto, new co-organizer institutions have helped disseminate the results achieved by the Conferences while granting these a strong global character in terms of convening power, submittal of papers, and the generation of collaborative knowledge. We deeply appreciate the disinterested contribution from GDMB of Germany, MMIJ of Japan, and TMS and SME from USA. 

This time, the current global situation is not only a scenario where competitive prices are being realized but also where strong and serious uncertainties are being handled in connection with the global economy; energy and key resources prices. 

Globally, ore grades have declined to historically low levels and, therefore, the recycling and recovery of what used to be waste material, nowadays represent great opportunities for the overall development of new projects. Water uses in production processes and the solutions applied no doubt represent a source of knowledge for the community gathered at this venue. Likewise, new long-term and mid-term forecasts to be made in the future

will certainly set their focus on eventual challenges and on mining and metallurgical development opportunities in the decades ahead. The total of 330 papers submitted in response to the original call will present the main changes to take place in metallurgical processes, as well as the state-of-theart techniques responsible for providing effective solutions to new challenges posed by metallurgical processes. The widespread interest generated by innovations, particularly in the area of pyrometallurgy will undoubtedly occupy a special place in the course of the Conference, thanks to the research and development of technological solutions conducted in countries like China, for example. The 2013 Conference has issued 7 volumes of Proceedings containing all the papers and management initiatives presented in each of the 10 symposiums hosted by the Conference. #### **MODELLING BUBBLE HYDRODYNAMICS IN FLOTATION** 

C.O. Gomez and J.A. Finch _McGill University 3610 University Street Montreal, Canada H3A 2B2 cesar.gomez@mcgill.ca_ 

M. Maldonado _Departamento de Ingenierнa Metalъrgica Universidad de Santiago de Chile Avenida Libertador Bernardo O’Higgins 3363 Santiago, Chile_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Three parameters are generally used to describe gas dispersion in a flotation machine: superficial gas (air) velocity, gas holdup and bubble size.  Techniques and sensors to measure local values of these parameters, including industrial flotation units, have been developed.  A model relating these variables, which was developed based on a drift-flux analysis of bubble hydrodynamics, has been available for many years.  The model has been mainly used to predict one variable (typically bubble size) from measurements of the other two.  Gas dispersion measurements in laboratory and industrial units have demonstrated that in many cases significant differences between measurement and model prediction exist.  A reliable model to predict properties of bubble populations would help in the selection and operation of flotation equipment. This work takes laboratory air-water data sets to establish the adequacy of the equations in the drift-flux model.  The results demonstrated that ignoring the effect of frother on bubble terminal and swarm velocities is the reason for the poor model prediction. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

4 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The separation of particles by flotation is the most widely used technology to concentrate base metal minerals.  Particles are selectively collected on the surface of rising air bubbles and separated into a concentrate.  The efficiency of the process depends primarily on the characteristics of the bubble population generated in the machine and the resulting system hydrodynamics.  To date we do not have the ability to predict the size distribution and spatial distribution of bubble populations.  A reliable model would contribute to the design and selection of equipment

and to the development of operating strategies leading to increases in performance. 

There are numerous theoretical and experimental studies on the generation and motion of bubbles in a fluid, recently reviewed by Kulkarni and Joshi [1].  Most of the studies refer to applications not relevant to flotation as no frother was used and bubble sizes were large (> 5 – 10 mm).  When frothers are used, the bubble size generated by the machine is preserved to varying degrees and bubble populations with small and narrow size range are obtained.  It has also been demonstrated that bubble velocity is related to its shape [2, 3, 4].  One study [4] demonstrated that changes in the shape of a single bubble achieved by varying frother concentration had the same shape-velocity relationship as a bubble whose shape was controlled by varying viscosity. 

The hydrodynamics of bubble swarms are commonly described by three parameters: superficial gas velocity Jg (or gas velocity, volumetric air flow rate per unit cross-sectional area of cell); gas holdup εg (volumetric fraction of gas); and bubble size db (an average diameter calculated from the size distribution).  Devices to measure these parameters in laboratory and industrial units have been developed and used to relate gas dispersion to metallurgical performance [5, 6, 7, 8, 9].  Bubble swarm hydrodynamics have been modeled using drift flux analysis employing these parameters [10,11], but the effect of bubble shape was not considered.  The models have been used to calculate one of the parameters, generally bubble size, from known values of the other two.  Our experience indicates that even in two-phase (air-water) systems the model predictions were not accurate: for example, bubbles of different size generated in a laboratory column using several frother solutions with the same gas flow rate, produced the same gas holdup which drift flux could not predict [12]. 

The drift-flux model requires equations to calculate bubble terminal and swarm velocity.  The purpose of this paper is to use two sets of published laboratory air-water data to establish the test the drift-flux model and try to account for the effect of frothers on bubble velocity through the relationship to bubble size. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

5

#### **Prediction of bubble terminal velocity** 

Correlations to predict bubble terminal velocity, originally developed for solid objects (particles), were applied in some cases successfully to small bubbles rising in clean and contaminated waters. However, bubbles larger than 1 mm move with terminal velocities significantly lower than that predicted assuming a sphere, as they adopt nonspherical shapes and rise following zigzag or spiral trajectories.  Correlations to calculate drag coefficients for bubbles in liquids were developed by fitting data to expressions obtained by dimensional analysis.  Four dimensionless numbers have been normally used in these correlations: i) Reynolds number (Re) which compares inertia and frictional effects; ii) Eцtvцs number (Eo) which compares buoyancy and surface tension effects; iii) Morton number (Mo) which compares properties of the liquid and gas phases; and iv), Arquimedes number (Ar) which compares buoyancy and frictional effects and represents the driving force for bubble motion. The predictions from the numerous correlations proposed to calculate drag coefficients for bubbles of sizes up to 4 mm vary widely [4].  Surface contamination (in flotation systems by the use of frothers) causes the interface to become rigid and bubble shape and velocity approach those of solid (hollow) spheres.  Recent work has demonstrated a strong relationship between bubble shape and velocity [2, 3, 4]; bubble shape is a parameter which has not been considered in drift flux analysis of bubble hydrodynamics.  For the purpose of this work, those correlations that predict minimum and maximum velocities for bubbles smaller than 4 mm will be considered:

The models are based on equations to calculate bubble terminal velocity and the slowing down as bubble concentration (gas holdup) increases. The equations have been developed for the sedimentation or fluidization of solid particles, which cannot incorporate the effect of frothers on bubble shape and velocity. This was demonstrated through the model application to two sets of published data. The experience leaves the impression that the approach may work if equations which include the effect of bubble shape are considered. #### **ABSTRACT** 

In the last decades flotation equipment has shown a significant increase in size. At the present moment, most of concentration plants operating in Chile have been fully equipped with 130–250 m³ mechanical cells and new projects are considering 300 m³ cell on their flotation circuits. This dramatic increase in size poses new challenges in terms of developing better approaches to optimize the operations. 

Originally, Minera Los Pelambres’ rougher Cu – Mo flotation stage was equipped with 130 m³ in volume WEMCO cells with no internal launders on it. This paper describes the metallurgical comparison between two parallel flotation lines, one of them with recently internal launders installed on the three first cells. For this purpose, a six month sampling campaign was developed in order to obtain the metallurgical parameters of concentrate grade and recovery. 

The analyzed data demonstrated an improvement in the Cu and Mo recovery of about 0,11% due the effects of internal launders on cells stabilization and increase on the available concentrate discharge perimeter. This result led to extend the installation of these devises on the other three lines remaining on the three firs cells.

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

A metallurgical improvement in the rougher flotation improvement was obtained with the installation of the internal launders on the three first cells. These results are: 

- Higher mean recovery for both, Cu and Mo species. 

- Lower enrichment ratio for Cu and Mo due the increase of the mass reported to the concentrate. 

- Better stability on the operation.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

A database of Sauter mean bubble diameters, D32, and superficial gas rates, JG, measured in different industrial flotation plants, is presented. Results involved mechanical flotation cells of 10 – 300 m<sup>3</sup> from rougher, cleaner and scavenger circuits and columns from cleaner circuits. A significant effect of superficial gas rate on bubble diameter was observed in mechanical cells with different bubble generation mechanisms, cell designs (self-aerated or forced air) and different operating conditions (frother dosage, impeller speed). This result implies a dominant effect of the superficial gas rate on gas dispersion. Also, higher D32 values were observed in flotation columns partly because of the bubble sparger system, but mainly due to lack of maintenance. From the D32 and JG estimations, the bubble surface area flux, SB, was evaluated in order to determine the typical range of industrial values. The gas dispersion database is useful to select proper operating conditions and to define control criteria in flotation circuits.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Flotation is a principal method for mineral concentration in which separation efficiency depends on chemical, operational and machine performance. Research focus among these three aspects has varied over the years. Recently, machine aspects have been revisited. Gas dispersion, being an important hydrodynamic characteristic in flotation, is one of the key variables related to equipment performance. 

Gas dispersion has been commonly expressed in terms of the bubble size, gas holdup,  G, and superficial gas rate, JG. Those parameters have been related by means of the bubble surface area flux, SB (SB = 6 JG/dB, where dB is usually the Sauter mean diameter, D32), which has been correlated with flotation rates in mechanical cells [1] while the linearity of these correlations has been discussed in [2]. More recently, empirical correlations between D32 and SB for pilot and industrial flotation columns were presented [3, 4]. According to [5], gas holdup is correlated with the bubble size because of the bubble rising velocity. At diameters below 2 - 3 mm, rise velocity decreases in direct relationship with bubble diameters. 

Superficial gas rate is expressed as the volumetric gas flow rate per crosssectional area. The JG parameter can be measured by collecting bubbles from the pulp zone into a tube immersed in the flotation machine [6, 7]. Bubble size distribution, represented by Sauter mean diameter, can be obtained using optical methods or visual techniques together with image processing software [8]. Finally, gas holdup can be estimated from conductivity measurements [9] or from confined volume in the collection zone [

7].

#### **Bubble size distribution, superficial gas rate and gas holdup measurements** 

Bubble size distributions (BSD) were measured using the McGill bubble viewer for image acquisition (Figure 1, top). The image processing software USM-IMA was used to obtain the BSD and the statistical parameters from the bubble population, e.g. Sauter mean diameter D32 [8]. The USM-IMA is semiautomatic software developed in MATLAB 2009 [12], which allows single bubble diameters to be estimated as the equivalent ellipsoid diameter. Also, simple clusters of bubbles can be automatically segmented and processed using either the Watershed or the Hough Transform. Complex clusters of bubbles and large bubbles can be manually estimated in order to avoid biased results. Each BSD measurement reported in this paper includes more than 1500 bubbles (Figure 1, bottoms). 

For the bubble capture, the MBSA sampling tube was placed between the cell launder lip and the froth-crowder based on accessibility. The sampling depth was between 15 and 30 cm below the pulp-froth interface in the quiescent zone of the cells (Figure 1, top). This position allows the pipe to capture the bubbles from the pulp zone even when the interface drops due to operational disturbances. Furthermore, measurements at the quiescent zone avoid turbulence effects. 

Figure 2 presents examples of bubble size distributions for mechanical cells (300 m<sup>3</sup> ) and columns (2 x 8 x 10 m<sup>3</sup> ). In mechanical cells, a good agreement between the histograms of the BSD and the lognormal distribution was observed. Also, a good agreement between the histograms of the BSD and the log-logistic distribution was obtained in flotation columns. In both cases, the statistical parameters were estimated by using the Statistics Toolbox of Matlab 2010 [13]. 

The MBSA was adapted to determine the superficial gas rate, JG, which was obtained by water volume displacement over time. The superficial gas rates alon

g with the D32 values allowed the calculation of the bubble surface area flux, SB (m2 /s/m2 ). The local gas concentration (holdup) below the pulp-froth interface was measured using 1.2 L device. This sensor allows a portion of pulp (along with dispersed air) to be captured in the collection zone. The gas holdup can be estimated from the difference between the sampled pulp and the total volume of the sampler. #### **CONCLUSIONS** 

In the present study estimations of gas dispersion parameters were performed in different industrial flotation plants. The main findings were: 

- The bubble size distribution measurements allowed for the detection of abnormal gas dispersion conditions based on the frequency of large bubbles. 

- A significant effect of superficial gas rate on bubble diameter was observed in mechanical cells from different flotation plants. This result implies a dominant effect of the superficial gas rate on gas dispersion. 

- Sauter mean diameters lower than 2.5 mm were related to low JG; diameters higher than 2.5 mm were related to high or moderate to high JG values in mechanical cells. 

- D32 > 4.0 mm were observed in flotation columns mainly because lack of maintenance in the gas dispersion systems (spargers). 

- Hold-up ranged from 5% to 21% in mechanical cell, in which εG < 12% were related to low gas rates (JG < 1 cm/s) or high D32 values (D32 > 3 mm). 

- In mechanical cells, SB values ranged from 21 - 62 m<sup>2</sup> /s/m<sup>2</sup> , where SB < 30 m<sup>2</sup> /s/m<sup>2</sup> were related to either JG < 1 cm/s or D32 > 2.5 mm with JG = 1.0 – 1.8 cm/s. 

- In flotation columns two conditions were observed: (i) low SB values were measured (< 20 m<sup>2</sup> /s/m<sup>2</sup> ), which corresponds to inefficient gas dispersion and (ii) SB ≈ 30 m<sup>2</sup> /s/m<sup>2</sup> with JG > 2 cm/s, which corresponds to inefficient gas dispersion

considering the high JG operating values.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

For over two decades, LOOP (French acronym for _Process Observation and Optimization Laboratory)_ researchers have been working at developing and/or improving specific sensors for flotation columns and their use for process control.  Several papers have already been published for the Mineral Processing industrial and scientific community in peer-reviewed journals and conference proceedings, e.g. for the Copper Conference series.  This paper summarizes the latest milestones completed by the group, since the last Copper conference held in Chile (2003), emphasizing on results presented in North America and Europe since Copper 2010.  On the instrumentation side, developments encompass a more accurate method for measuring electrical conductivity for flotation column sensors, a device for estimating the bias rate, a better procedure for evaluating bubble size from images taken by bubble viewers, and a method for on line estimation of frother concentration.  In terms of process control advances, the discussion will focus on results for bubble size control in a two-phase system, and the application of a 3x3 multivariable predictive control to a pilot flotation column running in parallel to industrial columns in a Quйbec concentrator. #### **INTRODUCTION** 

Since the first successful industrial implementation in 1981 (Les Mines Gaspй, Canada), flotation columns have been used in several mineral applications (coal, base metals, phosphates, etc.), mainly in cleaning stages as a result of their froth washing capabilities.  Despite their widespread usage, measuring some column-specific variables, and consequently their use for process control, is rather limited.  The process efficiency, reflected by the concentrate grade and recovery (primary variables), is dependent on socalled “secondary variables” such as froth depth ( _Hf_ ), bias rate ( _Jb_ ), gas hold-up (  _g_ ) and bubble surface area flux (BASF or _Sb_ ).  Only the first one is presently monitored in plants, usually through floats coupled to ultrasound, and controlled by manipulating the set-point of the tailing flow-rate. The gas hold-up is the relative column volume occupied by bubbles, thus available for particle collection, i.e. directly related to valuable mineral recovery.  Even though off-the-shelf sensors are commercially available [1,2], it is seldom monitored in industry and obviously not controlled.  The bias rate is defined as the net downward flow of water crossing the interface, and as such it dictates the quality of the column cleaning action.  Unfortunately it is not measured either. 

BSAF is defined as the rate of bubble surface rising through the column.  As such, it is the variable most directly associated to the collec

tion process, and thus to recovery.  However, the BSAF calculation implies knowing the average bubble diameter ( _Db,avg_ ), a variable that has started being measured off-line only recently [3] . An attempt to use the BSAF for optimizing the recovery estimates the _Db,avg_ through a drift-flux analysis (DFA), based on  _g_ values from a CiDRA GH-100© [4].  As mentioned by the authors, this approach though, implies some assumptions related to the DFA (e.g. pulp viscosity).  Having a robust on-line _Db,avg_ measurement will certainly encourage the use of BSAF for industrial column control.  Nonetheless, the _Db,avg_ is a misleading concept since flotation bubbles are quite different in size; therefore the bubble size distribution (BSD), and the corresponding BSAF <u>distribution, would be more relevant.  As later</u> indicated in this paper, work is in progress on this issue. 

Bubble size depends mainly on three factors: gas flow rate ( _Jg_ ), sparger characterristics (orifice size, porosity, shear water, etc.), and frother type and concentration.  Any effort for controlling bubble size will require manipulating these variables.  Whereas _Jg_ and sparger characteristics **/** settings can be adjusted, frother concentration cannot.  Some off-line measurement methods have been suggested, but the laboratory procedure introduces long delays incompatible with on-line control.  Aiming at an automatic control application, Maldonado recently proposed an on-line estimation method [5], using _Jg_ and  _g_ values, from already available commercial sensors. 

In summary, with the exception of froth depth, continuous monitoring of flotation column variables is so far limited to flow rates (gas, feed, tailings, wash water), i.e. to available manipulated variables.  Process control (PID) is also mainly limited to froth level and some flow rates such as wash water _(Jww)_ and air _(Jg)_ . Primary variables, concentrate grade and recovery, are essentially targeted through rule-based systems.

However, the benefits of advanced model-based control and supervision techniques are nowadays well recognized, and this in many industrial fields [6,7].  LOOP researchers have tested a successful application of multivariable predictive control to a pilot-scale flotation column [8], and discussions with industrial partners are underway for a full-scale test plan.  Moreover, the BSD has recently been measured and modeled using a modified version of the McGill Bubble Viewer [9], thus allowing control of the Sauter mean bubble size ( _D32_ ) in a two-phase system laboratory column [10].  Both control applications are summarized later on in this paper. 

#### **NEW INSTRUMENTATION DEVELOPMENTS** 

#### **Conductivity measurements using a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)** 

As mentioned before, froth depth is successfully measured in industrial columns using a float.  For laboratory or pilot-scale units, such as those us

ed by our research group, this option is not possible because of the small cross section of the columns. Instead, froth depth monitoring relies on a semi-analytical procedure based on the electrical conductivity profile across the interface position [11]. The conductivity is measured by sequentially powering a series of “conductivity cells” (eleven cells 10 cm apart, each one made of two electrodes flush mounted inside the laboratory column) with a high frequency alternating current, to avoid electrolysis and polarization. Both the McGill  _g_ sensor and the Laval _Jb_ sensor (later on described), also rely on similar conductivity-based techniques. The main disadvantage of this method is the high load produced in the power supply when all conductivity cells are connected. Moreover, it is sensitive to noise, and the number of output bits of the analog-to-digital converters limits the resolution. This can become a limitation, when the conductivity spans a wide range of operation. Furthermore, since the relationship between the output voltage and conductivity is usually nonlinear, the resolution is related to the changes in the function slope. To overcome these problems, Riquelme et al. [12] used a different approach where each conductivity cell is sequentially connected to a square wave oscillator circuit. Its oscillation frequency becomes a function of the sample conductivity. This strategy, where the measured frequency allows estimating the conductivity, reduces the problem related to the noise and DC components, since the square wave frequency can be measured with a digital input. Measurement resolution can be improved by increasing clock frequency, less expensive than increasing the resolution of the analog-to-digital converter. Since the hardware handles digital signals, data can be transmitted over long distances without degradation. Moreover, the approach allows a wide operational range as shown in Figure 1 and only requires a single point for the calibration, which is very convenient in an industrial environment. A Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) is used to measure the oscillation period, display the data on a LCD screen, communicate the information to a computer via RS-232 and manage the switching between the various measurement cells. #### **NEW PROCESS CONTROL DEVELOPMENTS** 

#### **Multivariable predictive control of** **_Hf_ ,** **_Jb_ and

**  **_g_** 

A hierarchical framework is generally recommended for adequate process control. The resulting stack of ‘control layers’ are often depicted in a triangular structure.  From the base of the triangle, the first four layers are: instrumentation, regulatory control, advanced process control and real-time optimization.  Regulatory control consists of local SISO (single input – ingle output) control loops (PID) providing a steady operation for the flotation column inputs: feed (whenever possible), gas and wash water flow rates. It is also assumed that the feed has been correctly conditioned ensuring adequate pH and reagent concentration.  The advanced control layer aims at maintaining process (secondary) variables, such as the froth depth, bias rate, froth parameters, gas hold-up or bubble surface area flux, at their own set point, hopefully related to the metallurgical objectives (recovery and grade).  Real-time optimization (RTO), the ultimate goal, allows 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

42 

managing on-line the set points of secondary variables, leading, through a mathematical routine, to optimal metallurgical indices. 

Two experimental projects [8,19] show the potential of this control philosophy. The experimental set-up consisted in a Plexiglas column of 7.5 m height (15 & 5 cm diameter), using conductivity-based sensors for _Hf_ ,  _w_ and  _g_ , peristaltic pumps for handling the various streams, and ad-hoc flow meters for gas, water and pulp streams. Wash-water and air flow rates were managed by PI controllers implemented in a Moore Micro 353<sup>©</sup> controller.  Graphical interfaces and data acquisition were performed by a HMI/SCADA software iFIX<sup>©</sup> , operating under a Windows XP<sup>©</sup> . An Opto 22<sup>©</sup> I/O system was used to centralize sensor and actuator signals.  The control algorithms were implemented in MatLab<sup>©</sup> , all signals being sampled every two seconds. 

In both experimental cases, the considered secondary variables are the froth depth, bias rate (or  _w_ ), and gas hold-up.  A 2x2 model-based predictive controller (MPC) (manipulating the wash-water and gas flow rates) supervises  _w_ and  _g_ , and complements the standard PI used for froth depth control, manipulating the tailings flow rate.  Like for industrial application, froth depth control essentially aims at maintaining a stable column operation.  The  _w_ /  _g_ multivariable controller adds a very interesting feature: it was designed to optimize indirectly grade and recovery, via gas hold-up and bias rate setpoints.  More precisely, the strategy consists in selecting a set point exceeding the normal physical values for  _g_ , while simultaneously satisfying operational constraints, such as ensuring a positive _Jb_ to prevent gangue entrainment.  This is equivalent to maximizing the BSAF available for particle collection, thus maximizing recovery, and avoiding concentrate grade deterioration.  Other

possible constraints to be respected are: 

- _Jg_<sup>sp</sup> ≤ _Jg_ max to prevent hydraulic entrainment and the loss of the interface

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The work summarized in this paper and references herein, shows that adequate sensors and/or methods exist for measuring the most important variables of flotation column operation.  In particular, the _Db,avg_ ( _D32_ ) can be estimated <u>on-line</u> and used for control purposes, via BSAF or gas hold-up.  The on-line evaluation and modeling of bubble size <u>distributions will soon be feasible and could also be employed for process</u> control as it is, or through the concept of BSAF distribution. 

Model-based control of “traditional” secondary column variables has been accomplished in an industrial environment, and could be implemented in industrial columns using available commercial sensors.  Model-based control of the bubble _D_ 32, calculated from BSD measurements, is achievable in a two-phase column.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Frothers play two major roles in flotation: preservation of the formation bubble size and stabilization of the froth.  Many tests have been proposed to characterize these two functions but, in general, the focus has been on only one of these roles and measurements are done at conditions quite different from those existing in industrial cells.  A technique to characterize the two roles simultaneously at flotation hydrodynamic conditions, based on the use of a laboratory flotation column, was developed and successfully used to screen and select a replacement candidate for a particular concentrator.  Although operations require to test and compare frothers regularly, the problems associated with the installation and use of a laboratory flotation column for on-site testing are a serious limitation for the implementation of the technique.  The objective of this work is the development of a frother characterization test using a laboratory mechanical cell, a common piece of equipment in operations.  It is believed that measurement of the CCC and determination of the water overflow rate, in these units, will provide data to establish differences among frothers and characterize the strength of their roles.  The work reported at this stage is the result of tests completed to demonstrate this concept.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Flotation is the most important mineral separation technology used to concentrate metal sulphides for metal production such as copper.  It is based on the collection and separation of hydrophobic particles on the surface of bubbles.  The separation requires several consecutive processes to occur: formation of bubble-particle aggregates by collision of bubbles and particles, rising and concentration of these aggregates in a top layer, and finally their removal into a concentrate stream.  Flotation machines operates with two zones for these processes to proceed: a pulp or collection zone in which the aggregates are formed and rise, and a froth or cleaning zone where the aggregates concentrate and drain water as they rise to overflow the cell and report to the concentrate. 

The efficiency of the separation, as expected, has been closely linked to the characteristics of the bubble and particle size distributions because of their obvious relevance in the formation of bubble-particle aggregates.  In the last few years, however, studies have shown that frothers play several roles in flotation that profoundly affect both bubble size and hydrodynamics in both zones of a flotation machine. Frothers not only reduce bubble size, but also increase collection zone gas holdup by slowing down bubble rise velocity, and water overflow rate by affecting the froth structure and its ability to drain wate

r.  It has been demonstrated that measurement of bubble size [1], gas holdup [2] and water overflow rate [3] could be used to classify frothers.  The two most relevant roles for industrial operations are preserving bubble formation size, which is connected with bubble size control, and defining water carrying rate into the froth and water drainage in the froth layer, which is associated with froth stabilisation.  The magnitude of these effects depends on the frother used and its concentration, and knowing their values is necessary not only for frother selection, but also to decide operating conditions leading to stable operation and acceptable metallurgical performance.  In a given concentrator, with an established cell size and type, and mineral and particle characteristics varying within a narrow margin, frother selection and distribution offer an alternative for operators to make adjustments after feed changes or to improve performance. 

Frother characterisation efforts have been, in general, focused on determining either the effect of frothers on bubble size and velocity in water and pulp, which is important for the processes occurring in the collection zone, or on bubble coalescence and water drainage in the froth layer, of interest to understand the phenomena happening in the froth zone. In most cases, work has been accomplished using batch techniques, designed to measure one variable, running at conditions quite different from those existing in industrial cells.  The results obtained, although useful for classifying (ranking) frothers, cannot be used to understand the result of frother replacement or of concentration changes in plant operations.  These approaches fail to recognize and account for the strong interactions existing between the two zones; for example, it was demonstrated that water overflow rate correlated with gas holdup in the collection zone [3].  The need for a method for capturing both roles at hydrodynamic conditions closer to those existing in flotation machines has been recognized [1,6].

A frother characterisation method was proposed to test frothers through simultaneous measurements in the collection and froth zone of a laboratory flotation column [8,9].  The approach offered data collected at true flotation conditions and, at the same time, including the effect of interactions between zones.  Air was dispersed using a porous SS sparger and was well implemented to be automatically operated with a constant froth layer.  The procedure included the measurement of bubble size, gas holdup in the collection zone and water overflow rate for a selected froth height, when the column was run continuously with a frother solution.  Frothers were characterized and classified using three parameters: the critical coalescence concentration (CCC) determined from the bubble size decrease as the frother concentration was increased, the minimum gas holdup to have overflow for a selecte

Although the approach was tested without solids, it was successfully used to aid a sponsor to replace the frother in use by one of three options offered by chemical suppliers [7]. Operations require testing and comparing frothers regularly, but the problems associated with the installation and operation of a laboratory flotation column for on-site testing are a severe limitation for the implementation of the technique, in spite of the advantages of running tests with the local process water and solids. #### **Test Procedure** 

The development of a standard test to characterize frother roles using a laboratory mechanical cell requires to find operating conditions that permit to detect differences in the ability of frothers to preserve the original bubble size obtained during generation, and to reduce water drainage when bubbles are concentrated and rise in close contact through a froth layer. Characterization of these two roles was considered through the measurement of: 

- Critical coalescence concentration (CCC), which requires the measurement of bubble size as a function of frother concentration (values selected 2, 5, 10, 15, 30, 60 y 100 ppm); and 

- Rate or total water that overflows the cell for one or more frother concentrations. 

The procedure to follow for running tests and collection measurements with acceptable reproducibility must consider that frothers, in many cases, have limited solubility and are slow to solubilize.  Frothers may be volatile and solutions may decompose at room temperature and if exposed to daylight.  Large volumes (10 to 12 L) of frother solutions in the concentration (ppm) range are necessary to fill both the cell and the bubble size measuring device; the same solution must be used as a fraction of that filling the bubble imaging device is released into the cell during bubble size measurement. 

The procedure to run the tests included three aspects: preparation of the frother solution, measurement b

ubble size, and determination of water overflow rate or volume: 

<u>Preparation of frother solutions. The solution to be used in the bubble size and water</u> overflow measurements was prepared by dilution from a 100-ppm stock solution.  The stock solution (30 L necessary for the tests at the seven concentrations) required 3 g and 30 kg of frother and water, respectively.  The mixture was maintained overnight with a gentle agitation to ensure complete dissolution of the frother, and then stored in a dark cabinet.  An effort was made to run the bubble size and water overflow measurements the same day the stock solution was prepared, to avoid concentration changes by volatilization and decomposition, which would go unaware. 

<u>Bubble size measurement. The measurement is initiated by filling the cell (with 4.5 L)</u> and the bubble images collecting device with the selected frother solution.  The cell was started with the impeller type, impeller speed, gas flow rate and amount of water selected for the test.  After 1 minute of conditioning, the stopper closing the bubble collection tube was removed for bubbles to be sampled and directed to the exposing area.  After 3 minutes to allow a steady flow of rising bubbles to reach the imaging point, 200 to 300 images were collected in a one per second rate (Figure 4).  The images were processed using the program ImageJ, which calculated both area and pixel value statistics for every object (group of neighboring pixels darker than a threshold, selected by the program) in

#### **CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK** 

The results obtained in this work demonstrated that the concept devised to develop a frother characterization test, using a laboratory mechanical cell, was successful in the detection of differences in the ability of frothers to both controlling bubble size and stabilizing the froth.  The approach selected to characterize these two functions was measurement of the CCC and determination of the water overflow volume, respectively. 

The results were collected in air-water tests using samples of commercial frothers provided by sponsors.  Both measurements, CCC and water overflow volume, showed clear differences between frothers, and sorting their strength was straightforward.  The results also demonstrated that a strong or weak frother for bubble size control didn't necessarily mean a strong or weak frother for froth stabilization. 

Future work will focus on the development of a standard test to classify frothers. Tests will use different types of frothers, this time available as reagents, to avoid blends and contaminants.  A search for operating conditions maximizing differences between frothers will be carried out. #### **ABSTRACT** 

Centro de Investigaciуn (Research Centre) JRI S.A. ( **CI-JRI** ) develops a line of research oriented to studying thickening processes, whose objective are to establish general design guidelines, reagent evaluation, and operating conditions. They expect to harmonize standard settling measurements made in a laboratory with measurements made in batch and continuous pilot thickening columns, for each type of ore. 

Thickener design requires taking into account a number of variables that affect slurry behavior, and the mineralogical characterization of samples and their representativity is of prime importance because geological units, lithologies and alteration may appear during the useful life of the mine, especially during its first 5 years. These characteristics of the ore affect its physical characteristics such as granulometric profile, solid density and ionic charge, among others, modifying its behavior in the thickening stage. 

Ignoring these aspects leads to various operational problems in industrial tailings and copper-concentrate thickeners such as not achieving overflow quality or the percentage of solids required in the und

erflow. 

In recent years **CI-JRI** has designed and built two pilot columns, 1 and 4 meters high respectively, equipped with rakes and a feed system (feedwell). With these two implemented columns **CI-JRI** has been able to develop its own methodology for characterizing mining-slurry thickening in batch and continuous tests. 

This paper presents examples of the type of results that can be obtained and shows how useful this type of results are for establishing thickener capacity, concentration of solids in the underflow, effect of the flocculant and quality of the supernatant liquid, in a way very much akin to what occurs in an industrial operation.

Finally, the authors believe that the definition of a method open to the community is good for all parties in that it clearly defines the procedures employed in the tests, which  are ideally standardized and make the evaluation of the most significant variables (solids content variations, mineralogy changes, additives, additive doses, etc) possible.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The characterization of thickening processes has been studied for over a 100 years; studies developed by Mishler in 1912 and Coe and Clevenger in 1916, are still used successfully mainly due to their simplicity both of calculations and information required for their application. “More modern” methods of design are based on the work developed by Kynch in 1952, and, as of 1970, a rigorous settling and thickening theory starts to be developed thanks to the joint effort of mathematicians and engineers. These studies are currently oriented towards developing models applicable to compressive systems (flocculated slurries). A detailed historical description of how the study of thickening processes has evolved can be found in F. Concha and R. Burger’s paper [1] “A Century of Research in Sedimentation and Thickening”. 

A number of experimental studies whose main objective is to validate the concepts through batch and continuous tests in columns of different heights and diameters has been conducted in parallel to the theoretical study of thickening. 

Studies such as the ones developed by E.W. Coming (1940), E.W. Coming et al. (1954), H.J. Edde and W.W, Eckenfelder (1968), L.G. Eklund and A. Jernqvist (1975), Eklund (1976), J.B. Farrow et al. (2000), B.R. Gladman (2010) [2-8] among others, show behaviors such as that the depth of the compression area and rakes have an effect on the concentration of solids in the underflow, but standard design is not their goal. 

Equipment suppliers have developed and/ or used benchmarking for designing industrial thickeners, but for obvious reasons, these methodologies have not been disclosed. 

The Authors believe that the open definition of designing methods is good for everybody; therefore, it is necessary to define clear testing methodologies, ideally standardized, that will allow the most signifi

cant variables (variations of fine contents in the ore, changes in mineralogy, additives, additive doses, etc.) to be evaluated. 

The objective of this paper is to develop CI-JRI’s own methodology for the characterization and design of thickening processes and to show the progress made in thickening during the last two years at **CI-JRI** that enable us to study variables such as thickening height, the effect of rakes, and differences between batch and continuous tests. 

This paper presents the implementation of two columns – 1 and 4 meters high respectively – for developing thickening tests based on which **CI-JRI** has produced measuring protocols. Examples of types of studies that can be developed, as well as their applications in thickener design, are given, establishing capacity, concentration of solids in the underflow, effect of the flocculant, and quality of the supernatant liquid, in a way much more akin to what occurs in an industrial operation.

#### **EXPERIMENTAL METHODS** 

#### **Experimental procedure** 

The procedure defined at **CI-JRI** for studying thickening of a particular material includes three main stages: Characterization, thickening and analysis of results. 

#### <u>Characterization of the sample</u> 

It includes mineralogy, determining the density of solids by means of a Gay Lussac pycnometer, laser granulometry, rheology at five concentrations of solids, and settling rate at four concentrations of solids in 1-liter graduated glass cylinders. 

#### <u>Thickening in columns:</u> 

Thickening tests are conducted in columns of different heights, mainly 1 and 4 m, in which peristaltic pumps are used for controlling feed and discharge flow (in the case of continuous tests) and for controlling flocculant feed flow. 

Injecting flocculant into the system is done through a T connection in the feed area just before both flows enter the feedwell area of the column. 

In the case of batch thickening tests, there is no flow in the underflow area, but the columns have a sampling system implemented at the bottom, allowing the percentage of solids at the lower end to be controlled during the test. 

Generally speaking, existing flows are controlled in column tests. These controls allow mass balances to be carried out, thickening capacity to be determined and reagent dosages to be controlled, among others. 

As the tests are carried out, samples are collected at controlled intervals of time from different points of the column, and the water-sediment interface, the consolidated slurry-sediment interface, and settling velocity (when the feed flow ends) are measured. 

#### <u>Sample analysis and treatment:</u> 

The collected samples are characterized at the **CI-JRI** laboratory to determine variations of time in the concentration of solids, granulometry, rheology and overflow turbidity. 

The data are analyzed in order to determinate: temporary evolution for sampling points, fl

ow changes during the test, time variations of the height of the clear water-slurry _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 65 interfaces – slurry in settling and slurry in settling–consolidation, and unit areas calculated with several methods, and their comparison. #### **Experimental equipment** In the first stage - characterization of the material to be studied - the main types of equipment used were: a Microtrac S3500 particle-size analyzer, Gay Lussac pycnometers, a Haake RS600 rheometer with a Vane sensor, and 1-liter graduated glass cylinders, corresponding to batch tests without rakes that allow settling rate to be determined. The second stage – batch and continuous thickening tests – is carried out in 1 and 4-m columns that are schematically presented in Figure 1 and described in general in the following paragraphs: #### Column A It is a 1m-high acrylic cylinder with a 0.15m diameter. It has a rake connected at the lower end, and three pumps, two of which are for feed and underflow and one for flocculant dosing. An available slurry conditioning drum allows the slurry to be homogenized as it is fed to the column and pH values to be adjusted when necessary. It has an original feedwell, designed by **CI-JRI** , which can reduce the kinetic energy of the feed flow. The effect of using the feedwell is part of this study and is currently in its development stage. #### Column B It is a 4m-high acrylic column with a 0.4m diameter, made up of four 1m-high acrylic modules. #### **ABSTRACT** 

The AMIRA International P260 series of flotation projects was initiated in 1988 at the University of South Australia, and was sponsored by 17 companies. The major focus of P260 has been all aspects of base metal sulphide flotation, expanding to gold, and more recently to phosphate and other value ores. A key feature of the research has been a deep understanding of pulp and surface chemistry under processing conditions, as well as the mechanisms underpinning the sub-processes of bubble-particle collision, attachment and detachment in flotation. Research comprises a combination of physical chemistry and engineering, aiming at optimum value recovery and selectivity. Copper flotation in a variety of ore types and deposits (Cu/Pb/Zn, Cu/Au, Cu/Mo, etc.) has been a constant theme in the project, encompassing research for operations on four continents. Now in its 25<sup>th</sup> year, AMIRA P260 was recently evaluated by an independent consultant, RMDSTEM, as having returned over $1 billion to industry over the project life. This represents a 22:1 return on investment to the sector. In this paper, we present some case studies of Cu flotation research in the P260 project, together with highlights of research tools and knowledge development contributed to industry.

Here we present case studies that exemplify this approach that has served the project sponsor companies for two and a half decades. #### **SELECTED CASE STUDIES** #### **Copper/moly flotation from porphyry ores** One of the limitations in the design and operation of bulk copper/molybdenum flotation circuits is that conditions which are optimal for flotation of the copper sulphide are not necessarily optimal for molybdenite. To maximise throughput, the roughers and scavengers are often operated at high solids percent (35% solids w/w or more). The P260 project conducted an investigation at three different copper mines located in North and South America, owned by major players in the mining industry. Consistently, it was found that, while copper recovery in the rougher/scavengers was not affected greatly by changes in the flotation feed solids percent (w/w), molybdenite recovery decreased at high solids percent [18, 19]. This was ascribed to some peculiar properties of molybdenite particles, such as: (i) flat and elongated shape, which affects _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 76 hydrodynamics, and (ii) hydrophilic and reactive edges, prone to electrostatic interaction with the fine gangue mineral particles and formation of slime coatings, which are enhanced at high concentration of calcium ions in solution, typically resulting from lime addition [20]. A reduction of the flotation feed solids percent by means of dilution of the slurry (the solids throughput was not varied), in spite of a reduction in the total residence time in the rougher/scavenger banks, provided increased flotation kinetics and molybdenum recovery (Figure 1). The effect was more pronounced for some ore blends (high skarn) than others, but it was consistent across all the three operations investigated. The P260 project provided insights on the effect of solids percent on the flotation of copper and molybdenite, and at the same time provided plant operators with a strategy to increase and maintain a stable molybdenum recovery in the rougher/scavengers. #### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The AMIRA P260 project has continued to deliver outcomes to the mineral processing sector through its unique balance of applied and basic research, coupled to plant trials, while keeping industry priorities as the driving force. An integral part of the success of AMIRA P260 has been the close and active engagement of sponsor company representatives at each stage of question/project formulation, regular interaction and communications with technical, academic and student research. This underpins the depth of technology transfer from the project through to implementation and the achievements of real benefits, as verified by the independent RMDSTEM assessment of over $1 billion return on investment. 

The P260 project will continue to focus on maximising the benefits to industry including: 

- Increasing recovery of value minerals in coarse, composite particles and in fine particles through deep understanding of pulp and surface chemistry and hydrodynamic factors; 

- Selectivity improvements through rejection of sulphide and non-sulphide gangue minerals, in base metal concentrates; 

- Increasing recovery of gold, MoS2 and PGM’s; 

- Assessing and mitigating the negative impacts of reducing water consumption in flotation; 

- Developing useful characterisation tools, methods and protocols for use by sponsors operations and personnel; 

- Progressing the science and engineering of the flotation process; and 

- Educating a generation research-capable people for the processing sector.

*Mineralisation** 

The copper mineralization of the Antapaccay project is located mainly in intermediate intrusive rocks as dissemination, veining, and hydrothermal breccias and in contact with pre-mineral rocks like diorites, and sedimentary rocks (limestone, chalky lutites, limonites and sandstones) that formed mineralized breccias through contact, exoskarn and “stockwork” in sedimentary rocks, with a marked domination of chalcopyrite over bornite up to 350 m deep. At greater depth, this role is inverted and is associated with a level of gypsum-anhydrite. 

Two apparently isolated bodies have been identified. The south body is the larger and extends 1 300 m in a NW-SE direction and varies in width from 250 until 430 m. The north body measures 300m NW-SE and is 450 m wide. 

Contact with limestone generates the conditions for metasomatism to occurring generating irregular bodies of granite-magnetite+/-pyroxene exoskarn with patches of mostly chalcopyrite. In addition, zones of intense veining of grey quartz “stock-work” with a strong content of bornite and chalcopyrite always occurs near hornfels-intrusive contacts, reaching several meters into the hornfels. 

Based on the Geo-metallurgical and Resources model, the project’s economic copper mineralization is distributed in the following form: 1.9% Cu oxide, 70.0 % Cu sulphide porphyry, 12.9% mixed porphyry, 6.5% porphyry-breccia-gypsum, 5.9% mineralized breccia and 2.8% skarn, with the highest grades found in the mineralized breccias and the skarn. #### **Flotation Test Work** 

Flotation test work consisted of a characterization program and a variability program which included one hundred and forty seven (147) samples. 

The most abundant ore types responded well to very simple processing parameters. At primary grind sizes of 150 to 200 μm P80, over 90% of the copper was recovered in concentrates that graded about 37% copper. Gold was 80% recovered in the final concentrate. 

Regrinding the rougher concentrate ahead of the cleaning stages was determined to be an important factor influencing the copper concentrate grade. However, the concentrates could be processed at regrind sizes of 30 to 50 μm P80. 

There were differences in metallurgical response between some of the ore types. The porphyry and breccia samples performed well with very little variation in response in individual sub samples. The skarn and other rock classifications demonstrated considerably more variability in metallurgical response. These ore types contained many non-sulphide forms of copper that negatively impacted metallurgical response. The rock type classification proved useful in delineating metallurgical response and ore hardness for the deposit. 

The concentrates were essentially free of significant deleterious elements.

#### **CONSIDERATIONS AND GRINDING CIRCUIT DESIGN** 

The Antapaccay mine exploits a deposit of type massive porphyritic with low grade, the reserves are 520 million mineral tonnes with a copper head grade of 0.60%. The mine provided employment to more than 6 000 people during the construction peak and to about 1 460 people in the operating stage. The construction of the project was accomplished between 2010 and 2012, and the life of mine is expected to be 22 years. Progressive closing of the waste dams and the tailings dams from Tintaya mine will be done in conjunction with the Antapaccay operation. The closing of the Antapaccay facilities at the end of the operation implies remediation of the land, the waste dams and the tailings dam. 

Xstrata Project Development made a strategic partnership with Bechtel to act as the main engineering company for their projects, FLSmidth for mills

and flotation equipment, and Siemens for mills motors. Bechtel together with Graсa and Montero were the main construction contractors. On the other hand Xstrata itself made strategic procurements of mill liners, grinding balls and flotation reagents. 

#### **Circuit Design and Equipment Selection** 

Xstrata Copper in 2008 had six potential large scale copper concentrator projects in their project execution pipeline. One of the largest capital cost items and also the longest lead time items on  some  of  the  projects  are  those  of  the  equipment  for  the primary  grinding circuit.  The general engineering philosophy for the selection of such equipment has been to select the largest proven equipment available. This currently corresponds to a 12.2 m (40 ft.) diameter SAG mill and 7.9 m (26 ft.) x 12.2 m (40 ft.) ball mills. 

With the delivery of this type of equipment becoming critical, the decision was made to place an order to secure a production slot for either a 11.6 m (38 ft.) or 12.2 m (40 ft.) SAG Mill and two 7.9 m (26 ft.) ball mills for one of the first projects. The decision whether to select an 11.6 m (38 ft.) or a 12.2 m (40 ft.) SAG mill for the first project, initiated the recommendation that an evaluation of all of the projects be carried out by industry experts, with a focus on the Antapaccay project.

Processing of Cu-Mo ores includes two steps: a bulk flotation where molybdenite is recovered together with Cu and Fe sulfides, and a subsequent selective flotation step where molybdenite is separated from depressed copper sulfides. Flocculants are usually employed in the middling thickeners in the

copper plant, and in the Cu-Mo bulk concentrate ahead of the molybdenite plant. However, the floatability of molybdenite, similarly to other naturally hydrophobic minerals, is highly sensitive to the effect of both natural and synthetic polymers. In this work flotation tests demonstrate that conventional high-molecular weight anionic polyacrylamide flocculants (PAM) are strong molybdenite depressants. Low-molecular weight shear degraded polyacrylamides in spite of losing flocculation efficiency maintain depressing ability for molybdenite. Also a non-ionic flocculant, polyethylene oxide (PEO), has been studied in this project. Our results indicate that PEO is an efficient flocculant for molybdenite suspensions in a wide pH range. However, similarly to polyacrylamides, commercial PEO can also depress molybdenite flotation.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Modern processing plants must have closed water circuits in which process water is recycled back after removal of solids in the solid/liquid separation unit operations. With the present trend towards higher flocculant levels in the thickening (e.g. paste technology) and filtration dewatering the likelihood of flocculants build-up in recycle streams over time is very large. The possible presence of residual flocculants or degraded derivatives in water which is recycled back to a flotation process raises the question about the effect of flocculants on flotation of Cu-Mo ores, and in particular on flotation of molybdenite which is an inherently hydrophobic mineral. These effects were studied in coal flotation, and since coal along with graphite, molybdenite and talc belongs to the same group of inherently hydrophobic solids these conclusions also hold for molybdenite. 

In many flotation processes, for example, in rejection of pyrite from coal, rejection of talc and graphite in the flotation of sulfide ores, polymeric agents are commonly applied as depressants. At one point, the polymer dextrin was implemented at the Utah concentrator as molybdenite depressant in the selective flotation of Cu sulfides from molybdenite [1]. 

In the Cu-Mo sulfide ore processing plants the stage of bulk flotation of copper sulfides and molybdenite is followed by the second stage (moly plant) which includes selective flotation of molybdenite and depression of copper sulfides. It has been a common practice that the Cu-Mo bulk concentrate is stored in a thickener in which also flocculants can be applied to increase solids content in the feed to the moly plant. In doing so it is often assumed that the use of low molecular weight flocculants minimizes flocculation and so does not affect much flotation. However, Shirley [1] pointed out that in plant practice “most of commonly used flocculants are excellent depressants for molybdenite even if it has been collected with an oil.  Therefore, flocculants should not be used on middling thickeners in the copper circuit or the molybdenite plant feed thickener unless absolutely necess

ary”. 

The objective of this paper is to discuss the effect of anionic polyacrylamide flocculants and their degradation products - which are polymer segments of lowmolecular weight - on the floatability of molybdenite. Polyethylene oxide (PEO), a nonionic flocculant and its ability to depress molybdenite flotation has also been studied. 

#### **USE OF POLYMERS IN MINERAL PROCESSING** 

Various polymers - low molecular weight dispersants/depressants and high molecular weight flocculants - are utilized in mineral processing circuits. Since they must be water soluble, these polymers are highly hydrophilic macromolecules. Common examples in the former group are dextrins, low molecular weight polyacrylates (e.g. Cataflot, Dispex, etc.), polystyrene sulfonate (PSS10 used in coal-water slurries), and in 

115 

the latter group polyacrylamides are the best known.  Also starch is in the group of high molecular weight polymers used as flocculants (by the way starch in combination with lime was the first flocculant patented in 1928 for the clarification of a coal’s mine effluents [2]. It is necessary to be pointed out that from the chemical point of view both dextrin and starch are the same polysaccharides which differ only by molecular weight. 

Polyacrylamides, the most common commercial flocculants, are to some extent anionic (expressed as degree of anionicity) and so they can also be treated as copolymers of polyacrylamide and polyacrylic acid. High molecular weight PAMs with a degree of anionicity in the range 20 to 30 are claimed to be the most efficient in thickening tailings [3, 4]. 

It is generally accepted that polymers used as flocculants aggregate suspensions of fine particles by a bridging mechanism. The bridging is considered to be a consequence of the adsorption of the segments of the flocculant macromolecules onto the surfaces of more than one particle. The optimum flocculation occurs at flocculant dosages corresponding to a particle coverage that is significantly less than complete. Incomplete surface coverage ensures that there is sufficient unoccupied surface available on each particle for the adsorption of segments of the flocculant chains during collision of the particles. Thus, at low polymer coverage, the adsorbed polymer can destabilize the suspension by bridging flocculation, but since these macromolecules are hydrophilic the polymer adsorbed layers cause repulsion at a high coverage (high polymer dosage). These results in stabilization of the suspension, the phenomenon referred to as steric stabilization. 

There are many direct contact angle measurements which show that hydrophobic solids become less hydrophobic and loose floatability in aqueous solutions of watersoluble polymers. Klassen [5] in his monograph on coal flotation listed many polysaccharides as depressants for coal flotation. The use of dextrin to depress coal and float pyrite with xanthate was patented by DOE for desulfurizing flotation of fine coal [6].  Pradip

and Fuerstenau [7] tested the effect of various polymers on the wettability of anthracite and showed that the anthracite becomes less hydrophobic in their presence. Similar results were reported by Moudgil [8]. Wie and Fuerstenau [9] reported strong depressing effect of dextrin on the wettability of molybdenite in acidic solutions; such a depression has recently been confirmed by Beaussart et al. [10]. 

Polymeric substances known as humic acids often appear in process water (obtained from lakes or rivers). These are poorly defined anionic polymers with phenolic and carboxylic groups, which were shown to affect strongly wettability of graphite [11] and also wettability of molybdenite [12].  These effects were particularly significant in acidic solutions where humic acids become less soluble and precipitate.  Pawlik et al. [13] confirmed that very hydrophobic bituminous coal can become totally hydrophilic at relatively low concentrations of humic acids. One of the important gangue minerals in the South African sulfide ores that contain platinum is talc. Since it is naturally 

116 

hydrophobic it tends to float well and it is common to depress it using guar gum (or other polysaccharides such as starch or carboxymethyl cellulose). 

#### **EEFFECT OF FLOCCULANTS ON COAL FLOTATION** 

This important aspect of coal flotation has been extensively discussed in the book by Pikkat-Ordynsky and Ostry [14]. In their tests they used slightly anionic polyacrylamide (PAM) with molecular weight of 3x10<sup>6</sup> and non-ionic polyethylene oxide (PEO) with molecular weight of 7 x 10<sup>6</sup> . Both flocculants were found to strongly depress coal flotation: the higher the flocculant dosage, the smaller the yield of the concentrate, higher its ash content and lower ash content in the flotation tailings. These effects begin to be visible at a dosage of 1 g/m<sup>3</sup> of PAM and were more pronounced for the flotation feeds with a high yield of very fine particles.  The results of their flotation tests on the effect of PAM on flotation of bituminous coal show that at 150 g/m<sup>3</sup> of PAM depression is total. The lower yields of clean coal were explained by the adsorption of hydrophilic macromolecules onto coal particles that makes these particles hydrophilic and higher ash contents of the concentrate results from non-selective flocculation of coal particles with gangue. Perfectly in line with these conclusions are Hey’s results [15] who reported that kinetics of coal flotation slows down with increasing dosage of PAM. 

#### **POLYMERS IN FLOTATION OF MOLYBDENITE** 

#### **Molybdenite crystal structure and surface properties** 

Molybdenite has a layer crystal structure. This is a typical anisotropic mineral and the surface charge on different sides of the molybdenite crystal (faces and edges), and in general surface properties of these sides, are different. The use of electrokinetic techniques to measure zeta-potential of the particles of anisotropi

c minerals, the particles which carry different charges on different sides, is not based on any sound science [16]. This was documented for other anisotropic minerals, e.g. for kaolinite [17] and for talc [18]. The electrokinetic measurements for such minerals may lead to entirely wrong conclusions. Molybdenite also belongs to a group of anisotropic minerals and thus all the measurements that have been reported in literature must be treated with caution. Wettability studies and the use of contact angle techniques face a severe problem associated with sample preparation. For example, as reported by Arbiter et al. [19], for cleaved molybdenite surfaces the measured contact angles exceeded 80 degrees. However for the specimens polished parallel to its cleavage plane the contact angle was only 70 degrees. Chander and Fuerstenau [20] confirmed large differences in contact angles measured on hydrophobic faces and hydrophilic edges of molybdenite. These differences were also reported by Lуpez-Valdivieso et al. [21]. As Figure 1 shows, the contact angles measured on molybdenite faces were in the range of 60 degrees, while the edges were completely hydrophilic. These 117 measurements also confirm Arbiter et al.’s results [19] in that the contact angle values practically do not depend on pH. The zeta-potential measurements, for example the results provided by Chander et al. [22], show practically constant values at pH>6 (around – 40 mV) and linear decrease at pH < 6 down to -25 mV at a pH of 3. But since this is an anisotropic mineral which particles possess two different sides it is impossible to figure out what are the zeta-potential values for these different sides. 70

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

1. Depression of molybdenite by polyacrylamide and polyethylene oxide flocculants is in a good agreement with the general behavior of other layered native hydrophobic minerals (e.g. talc and graphite) which are commonly depressed by hydrophilic macromolecules. 

2. Polyacrylamide flocculants are strong depressants of fine particles of molybdenite and this effect increases as polymer concentration is increased. 

3. Shear degraded polyacrylamide products – shorter chain segments with low molecular weight– maintain a strong depressing effect on molybdenite, particularly at acid pH that is  around the zero-point of charge of molybdenite faces. 

4. No direct relationship between flocculant effectiveness and its depressing effect on molybdenite flotation exists. The products of polyacrylamide shear degradation turned out to be effective molybdenite depressants. In spite of their much lower molecular weight, which made these products poor flocculants, they turned out to be still efficient molybdenite depressants. 

5. The use of flocculants in the Cu-Mo flotation process (in the middling and bulk CuMo concentrate thickeners) must be limited because they and their degradation products exhibit a strong depressing effect on molybdenite flotation.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Sumitomo Metal Mining Co., LTD, Niihama Research Laboratories (NRL) has been developing Cu/As separation technology from chemical approach (investigating and optimizing solid-liquid interfaces) and physical approach (studying the effect of bubble diameter, pulp density, retention time in froth depth and jet velocity). 

The influence of oxidization on the contact angle of tennantite, chalcopyrite, bornite and pyrite was investigated. When the surface was not oxidized, tennantite indicated similar contact angle to non-arsenical copper minerals, chalcopyrite and bornite. The contact angle of tennantite became smaller than that of the non-arsenical copper minerals when weak oxidization was applied. 

Effect of physical parameters of flotation equipment on separability of arsenic was also investigated. The results agreed with propos

ed flotation models. The separability of arsenic improved as the pulp density increased and maximized at 14 m/s of the jet velocity. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 134 #### **INTRODUCTION** Arsenic is a typical undesirable element that causes toxicological and environmental problems in the copper smelting process. Although hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical treatments could be applied to remove arsenic into bi-products, increasing severity of environmental legislations has resulted in a progressive reduction of the amount of arsenic allowable in the bi-products (Fornasiero et al., 2001; Guo and Yen., 2005; Dai et al., 2005; Subramanian et al., 2005; Tongamp et al., 2010). Consequently, high penalties are imposed by smelters to treat copper concentrates containing 2000ppm or higher arsenic generally. It would be more economically and environmentally beneficial to remove the arsenical minerals on an earlier stage such as flotation. Their separation is nevertheless difficult as they generally have similar flotation behavior to the valuable minerals with which they are associated in practical operations. NRL has been developing Cu/As separation technology from chemical approach (investigating and optimizing solid-liquid interfaces) and physical approach (studying the effect of flotation equipment). #### **MATERIALS** #### **Surface analysis** Table 1 lists mineral specimens provided for surface analyses and contact angle measurements. 0.37| *at 80% copper recovery #### **Flotation tests (Jameson cell)** #### Flotation model _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 147 Two models of minerals separation are known for flotation. One is surface energy model and the other is kinetic energy model. The surface energy model is proposed that mineral substitution occurs on the surface of air bubbles to be stable in its surface energy of air bubbles. The details of simulation model are as follows; - 1) Even if a low hydrophobic mineral attach to air bubbles, a high hydrophobic mineral pushes out it and adsorbs to air bubbles. - 2) When air bubbles are combined and surface area of air bubble is small, different hydrophobic minerals are about to attach on surface of its bubble a low hydrophobic mineral falls off. The key parameter to improve Cu/As separation is as follows; - 1) Contacting probability is higher and contacting frequency is longer between air bubbles and minerals. - 2) Contacting frequency of air bubbles is longer to be combined air bubbles. If mineral diameter is constant, contacting probability is in inverse proportion to bubble diameter. Frequency time between air bubble and mineral is in inverse proportion to air and slurry velocity which are installed to flotation machine. Retention time of air bubble is determined from froth depth. Therefore, the influence of bubble diameter and froth depth on separability of arsenic was investigated in this study. The kinetic energy model is proposed that definite kinetic energy is necessary so that mineral attach on bubble surface, and the energy depends on the mineral hydrophobicity, and big energy is necessary as a low hydrophobic mineral. If mineral diameter is constant, separability improves when a high hydrophobic mineral is given kinetic energy (velocity) of a minimum necessary to floats and mineral is not able to detach when excessive kinetic energy (velocity) is given. Therefore, the influence of jet velocity on separability of arsenic was investigated in this study. #### Evaluation method of recovery In flotation, as film of air bubbles is formed slurry, non-purpose minerals in slurry float with froth. Therefore the mixture of non-purpose minerals needs to be deducted when Cu/As separation is evaluated. Because non-purpose minerals float with water, copper or arsenic recovery is adapted to revised recovery in this study as shown in equation (1). #### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Tennantite is more easily to oxidize than bornite and chalcopyrite. Tennantite was activated by attachment of cupric ion released by oxidization of the copper minerals. Chelating agents, especially TETA (triethylenetetramine) captured the cupric ion and deactivate tennantite effectively. Combination of TETA addition, aeration with pure oxygen and elevating pH to 11.0 was effective to depress tennantite against non-arsenical copper minerals. Optimizing the conditions, the arsenic to copper recovery ratio decreased from 0.99 to 0.37 in the flotation of an arsenic baring concentrate. 

Effect of physical parameters (bubble diameter, pulp density, retention time in froth depth and jet velocity) of pump speed, wash water and air flowrate on separability of arsenic was also investigated based on the proposed two flotation models, which are surface energy model and kinetic energy model. The separability of arsenic improved as the pulp density increased and maximized at 14 m/s of the jet velocity.
