#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Esperanza mine is located at 150 kms from Antofagasta in the north of Chile, and at 3 km from “El Tesoro” Mining, near Sierra Gorda. The height above sea level is around 2.300 meters. 

Basically, the operation consists of a conventional concentrator plant to process sulfide copper-gold ores which come from Esperanza open-pit mine. The treatment of sulfide ores is carried out through SAG grinding process and beneficiation by flotation, with a throughput of 95.000 tons per day to produce 685.000 tons per annum of concentrate with 28% of copper and 15 gpt of gold. 

This paper shows a brief description of the process. It also shows the characteristics of the water used in the process. Moreover, this work analyses the water effect of main units operations and in corrosion process. 

#### **Ore Treatment** 

Esperanza is a porphyry copper-gold deposit, whit a copper grade of 0,54% and 0,23 gpt gold . The mine has proven reserves of 480 million tons. The concentrator uses conventional milling and flotation production process. The average plant throughput is 95,000 tons per day. 

Grinding process is carried out in a SAG mill of 40’ x 26’ of 30000 HP and two secondary balls mills of 25.000 HP each one. The overflow of cyclones goes to flotation while the underflow can go to the ball mills or to the flash flotation cells. The pebbles produced by SAG mill, go to the pebbles crusher. The product from the crusher is taken by the two balls mills. 

The product from the grinding circuit is sent to the flotation circuit, which has two possible configurations, the normal and ev

entual circuit. In general, the circuit consists of a rougher flotation, a regrinding closed circuit, one or two optional stages of cleaning flotation and one scavenger. The normal configuration uses one cleaner stage in column cells. On the other hand, the eventual circuit uses a first cleaner in conventional cells and a second cleaner in columns. In this configuration, the cleaner scavenger stage is shorter than in the normal circuit. The use of the normal or eventual circuit configuration (one or two cleaners) depends on the pyrite grade in the ore. As a rule, until 2% pyrite can be process in the normal circuit. Over this value, the eventual circuit is used. The depression of pyrite is carried out by the use of a proprietary technology based on the use of sodium meta-bisulfite (MBS) in the cleaning stage and no lime addition. The goal is to obtain concentrate grades of 28% copper and 15 gpt gold. _Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 157 Concentrate thickening is carried out in a highrate thickener of 36m of diameter. The overflow is sent to the process water pool and the underflow which is 65% of solid, is pumping to the filtration plant in Michilla from where it is shipped. #### **Concentrate Sedimentation** 

Due to the use of MBS in flotation circuit, the Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion concentration and therefor the pH of final concentrates tends to be lower than those obtained in conventional flotation process with lime. 

Laboratory test indicates that settling rates for pH 10,5 are slower than those for pH 7,5 at the same flocculant dosages. 



Figure 9 – pH effect on settling rate. 

Most minerals particle surfaces are negatively charged when they are in liquid medium. Extremely fine particles (< 10 um) are highly charged, hence the repulsive forces due to the superficial charge are more significant than van-der Waal´s attraction ones [6]. 

Some cations like Ca<sup>2+</sup> can neutralize the particles superficial charge and allow acting the attraction forces to generate agglomerates. Due to the use of MBS in flotation circuit, the Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion concentration and therefor the pH of final concentrates tends to be lower. This provides a stable colloidal suspension and therefore, problems in settling rates and overflow clarity. Figure 8, shows the effect of pH in overflow clarity for different flocculant dosages. Major overflow clarity was obtained for pH 11, for all flocculant dosages [6]. 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

166 



Figure 10 – pH effect on overflow clarity. 

If a typical sedimentation model is considered, like Coe & Clevenger at the same conditions, the total area required to process a given tonnage at pH 7,5  is 40% larger than at pH 10,5 due to the difference in settling rates [6]. 

In consequence a new concentrate thickener is being implemented in Esperanza to achieve an optimal sedimentation process.

An interesting features of the tailing produced with sea water is that after dried dust is not produced in the dam. The salt precipitation from the sea water produces a hard cover over the tailing avoiding the dust generation.

This Concentrator plant processes about 3,500 DMT/day and produces 43,000 DMT/year of concentrate with 28% copper content and some silver content.

#### **IMPACT OF FINES CONTENT VARIATIONS ON THE RHEOLOGY OF COPPER SLURRIES** 

P. Garrido, T. Watt _Centro de Investigaciуn JRI S.A. 2343 Luis Uribe Santiago, Chile pgarrido@jri.cl_ 

Nestor R. Rojas _Instituto de Minerales CIMEX, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Medellin, Colombia._ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The design and control stages of tailings thickening, transport, and final disposal processes require rheological studies which need to be conducted based on the concentration of solids to determine viscosity and yield stress. These studies should include the variability of geological units and, among their characteristics, lithology and alteration. These different units show variations in their physical and rheological properties, which have a direct influence on particle size distribution, settling rate values, flocculants efficiency, viscosity and yield stress values. 

This paper presents the existing relationship between particle size distribution, mainly fine material (under 74, 38 and 25 microns), and the yield stress values of copper tailings. It also presents results of the rheological characterization of samples of different lithologies and alterations, which have different particle size distributions and complement this study. 

The results obtained indicate that the rheological properties of copper tailings are affected by fine material content, concluding that the higher the fine material content, the higher the yield stress and viscosity values will be. The above is only true for fines contents above a 20% approximate value; its effect is not observed in percentages below this value.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Over a million tons of tailings are generated in Chile each day and deposited in arid zones of this country where a sustain

able management of water resources is required. The challenges this situation implies are associated to the need to recover the largest possible amount of water present in the tailings and achieve their stable and safe final disposal. Both challenges are met if we are able to achieve highly thickened and transportable tailings. 

Rheology is the main field associated with the study of hydraulic characteristics and design of systems for the concentration and final disposal of tailings slurries, primarily viscosity and yield stress parameters. 

The methodology most used for determining yield stress is the vane method described in detail by Nguyen and Boger (1983, 1985) [1-2]. But when the objetive is to determine yield stress and suspension viscosity, rotational rheometers with cylindrical sensors and cups as described in the papers by Nguyen and Boger (1987) [3], Dabak and Yucel (1987) [4], Tangsathitkulchai (2003) [5], among others, are used. 

Other studies allow us to establish the effect of variables such as solids concentration, pH, and zeta potential on rheological parameter values and, to a lesser extent, the effect of particle size distribution, Mikulбek et al. (1997), Zhou et al.(2001), Turian et al. (1997), M. He et al. (2004) , Logos and Nguyen (1996), Leong (1995) [611]. Most of these studies have been conducted with suspensions of laterite, gypsum, titanium dioxide and bentonite ores whose characteristics are considerably different to Chilean tailings. 

Through studies conducted at the Centro de Investigaciуn JRI S.A. (Research Center), ( **CI-JRI** ), it has been possible to establish a range within which particle sizes present in copper tailings fluctuate, and we can consider as a reference that material below the 70 µ m size fluctuates between 45 and 80%, material below 38 µ m between 35 and 70%, and material below 25 µ m between 30 and 64%. 

The objective of this study is to demonstrate the effect of particle size distribution on yield stress values by means of samples prepared artificially and real samples from different lithologies and alterations.

#### **EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY** 

The methodology used in both Case Studies is described in detail in this paper. 

#### <u>Case Study 1</u> 

It refers to the rheological characterization of copper tailings whose particle size distribution is modified by incorporating different percentages of its own material, but of finer sizes. The finest sizes considered were: under 200 Tyler mesh (74 μm), under 400 Tyler mesh (38 μm) and under 500 Tyler mesh (25 μm). 

#### <u>Case Study 2</u> 

A detailed description is made of the rheological characterization of copper tailings generated in a pilot plant and referring to samples of different lithologies and alterations. In this case, the objective was to identify the effect of particle size distribution variations on yield stress values in a specific lithology-alteration.

#### **ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES OF BRO

WNFIELD PROJECTS** 

Fernando Pino Osorio 

_Senior Process and Commissioning Specialist Jacobs Chile Av. Nueva Tajamar 481, 19th floor, North Tower Las Condes, Chile Fernando.Pino@jacobs.com_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Projects are classified as Greenfield or Brownfield, the latter corresponding to those dealing with expansion, modification and/or optimization of existing operations. Usual thinking is that Brownfield Projects are easier to define and develop than Greenfield or new Projects; however, evidence shows that rather the opposite is true. Advantages of Brownfield Projects are the available improved knowledge of ore characteristics, metallurgical processing, unit operations, equipment performance and personnel know how. However, there are serious hurdles to overcome, such as: coordination between the EPCM Company, the Owner Project Manager and the Operations Manager; building additional facilities within a running operation under acceptable safety conditions; need to maintain production level during construction; connections or “tie-ins” of new facilities to the existing ones; possible modifications required due to technological evolution or changes in the ore nature. In this paper, some general recommendations are drawn from the analysis of selected typical cases, comprising tie-in identification, design, engineering, coordination and implementation; and planning the execution of modifications during normal and extraordinary plant detentions. Additionally, cases are analyzed for which innovations can have important effects on commissioning and start up schedule for both project types. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

198 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Projects are usually classified as Greenfield and Brownfield. The first type corresponds to new projects and the second one to expansion, modification or optimization of existing operations. There is abundant literature about management of Greenfield projects; however, not too much for Brownfield projects. It is common to believe that the Brownfield projects are much easier to define and develop than Greenfield projects; however, evidence shows rather the opposite situation. 

This paper discusses the author’s experience on Brownfield projects, over more than forty years in designing, operating and commissioning ore dressing and extractive metallurgy plants. The goal of this paper is to achieve some general recommendations from the analysis of real cases, and to share this experience with the mineral processing community. The paper emphasizes the impact of Brownfield characteristic, advantages and disadvantages on project development and management and, perhaps, the most relevant issue: tie-ins identification, design, engineering, coordination and implementation. The paper layout follows the organization of check lists of ideas and actions to be considered. 

#### **BROWNFIELD PROJECTS CHARACTERISTICS** 

#### **Reasons to develop Brownfield projects** 

Typical causes to develop Bro

wnfield projects are: 

- The Project is developed by stages, and the expansion was considered from the very beginning. 

- Economies due to increased operations scale and use of existing infrastructure. 

- Need of increasing the treatment capacity due to diminishing ore grade. 

- Need of increasing the treatment capacity to compensate gaps due to deviation of real ore geometallurgical characteristics compared to the characteristics used for the Process Design Criteria. 

- Need of process or unit operations modifications due to failure of technological innovations. 

- Ore reserves have been increased because discovering of new geological resources or thanks to better market conditions. 

- Changes in ore characteristics, such as ore hardness, particle size distribution, mineralogy and metallurgical recovery, and others. 

- Incorporation of technological innovations or process improvement. 

- Addressing more stringent environmental regulations. 

- Marginal expansions to eliminate treatment or production capacities bottlenecks or operating or metallurgical problems. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

199 

#### **Advantages of Brownfield projects** 

Some main advantages of Brownfield projects are: 

- Improved knowledge of ore resources and ore reserves, ore characteristics, metallurgical process, unit operations, equipment performance and personnel knowhow. 

- Good project economic indexes due to use of existing infrastructure, manpower and organization. 

- Use of existing design engineering and duplication of existing equipment. Some facilities could be almost a copy and paste of the existing operations. 

- Commissioning and start-up of known processes, equipment and facilities. 

- Possibility to upgrade the operations and results by including new process and technological advances. 

#### **Disadvantages of Brownfield projects** 

On the other hand, important disadvantages and restrictions appear: 

- Generally speaking, for the same package of works, a Brownfield project needs a greater cost and time than a Greenfield one. Some production losses need be considered and evaluated before the decision to invest. 

- Usually, construction has to be carried out in an operating facility. Safety conditions are extremely severe. HSE rules of operations are usually different to HSE rules of construction. In these projects, both have to be accomplished at the same time. 

- Coordination between the EPCM Company, the owner’s project manager, the operations manager and the construction contractors is a real difficult challenge. 

- Lack of space to implement the modifications or expansion is a real difficulty to design the expanded layout. 

- Many times, from the start-up of the original project to the expansion, some plant modifications have occurred and not been registered in drawings and documents. Of special importance are modifications in piping, electrical and control circuits. 

- Normally, first priority has to be given to

operational and maintenance activities. Many claims for lost profits are generated by construction contractors. 

- Minimizing the time when the plant is out of service is a condition of the project. If project activities are planned to be performed during a plant general maintenance, too many teams will be working in the same places at the same time, construction equipment and other resources availability could be a restriction. 

- A lot of interferences need to be solved. When an innovation in some point of the process is introduced, the old configuration sometimes needs to be kept working by means of a by-pass until the new one is proved. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

200 

- When a special plant stop is programmed to perform project modifications or tieins, a very detailed execution planning is needed, because the modified plant has to continue producing immediately after restarting-up, with neither precommissioning nor commissioning.  The need to maintain at least the previous production level after the modifications is a must. The plan has to include supplies, resources, procedures, protocols and contingency plans. 

- Sometimes, introduction of innovations are required, due to technological evolution or to adjust the facilities to the real ore and process requirements. These innovations could have important effects on the construction, commissioning and start up schedule; however, this issue is valid for both Greenfield and Brownfield projects. 

- Lack of knowledge of the characterisitics, restrictions and difficulties of the Brownfield project by some or all the project actors is probably the main reason of deviation of the programmed budget, schedule and results compared to the original evaluation of the project. 

#### **DEVELOPMENT OF A BROWNFIELD PROJECT** 

There are two main types of plant expansion or modification projects: the first one is developed completely inside of existing operations, and the second type consists of construction of external additions to existing operations, and intended to be connected to them; a third and very frequent type is a combination of both. The second type is managed almost as a Greenfield project until the precommissioning and then tied-in with the existing facilities. The infrastructure and some facilities are commonly shared by the new and the existing facilities. 

As a general rule, the interferences  with operations, the needs to manage a large number of tie-ins, the needs of plant integration and the effects on production programs are not well evaluated. Sometimes these projects are conceived within the operating group, with a very optimistic scope of work, execution plan, project schedule and project budget; if this situation is not corrected during the early stages of the project it is a  call for disaster. 

During the conceptual and basic engineering stages, at least the main interferences and tie-ins have to be planned and minimized. If this is not possible, their

effects on costs, budget and production programs have to be evaluated. Stopping the plant because of project works seems to be a wrong decision, but the additional cost, longer schedule and project risks could really result much more expensive. It is very important to recognize the relevance of the tie-in engineering; development of a methodology and formal constructability analysis for the tie-ins implementation; formal and real compromise of the operating team to the project; and  evaluation of the safety risks involved in a Brownfield project. Today, the philosophy of all the international mining companies is clear: Health, Safety, Environment, and Community are really first. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

201 

Brownfield projects require people with rebuild experience and mind-set involved during the feasibility study stage of the project to assess the client requirements for shutdowns and to develop the concepts required for integration. The transition period between the existing and the new operation can be difficult to manage and needs to be designed into the project. Considering these activities during the conceptual and basic engineering is of the most importance; including them in the master schedule and budget. 

Formats of drawings and documents, equipment tags and procedures need to be early agreed upon. Preparation of  up-dated as built drawings and diagrams and control systems is a must. Need of developing temporary facilities, existing facilities disassembling, plant stops to implement modifications and possible effects on production programs also need to be identified as early as possible. 

Methodology to focus the tie-ins engineering has to be agreed in an early stage. Making this engineearing near the site has been a good practice; however, the normally much higher cost associated with this approach has to be evaluated. New information and communication technologies could be now of great assistance in conducting engineering far away from the plant. 

The amount of construction work requiring a plant shutdown should be minimized. However, in case that plant shutdowns are unavoidable, this essential work should be carefully scoped and planned. The shutdown scope should be defined and scheduled at least four months prior to the shutdown date, and preparations should start then. Construction personnel should be included in the design team in the early stages to ensure that constructability is built into the design, not as an after-thought. 

Construction Contracts Criteria have to be considered with key differences between Greenfield and Brownfield projects. Also, for both type of projects procurement is frequent cause of projects delays and define the overall project duration. Brownfield projects sometimes require using the same materials and the same brand and model of equipment than in the existing plant; then, it is necessary to verify if these are still being produced. Inclusion of technological advances an

d process modifications is frequent in Brownfield projects; its management needs great attention due to possible associated risk, and its effects are relevant for the design, implementation, start-up and operation of the projects. 

In the author’s experience, the most successful expansion (rebuild) projects have had dedicated client operating and maintenance personnel imbedded in the design team since day one. Individuals in the design office and on-site should be given the responsibility to manage shutdowns and the line authority, to be able to get things done. 

A design team should be based at site for several months in the early stages of the project with responsibility to design the integration and agree the process with the Client. This team should have an Operations member continually available to them and have properly controlled access to the plant for measurement and survey purposes. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

202 

Piping tie-ins should be managed by an on-site manager with a team of designers throughout the design period. Whenever possible, construction of new piping intended to replace existing piping should be run in a different location, thus limiting plant shutdowns to conduct final connections. 

Processes for “hot taps” in piping systems should be developed and approved with the client’s Operations Management, and implemented where necessary. 

The design philosophy should be “to get it right in the office” with field work limited to construction support only. 

The project schedule should be available to all project team. Hard copy of the schedule should be displayed in the project area. 

Effects of the project on plant operation and production have to be considered during the pre-inversion period, as well as the effects of carrying out the project inside an operating plant. Decisions of plant shutdowns due exclusively to the project have to be taken and evaluated during the Feasibility Study. 

#### **TIE-IN ACTIVITIES** 

According to our experience, one of the most important issues in Brownfield projects is managing tie-ins; sometimes, hundreds of tie-ins have been required. The concept of tie-in is the connection between an old and a new facility; however, it frequently includes many activities that are carried out during a plant stoppage. Planning of these activities is most relevant to the success of the project. 

Brownfield projects are complex by themselves and the tie-ins management introduces additional complexities. Tie-ins require careful planning; an ad-hoc organization, and an early assignment of a “Tie-Ins Manager” to estimate resources, manpower, program and budget, which is imperative. Normally, owners and EPCM project managers tend to minimize the tie-in impact for not disturbing the main project objectives; however, this is a very costly mistake. 

The following is a list of some main issues to consider for the tie-ins management: 

- Early identification of main tie-ins and interfere

nces. When the expansion or a section of the expansion is constructed independently to the existing facilities, normally the main tie-ins are the connections between the new and old facilities. 

- Preparation and programming of a tie-ins list, organized by engineering disciplines, magnitude, importance and effects on the operating facilities and production. An important group of tie-ins consists of those requiring plant shutdowns to be implemented; time required in each case should be estimated. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

203 

- Use of photography, video and 3D design is very helpful. 

- The use of Dimensional Control Technology (Laser Scanning) is an extremely valuable tool to accurately capture existing conditions. 

- Process and operations has to be attentively reviewed to discover the interferences and the opportunities to minimize the lost of production due to the project and tie-ins implementation. 

- A full time task force should be assigned to the tie-ins design and implementation. Tie-ins development requires an active participation of the project owner, operating and maintenance personnel. Sometimes, the process owner directs the task force and the engineering company gives all the necessary assistance. 

- It is most important to precisely identify the plant or plant sections that should be shutdown and the relationship among them, and relevant safety, operation, maintenance, production and program issues. 

- Normally, all project costs - labour, supervision, transport, accommodation and delivery at site - are high. Management attempts to do whatever possible at the design office to minimise the work at site. This is particularly true in Chile and Peru, where most important projects are built at 4 000 m above sea level, or even higher, and the work area is rugged, and difficult to get to.  These factors should dictate that engineering management should follow a “get it right in the office” principle, not “to get things nearly complete in the design office and then fix the rest up at site by field engineering”. It is not uncommon for the engineering fee to include penalties based on the amount of re-work at site. 

- All new independent sections have to be pre-commissioned before being connected to the plant. Shutdowns required to modify existing parallel lines, should take place only after pre-commissioning and connecting new lines. 

- Participation of the construction contractors in the planning, programming, engineering and construction of tie-ins has to be well defined, directed and controlled. Their commitment and responsibility have to be well established. 

- To avoid losses of production, use of temporary facilities is frequently required. 

- Comparison of the plant maintenance program and the project program has to be an early activity to achieve optimum use of plant detentions. As both are on-going programs, continuous follow up and update are required. 

- Early procurement of fittings, piping, s

upports, prefabricated structures and others is important because implementation of tie-ins depends on windows of opportunity given by the main construction program progress. 

- It is very convenient to assign inspectors in the vendors fabrication shops to avoid mistakes in spools, transfer boxes, chutes, lined piping and others, to assure programs and quality control, and take rapid decisions. 

- Contingency plans B and C are required to avoid non reasonable interruptions of production. 

- Planning and procurement of the main and complex tie-ins require a special organization, to avoid relevant losses of production. Each main tie-in needs to be 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

204 

managed as a mini-project. Engineering, procurement, fabrication, preassembling, contractual situations have to be well established. 

- Equipment requisitions for plant modification and rebuild work need to fully list the items required. This enables everyone involved in the EPCM chain (engineers, procurement buyers, expeditors, inspectors, shippers, goods receipt at site, contracts) to work on the same list. 

- When an existing pipe is to be replaced with a new line of larger size or a different specification, the easiest way from a design viewpoint is to put the new line in place of the old line. This approach is the worst option for Construction and Operations, as the pipe system will need to be taken out of service while the change is made. Sometimes this will require a major shutdown of the plant. Construction work during a shutdown puts pressure on everyone involved and should be avoided at all costs. A typical approach to rebuild and expansion projects is to review all the piping connections as soon as the P&IDs are “issued for design” to eliminate all but the most essential examples of where new pipe follows the same route as existing. 

- When the plant works by alternating campaigns using different type of ores, this opens windows of opportunity for a good tie-in implementation program. 

- When new engineering solutions are considered at some points of projects, sometimes it is necessary to keep the old facilities as a by-pass until the innovation is proven. 

- Some special technologies should be considered to avoid plant detentions, as the use of hot-taps in piping, for example. 

#### **PRESENT DESIGN TECHNOLOGIES** 

Today, basic and detailed engineering for Greenfield projects use 3D modeling platforms. This technology offers great assistance for managing of Brownfield projects. For existing projects, Mining Companies would have to prepare or update their models to an “as built” stage; this can be accomplished with the use of Laser Scanning to capture as-built conditions; especially for tie-ins. This should be considered and it can be a cost effective decision. Identification of tie-ins and interferences will be substantially improved. Engineering Companies will need to have qualified personnel to accomplish this challenge. 

Anot

her interesting facet of the technology, just under exploration by designers, should be an intensively use in Brownfield projects of small portable devices, which are designed for an intuitive everyday use. They can capture images and videos of high quality, some of them even allow hand sketches and a number of other tasks in a field. Undoubtedly, these devices will help the engineer to understand in a greater depth the daily design challenge to face this type of projects. 

The combination of the previously mentioned 3D design and the images obtained with tablet computers will help the designer achieve a safer design, optimize plant 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

205 

stoppage programing, accomplish tie-ins and interferences identification, to get integrally successful projects. 

#### **PROJECTS INCLUDING INNOVATIONS** 

The mining industry attempts to use proven technologies; however, in expansion or modernizing projects it is almost always necessary to include larger sizes of equipment or new technologies. This applies to both Greenfield projects and Brownfield projects. Special attention should be paid when innovations are included in projects, in which case much of the major failures or fatal flaws are related to this incorporation. In any case, decreasing of ore grades, increasingly complex minerals and the emergence of new technologies push incorporation of innovations. 

#### **SELECTED CASES FROM THE AUTHOR’S EXPERIENCE** 

<u>Case A:  Smelter Technology Innovation, and Sulphuric Acid Plant to treat converters gases</u> 

The project uses siphon converters to increase the SO2 gases content, and it includes a sulphuric acid plant. It was a very difficult project because it was constructed with the smelter running. During the start-up, the converter siphon was repeatedly clogged, and the gases cooling system, from 1 000 °C to 400 °C to feed the existing electrostatic precipitator, had to be modified. After some years siphon converters were replaced by El Teniente converters. 

#### <u>Case B: Smelter Expansion from 180 000 to 280 000 short t/a Cu, and Oxygen Smelting development</u> 

The project considered the converter oxygen smelting process, using reverb copper matte as a seed, oxygen enriched air to blow the converter and smelting of additional concentrates in the converters. Initially, the oxygen smelting process failed and a third reverb furnace was constructed. Design and use of oxy-fuel burners were implemented to increase the capacity and improve the heat balance in reverb furnaces. In parallel, a modified converter to implement the oxygen smelting process was developed, designed, pilot tested and commercialized. This development took some years and became the technology of choice for the modernization and expansion of a number of Chilean and foreign smelters. 

#### - <u>Case C: Continuous expansion of a Cu/Au/Ag Concentrator/Leach CIP/ Roasting Plant</u> 

Crushed high grade enargite copper ore, containing g

old and silver, was washed to decrease its acidity, and then ground and concentrated by flotation. The flotation tails were cyanide leached and treated in an ADR plant. High arsenic concentrates were 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

206 

roasted and high purity arsenic trioxide was obtained. About 30 000 t of copper, 300 000 oz of gold, three million oz of silver and 10 000 t of As2O3 were annually produced. 

The original project considered 40% solids as flotation feed; however, due to the slurry high viscosity, the solids content was decreased to 28-30%. Inclusion of a tails flotation thickener was necessary, to get independence between flotation and leach plants. A grinding and flotation circuit of rougher flotation tails sands and the incorporation of a flash flotation in the ball mill cyclones underflow permits various points of gold recovery increase. A second primary grinding mill and modifications in the crushing and washing plants duplicated the ore treatment capacity. Due to the expansion of the concentrator and the increase of the ore copper grade, a second and then a third roaster were included. The second roaster was constructed beside the first, using the same infrastructure, control room and As2O3 recovery and packing plant. The third roaster was also constructed beside the existing facilities, but incorporating a new As2O3 packing plant. The control system was originally based on analogical instrumentation and it was changed gradually to digital systems, without stopping the plant. 

Most projects were generated by the operations group and home engineered and construction managed. 

#### <u>Case D: Crushing, LX, SX, EW Plant expansion from 60 000 t to 100 000 t of copper per</u> 

#### <u>year</u> 

Crushing plant treatment capacity was increased from 22 000 t/d to 45 000 t/d. The project included a new primary crushing, a coarse ore stockpile and a secondary/tertiary crushing and agglomeration plant, an independent leach pad, two new SX trains and a new EW aisle in-line with the existing one. The new primary crusher fed a tower located between the old and the new stockpiles, where a diverter chute was designed to feed the new or the old stockpiles. After the expansion, the old stockpile was connected and the old primary crusher was put out of service. The project tried to decrease as much as possible the interferences between old and new facilities; and main difficulties were encountered to integrate the two new SX trains to the three existing trains. 

#### <u>Case E: Crushing, LX, SX, EW Plant expansion from 180 000 t to 256 000 t of copper per year</u> 

Crushing and material handling plants expansion to increase treatment capacity from 8 000 t/h to 10 700 t/h, upgrading as much as possible the existing facilities, and adding a tertiary crushing plant. Allowance to reach 300 000 t of copper per year was left. The vendor of the primary crusher increased its speed and modified the mantle design, to increase the

OSS and capacity. Secondary crushers’ vendor modified the crusher chambers to accept the bigger primary crushed product. Secondary screens were replaced by multi-slope screens. Belt feeders and belt conveyors were upgraded increasing the speed and power, mainly augmenting the number of motors and drives. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

207 

Tertiary crushing was an independent plant and the last conveyor of the secondary crushing had a telescopic head to feed directly to agglomeration and heap leach or through the tertiary crushing plant. Heap leach pad width was expanded and the stacking and recovery bridges enlarged. All the piping systems were upgraded and new ponds were included. A fourth independent SX train was included and the tank farm was almost duplicated. A third EW Section, in line with the two existing ones, was included. 

The whole SX and EW areas were shut down only one day; and more than 400 hundred tie-ins were identified, engineered and implemented with the plant in operation. For the crushing plant, material handling and leach pad expansion, a dedicated plant detention of ten days was agreed between the EPCM main contractor and the owner. An initial screening of the complete list of activities for this area was made, trying to identify the shortest possible list of activities to be conducted during the shutdown. A task force, under the direction of the Jacobs Start up Manager was formed, including personnel of operations, client project group, schedulers, construction managing group, contractors and vendors. Planning, design and programming of this shut down was prepared with great detail and successfully implemented. 

#### <u>Case F:  Expansion of a big Concentrator Plant</u> 

As a commissioning engineer, involved in planning a Project Startup, a lot of experience was gained from the expansion project of a big concentrator. No special plant stoppage to carry out modifications, besides normal SAG mill maintenance detentions, was considered in the project schedule. An evaluation exercise showed that the loss of production due to special stoppages was much bigger than the increase of project cost. About a thousand tie-ins were implemented; classified in three categories: a) to be solved inside the plant in operation, b) to be solved during the SAG and ball mills maintenance periods and c) special cases to be deeply studied to avoid special stoppages.

#### **THERMODYNAMIC CONSTANTS OF MINERALS OF THE OXIDATION ZONE OF COPPER – ANTLERITE AND PSEUDOMALACHITE**

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Minerals of the oxidation zone of copper deposits belong to the most difficult for enrichment. To transfer them into the easily floatable sulfide components it is necessary to have new technologies and methods of enrichment associated with solving of a number of theoretical issues to which the chemical enrichment refers. Optimization and intensification of the technology process for the purpose of more complete and complex utilization of raw materials require certain knowledge of thermodynamic properties of the oxidized minerals since the thermodynamic analysis and a preliminary simulation of the process are necessary for creation and choice of ore processing schemes. A basic sulfate of copper antlerite and a basic phosphate of copper pseudomalachite relate to these minerals along with malachite, azurite, atacamite, chrysocolla, brochantite, etc. This paper generalizes the results of experimental studies of thermodynamic properties of antlerite and pseudomalachite obtained by a number of the calorimetric methods (lowtemperature adiabatic calorimetry, the Tian-Calvet high-temperature melt solution calorimetry). This resulted in obtaining such fundamental thermodynamic constants as the heat capacity, entropy, the change of enthalpy, the enthalpy of formation and the Gibbs energy of formation used in simulation of technological processes of processing of the oxidized and mixed copper ores.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The oxidized and complex copper ores have recently attracted an increasing attention of researchers due to depletion of sulfide ore reserves. The quality of mineral raw materials supplied to concentrating mills is affected by the composition of ores of the oxidation zone consisting predominantly of carbonate and silicates, sulfates and hydroxosulphates, phosphates and chlorides. In this case, the presence of one or another oxidized copper mineral cannot be excluded a priori, since they are specific to each zone of oxidation; and therefore it is necessary to have information on the material composition, chemical and physical properties, and conditions of formation of these minerals. For process simulations of processing such type of ores is also necessary to have reliable thermodynamic data on the minerals entering into their composition. 

The issue on structure and properties of natural phosphates of copper has been discussed in the scientific literature for quite a long time. Due to the similarities in appearance and

crystal structure of minerals in this group, as well as the presence of polymorphism and variable water content, there is uncertainty in a description of minerals and their crystal-chemical formulae. A natural hydrous copper sulfate – antlerite belongs to sulfate minerals of the oxidation zone of sulfide copper deposits alongside with brochantite, posnjakite, langite and others. Thermodynamic properties of the compounds of this group have been investigated for brochantite [1], whereas thermodynamic functions for the rest sulphate minerals of copper practically have not been studied. There is no information on thermodynamic properties of pseudomalachite in the scientific literature. The data on thermodynamic and thermochemical properties of antlerite are limited to calculations of the equilibrium constant of the reaction of formation of this mineral and the Gibbs free energy of formation using the estimated value of entropy. 

This paper presents the results of calorimetric studies of thermodynamic properties of one of the most common natural phosphates of copper – pseudomalachite Cu5(PO4)2(OH)4, and the results of the experimental study of thermodynamic and thermochemical properties of a natural hydrous copper sulfate – antlerite Cu3SO4(OH)4.

In the area of temperatures below 10 K an anomaly of the heat capacity had been detected, possibly due to the presence of the JahnTeller effect or the Schottky phenomenon, which was confirmed by subsequent measurements, too [9]. In the experimental heat capacity of antlerite in the area of 4-20 K a pronounced anomaly of λ-type was also observed (Fig. 4). #### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Thus, for the first time a low temperature heat capacity of the oxidized copper mineral antlerite Cu3SO4(OH)4 has been measured by adiabatic calorimetry over the temperature range of (4.47-324) K. Based on the results of calorimetric studies the existence of a phase transition in antlerite at the Nйel point 5.3 K has been confirmed. Taking into consideration this transition the values of the heat capacity have been extrapolated to absolute zero, and the thermodynamic functions of the compound over the range of (0-320) K have been calculated. The thermochemical constants of the compound have been determined by the results of the high-temperature melt calorimetry. These values are more accurate than the data for synthetic samples measured earlier. 

As a result of the carried out investigation of the heat capacity of a natural copper phosphate – pseudomalachite, its thermodynamic functions have been determined up to the temperature of 320 K. Thermodynamic parameters of the detected anomalous effect of the heat capacity have also been determined. These parameters indicate that two equally probable states in pseudomalachite turn into a single new state.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

This presentation looks at some of the advancements in operating and monitoring that have accompanied the implementation of deep sea tailings placement (DSTP) in the Asia Pacific region over the past 20 years. It describes the guidelines and criteria that have been developed to ensure that DSTP systems are properly assessed and located prior to approval and throughout operation and closure. In considering the potential applicability of these experiences to countries such as Chile, substantial research will clearly be required to establish equivalent criteria to achieve the same objectives and environmental safeguards in the Chilean socio-political context. However, just as important for gaining acceptability will be the acknowledgement by governments and all sectors of the community of the existence of the dilemma – now or at some time into the future – that if the currently accepted land storage methods reach their physical or safety limits, alternative storage methods will need to be considered.  DSTP cannot be a solution without broad community acknowledgement that a dilemma about future mine tailings management needs to be faced. It is the role of governments, informed by scientific study, to evaluate the best solut

ion for future tailings management for the country in each case.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

As the world demand for copper increases, so the sizes and production rates of copper mines are also increasing, with the associated burden of managing the large volumes of tailings produced. Successful management of tailings presents technical challenges for mining operators, their regulators and communities wherever mining occurs. Typically, management of tailings has either involved impoundment in constructed storage facilities on-land, or discharge to lake, river or to sea, but constraints apply to all these options. In countries such as Indonesia and Papua New Guinea (PNG), the largest copper mines such as Grasberg, Ok Tedi and Bougainville currently use or have used riverine disposal as there was no feasible alternative at the time. Each mine has had consequential impacts to the receiving rivers and floodplains and it is unlikely that disposal of tailings to rivers would be proposed or approved for any future project of such size. The same may be said for any disposal to shallow coastal areas, if resultant increases in surface turbidity or shoreline impacts from tailings could not be prevented. 

In the Asia Pacific region, the overall feasibility of construction of land-based storage facilities for large volumes of tailings is often severely constrained by the physical geography of the site and this disposal method is mostly restricted to small mines. Finding suitable sites that are economically feasible becomes more difficult in steep mountainous regions characterized by high rainfall and high seismicity. Mines on small islands also face limited availability of land that is not otherwise of high agricultural or forestry value.  In mountainous terrain, dam walls have to be very high, and even with modern engineering techniques, building tailings storage dams in hostile climatic and seismic settings increases risks of failure over the long term. 

To obtain the benefits of mineral resources, archipelagic nations such as PNG and Indonesia have faced the dilemma of finding satisfactory long term solutions to the handling of large volumes of tailings. Marine tailings placement alternatives were first explored in PNG and Indonesia during the 1980s and 1990s respectively, seeking to achieve the best possible technology for placement of tailings on the deep seafloor, thereby by-passing the adverse impacts on the land and to nearshore marine ecosystems. 

This presentation describes some of the experiences of mining projects in the Asia Pacific region using Deep Sea Tailings Placement (DSTP). It describes the criteria and guidelines that are now in place to ensure proper site selection and protection of coastal marine environments and fisheries, and studies that might be needed to assess. 

#### **DEVELOPMENT OF MARINE TAILINGS PLACEMENT SYSTEMS** 

The most well studied marine tailings placement systems be

gan in the early 1970s with the Island Copper Mine, on Victoria Island, British Columbia, Canada, and the Kitsault Molybdenum mine, on the mainland of northern British Columbia, Canada, 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

225 

reported by several researchers [1-3]. Both discharged tailings from pipelines at around 40-50 m depth into coastal fjords in the order of 150 to 400 m depth. Both were subject to operational and post closure monitoring, which has shown that the tailings have remained substantially within the target fjord, with recolonisation of seabed fauna and succession observable soon after closure. At Island Copper, the marine ecosystem sustained its fisheries and plankton throughout mine operations. There were detectable population changes and losses in the seafloor benthic fauna (where deposition rates exceeded 20 cm/yr), but these recovered to a sustaining ecological succession within 1-3 years. The only permanent change after 25 years and the placement of some 400 Mt of tailings was the change in seabed to a mud bottom, and a slightly reduced capacity of the fjord containing the tailing solids. The Atlas Copper Mine on Cebu Island in the Philippines was the first mine in the Asia Pacific region to use marine tailings placement. It operated from 1971 to 1988, however its discharge depth was only 10 m over a 30 m seabed. Tailings were discharged via an overhead pipeline extending 500 m from the shore, from which substantial tailings plumes were evident (Ellis [1]).  While none of these systems would meet current criteria for deep sea tailings placement, each has contributed to our understanding of how marine tailings placement systems work and, accordingly has led to improvements in installation design and the depth criteria for safe disposal. 

#### **Deep Sea Tailings Placement - definition and benefits** 

Deep sea tailing placement (DSTP) is a deep ocean form of marine tailings placement, which involves controlled submerged discharge of a tailings slurry onto a continuously sloping the ocean floor, from where it flows as a density current down the slope to a deposition area deep on the ocean floor. Submarine canyons are favorable because the tailing density current follows the axis of the canyon and the walls help confine its lateral spread. The main goal is to locate and design the DSTP system to facilitate its downslope flow to the sediment of the deep ocean bed, where it becomes part of the physically and chemically stable natural sediment. Properly constructed, this avoids contact or mixing between the tailings and the most productive surface waters and coastal reefs where most fisheries occur. This method is effectively restricted to coastal locations where deep oceanic water and steep seabed bathymetry is available close to shore, because increasing distances from mine to coast, and from the coast to the continental slope progressively affect engineering feasibility. 

Current best practice guidelines for the c

onsideration of DSTP require that the depth of the pipeline outfall should be: 

- Below the deepest extent of the surface mixed layer (plus an additional margin of safety), such that the tailings is always discharged well below the density discontinuity between the surface mixed layer and top of the thermocline, and is prevented from rising upwards; 

- Below the euphotic zone, (plus an additional margin of safety) or the depth limit of photosynthetically active light (typically 1% of surface light); 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

226 

- Below the depths where any upwelling could potentially transport material into the surface mixed layer or to the ocean surface. 

Typically, outfall depths range from 100 m to over 300 m and the final depth of tailings deposition is arbitrarily defined as at least 1,000 m. For the tailings slurry to flow downslope to these intended deposition depths, its density must exceed that of the ambient seawater and all entrained air bubbles must be removed prior to discharge. While the overall slurry density is greater than that of the ambient seawater, the density of the liquid fraction alone may be less, and will be entrained into the surrounding water, separated from the main density current. This usually occurs at minor density discontinuity layers in the deep ocean water column. Any fine particles entrained in liquid fraction separating from the main density current will have density greater than seawater and their rate of sinking and dispersion will depend on relative current strength. Therefore it is important also to ensure full knowledge of the tailings liquid quality before discharging. 

Post mine closure, a successfully designed and operated DSTP system avoids the risks of having to manage, in perpetuity, tailings storage facilities in high seismic and high rainfall areas. There will however, be significant post-closure monitoring requirements but the tailings will gradually become recolonized as they stabilise and become buried by naturally accumulating sedimentation. Provided that it is designed and operated safely, the most significant advantage in the Asia Pacific archipelagic regions is that it allows safe development of mineral wealth that would otherwise be impossible to access without significant land or coastal impact. The main disadvantages are the loss of any future option to reprocess the tailings, the need for thickening prior to discharge for recycling process water, and system failure if it is designed with insufficient knowledge of the environmental constraints and does not operate as predicted. 

#### **Locations of mines using Marine / Deep Sea Tailings Placement** 

Marine tailings placement has now been implemented at geographically diverse locations such as in fjords in Canada, Greenland and Norway, in the Black and Mediterranean Seas in Europe, in southern Chile and in volcanic islands in Indonesia and PNG, and in coastal location PNG. The earliest and longest operating

systems are the alumina plants in the Marseilles area (Barasse and Gardanne) which since 1967, have discharged the alkaline red mud residues from processing of bauxite into the submarine Cassidaigne canyon (north-western Mediterranean Sea) through pipes situated at 320– 330 m in depth, with a significant proportion reaching >2,000 m (Dauvin [4]). The Barasse pipeline ceased in 1988 but Gardanne is expected to phase out by 2015. This information is needed for engineering design, e.g. to ensure that ballasting of the offshore pipeline will withstand current and wave forces, as well as for environmental impact assessment and impact mitigation. Impacts will also depend on the physical, geochemical and toxicological characteristics of the tailings from the point of discharge to settlement and consolidation. Environmental studies involving deep oceanic research are complex and difficult and require specialist oceanographical equipment and scientists to operate. Historically, best sampling efforts were made with locally available vessels but dedicated oceanographic vessels have become a pre-requisite for baseline seabed surveys to minimise uncertainties for the assessment of a DSTP option. There is a need to keep pace with ever more stringent demands for information (and the availability

of technology to access that information), although it is unlikely a situation where there are no residual uncertainties will ever be achieved.  For example at Batu Hijau, each new permit requires new/additional/updated studies such as updated model prediction and field validation. However, there is now an increasing body of knowledge from performance monitoring of analogues in a range of situations to better address those uncertainties. 

#### **The main impacts and concerns** 

Marine life will inevitably be impacted or displaced by DSTP, just as terrestrial life in the area of the tailings storage is severely impacted by the construction of a land based tailings facility.  The benthic communities on the seabed in the path of the descending tailings stream, and those in the depositional footprint will be smothered and most EIS studies predict the effective loss of these seafloor communities. In reality, impacts are seldom that extreme, and experience from monitoring shows some colonisation of actively depositing tailings, though at reduced numbers. The observations at Island Copper (Ellis [1]),  Lihir (SAMS [5], and at the Gardanne operation in the Mediterranean (Dauvin [4]), all show abundances and biomass of meiofauna (microscopic benthic animals) to be lower in tailings than in unimpacted areas but nevertheless present.  At the Batu Hijau operation in Indonesia, mesocosm and microcosm experiments showed the capacity of meiobenthic fauna to recolonize tailings to levels indistinguishable from control (defaunated) sediments between 100 and 200 days (Gwyther et al. [6]). No doubt rates would be slower at greater depths. SAMS [5]) found differences in benthic communities were still detectable 3 years after closure at Misima. 

The potential for metals in tailings to accumulate in fish through the food chain, affecting the edibility of fish and posing risks to human health is always a matter of concern to local communities and coastal fishing interests. Exposure of fauna to metals can occur through geochemical changes at seafloor/water boundaries, or in the water 

_Proceeding of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

229 

column. During the downslope descent of the tailings density current, partial separation of the solid and liquid phases causes localised subsurface plumes to develop, comprising tailing liquor, seawater and very fine suspended sediment particles. However, extensive routine monitoring of metal content in fish tissues at Misima, Lihir and Batu Hijau has never detected any elevation above baseline conditions, and such elevation that is measured is the same as that accumulated from naturally-occurring sources (see Brewer et al. [7]). Studies that investigated metal uptake by different elements in the food chain found some detection of mine-related metals in midwater plankton but at no other trophic levels (Coffey Natural Systems [8]). 

Related to this is the phenomenon of upwelling, and its potential to redistribute tailings into surfac

e waters.  The potential for this occurrence depends on the depth from which upwelling occurs and its strength and persistence relative to gravitational descent of the tailings. These are factors that must be investigated and incorporated into siting and engineering design. Upwelling has not been strong or persistent enough for any observation of tailings rising into surface waters at any of the DSTP projects in PNG or Indonesia. At Gardanne in the Mediterranean, red mud deposits on the continental shelf due to the transport of the suspended material from the pipe mouth was reported as an exceptional phenomenon, but one that was observed in 1981 during a sustained Mistral period that lasted about three months. The currents in the deep waters of the canyon are not sufficient to mobilize deposited sediments, and due to gravity and the high density of the red mud, most is distributed along the axis of the canyon (Dauvin [4]). 

#### **Engineering risks** 

The main risks to a DSTP facility are from failure of the tailings pipeline or leaks from excessive wear and abrasion.  The design requires at least the same level of geotechnical and seismic investigation as a land based tailings facility.  The pipeline must be installed in a stable seabed location, away from areas showing evidence of submarine slip scars, and properly weighted to avoid movement by waves or currents. Deaeration of the tailing slurry must occur prior to discharge to prevent air entering the tailings outfall pipe. Pipe wear and corrosion must be anticipated and the design provide for this, including monitoring and shut-down procedures to restrict losses of tailings in the event of failure. 

Dual systems are beneficial to allow for continuous operation while maintenance and/or replacement of an outfall pipe takes place.  Systems are now implemented (e.g., at Batu Hijau) that routinely check for pipeline wear using an ultra-sonic pipeline integrity checking device, with stipulated conditions for pipeline change-out when wear exceeds certain levels. Such standard operating practice significantly reduces the risks of pipeline failure. 

Suitable seabed gradients at the pipe outfall must be sufficient to facilitate continuous downward flow of a coherent density current without risk of accumulation

and blockage of the outflow, or dispersion into surrounding areas. This requires case by case assessment of the tailings characteristics and seabed slopes to facilitate flow to the target deep seafloor area. 

#### **Guidelines and criteria** 

#### <u>What opponents to DSTP say</u> 

The main criticisms leveled at marine tailing placement and DSTP assessments claim that the scientific knowledge of the deep sea is not well enough understood to predict potential fate and environmental impacts of the tailings. Further, the criticisms come with the accusation of lack of independence of the science undertaken, whether or not the regulatory age

ncy seeks peer review. Such perception has and likely always will surround work funded by project proponents. 

There have been major advances in oceanographic sciences in recent years and the ability to obtain data on circulation and seabed conditions is far greater now than was the case twenty or even ten years ago. Even so, it is never possible to eliminate all scientific uncertainties and the practicalities of mounting complex oceanic research on a case by case basis are beyond any realistic independently funded means. Hence, the accusations persist. 

It is often stated that DSTP would not be permitted in countries like Australia. This is never likely to be tested, where conditions are the opposite of those in the islands of PNG and Indonesia to the north. Flat, arid and stable land is not in short supply in Australia, and distances to access continental slope depths lie many tens or hundreds of kilometers from the coast in Australia. It has to be recognized that there is no ubiquitous solution to tailings management that fits all geographic and climatic regions. 

#### <u>Independent review</u> 

In PNG, a project was undertaken in 2007/08 to provide an independent evaluation of DSTP in PNG, as part of the mining sector support program funded by the European Union. Its objectives were to critically assess all existing information on past and present mining operations using DSTP in PNG and provide guidelines for future DSTP assessments and marine environmental studies. 

The review was conducted by the Scottish Association for Marine Science (SAMS [5]), which examined operating (Lihir), closed (Misima) and proposed (Ramu) DSTP projects in PNG. The outcome of the study was the development of an independently-derived set of general guidelines and criteria for mining operations in PNG considering DSTP as a tailings management option (Appendix 10 to SAMS [5]). These draft guidelines set out the minimum bathymetric and oceanographcal requirements for engineering, and the baseline and monitoring studies, and duration of

studies, that must be undertaken to assess and validate impacts, applicable to all phases of a project from feasibility, construction, and operation to post closure. The details within the guidelines cover: 

- Preliminary site evaluation including physical, locational criteria and ecological constraints; 

- Environmental baselines, (full water column oceanography, sediments, biological and geochemical characterization, and predictions of fate of tailings) **;** 

- Tailings geochemical and toxicity assessments; 

- Minimum requirements for discharge depths and target accumulation area identification; 

- Monitoring; and 

- Design safety requirements. 

The SAMS draft guidelines have provided the independent scientific input and have raised the bar in terms of the extent and duration of baseline studies and monitoring required for projects considering a DSTP. Though draft, the

y are also effectively in use in PNG, if requested in terms of reference for impact assessment studies of a DSTP option. 

#### **The Batu Hijau example** 

PT Newmont Nusa Tenggara (PTNNT) operates the Batu Hijau copper/gold mine on Sumbawa Island, Indonesia, in which ore is processed at a rate of approximately 130,000 tpd. The tailing residue is discharged to the deep ocean floor from a pipeline, with its terminus located at 125 m depth at the head of a steep submarine canyon (the Senunu Canyon), some 3.2 km offshore of the southwest coast of Sumbawa. Below the pipe exit, the steep gradient of the canyon facilitates tailing flow as a density current to its final deposition at depths below 3,000 m. The mine started operation in 2000 and is expected to continue until 2030s. It is the largest DSTP operation in the world. 

During the environmental impact assessment process, DSTP was chosen over land-based storage options for the following reasons. 

- On-land storage would have required 2,300 ha of forest/agriculture land and relocation of villagers; 

- Water management – annual rainfall 2,500 mm 

- On-going risk of dam wall failure (high rainfall and earthquake risk) 

- On-going management requirements; 

- Suitable bathymetry / slope for DSTP down to >3,000 m 

- Impacts confined to deep sea areas of lower biological productivity (i.e., protection of reefs and biologically productive surface waters; 

- Ultimate recovery of seabed will occur, aided by natural deposition.

From the studies completed, the environmental impact statement (PTNNT [9]) predicted that the tailings slurry would flow down the Senunu Canyon and accumulate at depths of 3,000 to 4,000 m at distances of 50 – 100 km from the coast. It also predicted that the benthos would be lost (smothered) in the tailing footprint, and deep slope fish would be displaced from the area occupied by the descending tailings density current. As the objectives were to protect the shallow water, the third main prediction was that the tailings would not rise into the biologically productive surface mixed layer because of its density and the steepness of the deep sea canyon slope. 

The DSTP system is extensively monitored by the company as well as by third party institutions in Indonesia and overseas. It is in all likelihood one of the most monitored operations in Indonesia and the world, where permit is renewed every two to five years, informed by monitoring of environmental performance. The monitoring program routinely covers the water and sediment quality, reefs, reef fish, metals in fish, plankton, benthos, intertidal areas, seagrass and mangroves to check for any detection of tailings.  Periodic major oceanographical campaigns are also undertaken to validate accumulation areas on the deep seafloor and measurements of dissolved and particulate metals (e.g. [10-12]). The permit also requires regular socialization of monitoring results to stak

differences in ocean circulation and the ecological dependencies of fisheries may be profoundly different from those of the archipelagic situations of the Asia Pacific area. Much study will be needed to understand the constraints, and over sufficient time period to observe implications of the El Niсo Southern Oscillation, and other potential extreme events. This needs to be done to assess whether the required engineering parameters exist for DSTP before it can be considered as a potential option. Gaining community consent is never easy, particularly for coastal communities dependent on fishing; where the benefits are only the assurances that impacts will be minimised. It is critical for governments to have the information to decide whether the environmental impacts are reduced to as low as practicable and justifiable, to realise the socio-economic benefits from mining. Fundamental for gaining acceptability will be the acknowledgement by governments and all sectors of the community of the existence of the dilemma – now or at some finite time into the future – that if the currently accepted land storage methods reach their physical or safety limits, alternative storage methods will need to be considered, in order to maintain the wealth created by the mining industry.  DSTP cannot be a solution without broad community acknowledgement that a dilemma about future mine tailings management needs to be faced. It is the role of governments, informed by scientific study, to evaluate the best solution for future tailings management for the country in each case.

The analyses of all data collected during commissioning and optimization show that the hydrocyclone spigot and mill grate mainly influence the grinding cycle effectiveness. The wear behavior of entire grinding cycle equipment must be controlled as often as possible in order to prevent emergencies stops. Working parameters that could give on time indication are hydrocyclone pressure and pump’s energy consumption and must be continuously monitored. 

In conclusion: 

**Sand nozzle diameter** - in order to assure optimal working conditions of AG mill and hydrocyclone the sand nozzle diameter of the must be between 120 mm and 150 mm. Bigger spigot opening could cause AM break-down – grate blockage, problems with the pump and etc. 

Sand nozzle material – tests with different materials in order to assure constant working parameters and long life of the spigot were done. It could be concluded that: 

1. The rubber spigots are not applicable for the autogenious grinding, in our case, because of fast wearing. 

2. Ceramic spigots type 1 and 2 are not useful in the first stage of grinding for processing slag as well, because of unpredictable life time. 

3. The ceramic nozzles type 3 can be used too, but is necessary to plane new tests to definite it real life time.

Metso’s crusher simulation employs DEM with a proprietary fast breakage technique using the concept of incremental damage. #### **INTRODUCTION** 

Modeling and simulation of cone crushers in order to predict performance is of great importance when predicting the performance for the design and optimization of crushing plants. There are many models and simulation tools with a view to explain the processes; laboratory scale studies from academia concentrating on understanding the physical phenomena, and then expressing that by mathematical means. The industrybased studies are structured more towards gathering data on the performance of the crushers in relation to existing design and operating conditions. 

One of the first models of crushers was published in 1953 and 1954 by Gauldie [1-2] in which he presents a method for prediction of the throughput for a jaw and cone crusher. His assumption is that a material volume slides down the crusher cavity until it is nipped between the two crushing surfaces. The material is assumed to behave plastically and to be porous. At the same time, the material is considered non-sticky and a friction force determined by a friction coefficient is describing the sliding process between the crusher parts and ore particles. The results of the model are the throughput and whether or not the crusher can be choke-fed. One of the drawbacks of this model is that the free fall of the particles is not included. The free fall phenomena might occur at high eccentric speeds and it will affect the throughput of the crusher. The other drawback is that the model might not really preserve continuity. The model assumption that the feed material has bulk properties of porous plastic clay might lead to inaccurate results. 

Bearman [3] has proposed a set of predictive equations in a form of three dimensional graphs to predict the power consumption and product size of a laboratory scale crusher. The effect of feed size, closed side setting (CSS) and rock strength on the power consumption and product size has been examined. In addition to predicting the product size, a method of predicting the full product grading is also presented. The method is based on the Rosin-Rammler distribution and the authors concluded that this method could be used as a tool to predict the product grading of a full scale cone crusher. 

A method for prediction of cone cr

usher performance based on Gauldie’s flow model is presented by Evertsson [4]. His method can predict both product size distributions and total capacity of a cone crusher. By combining these results a Crusher Performance Map (CPM) is obtained. The CPM is a description of crusher performance over a wide range of variation in the operational parameters. The analytical model presented in this paper can be used to optimize a single crushing stage if the feed properties are known. 

An improved flow model for the cone crushers is presented by Evertsson in this paper [5]. The new flow model describes the movement of an aggregate of particles down a crusher using equations of motion. A constitutive relation between size distribution and the uncompressed bulk density of the material is presented. Along with compatibility conditions from the crusher geometry, mass continuity is preserved. The 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

249 

flow model provides detailed information about how different machine parameters affect the flow of the rock material through the crusher chamber. 

A model to predict crushers’ performance has been developed by Ruuskanen [6]. The model is predicting the product grading, product shape, crusher capacity, crusher power and Manganese consumption using the feed and the crusher parameters as inputs. The essential part of the model is to find, by using extensive experiments, the relationship between different parameters and then to describe the crushing phenomenon in mathematical terms. The model is implemented in Metso’s Bruno simulation program, which enables the prediction of the overall crushing plant performance. 

All the models of the cone crushers described above have their own limitations and have been developed under certain assumptions which limit their capability of predicting the crusher performance under a wide range of operational and geometrical parameters. This paper will describe Metso’s current 3D Discrete Element Method (DEM) modeling techniques developed to allow a comprehensive study of the effect of different crusher variables on actual performance of the crusher. 

#### **DESCRIPTION OF THE DEM WITH FAST BREKAGE MODEL** 

The Discrete Element Method (DEM) is a numerical technique in which the equations of motion of every particle in the system are integrated numerically at every time step. Thus, the motion of every particle is known in great detail. DEM simulations are often used to simulate the flow of unbreakable particles in material handling applications within reasonable time frame. 

The application of DEM to crusher simulation must overcome an additional challenge. The particles passing through the crusher must be broken and the DEM requires additional realistic and fast breakage models. These breakage models must consider the ore properties and the loading information from the DEM simulations and calculate the resultant size reduction. On the other hand, the breakage model must provide th

e resultant forces that the rocks apply to the mantle and liner. 

The Newton’s Second Law of motion is numerically solved in DEM simulations for each particle in the system. If _mi_ is the mass of the particle moving with velocity _vi_ under the action of a collection of forces _fij_ including gravitational forces, friction, particle-particle, particle-fluid and particle-boundary interaction forces the Newton’s Second Law can be written as: 



The DEM modeling of the particles in this paper is done by using 3D polyhedral particles.

Early techniques to develop a breakage model used “clamps” constructed of subparticles “glued” together by contact forces that are able to withstand specific tensile stresses before being broken. This approach can provide good results but the computational time for such technique is significantly high. The new approach referred as Fast Breakage (FB) described by Potapov [7] combines DEM with Population Balance Modeling (PBM) and has largely overcome the limitation of the “clamps” breakage modeling. The inherent requirement for a realistic and robust breakage model is the conservation of mass and volume. The FB model developed by Metso is using polyhedral shaped particles. This paper presents the validation of the FB model against MP1000 and MP1250 Metso tertiary crushers.

The results were compared with experimental plant data on the respective crushers. The experimental work was carried out on crushers with relatively new wear liners in order to eliminate the effect of abnormal chamber profile on the comparison exercise. The estimated results are very close to the experimental data proving that Metso DEM Fast Breakage code is a very powerful tool which could be successfully used to optimize the design of the cone crusher liner profile or the crushers itself for better performance. The model will aid in the selection of crusher design and parameters for any given criteria or application, as well as the use in product development. The current DEM model is a micro model and is sensitive to all aspects of a crusher design and operation while the previous models were tailored for certain plants or experimental setups. The data provided by the model can be also highly localized and thus opens the possibility of developing wear models that will be sensitive to ore and crusher parameters. The current DEM Fast Breakage code is implemented

in Metso’s PROSim plant simulating software and it can be used to predict crusher plant overall performance.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

“Copper clays” is a common mapping term to describe parts of argillic and advanced argillic alterations associated with Andean type copper deposits. They are very fine grained materials with a bluish hue, which may or may not expand when humidified. These “copper clays” accompany chrysocolla, atacamite and secondary sulphide mineralization. Copper clays have been characterized by X-ray diffraction, Qemscan<sup>®</sup> and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM). In this presentation, TEM observations are contrasted with literature data on (1) the attempts to synthesize Cu-phyllosilicates, (2) the modification of phyllosilicates with Cu bearing molecules and (3) larger than claysize phyllosilicates incorporating Cu phases between individual sheets. For the studied copper clays, discrete copper phases were found to be intercalated between individual phyllosilicate layers on a nanometric scale. For acid extraction of Cu from these combined clay and Cu phase aggregates, rock texture and acid stability of the phyllosilicate species are of fundamental importance.
