#### **INTRODUCTION** 

“Copper-clays” (“arcillas con cobre, arcillas de cobre”) is a mapping term used in Andean type porphyry copper deposits [1], given to clay-like materials with a bluegreenish hue found in argillic and advanced argillic alterations. They are very fine grained materials, which may or may not expand when moistened. Cu-clays accompany chrysocolla, atacamite and secondary sulphide mineralization. Therefore

, whole sample copper grades o Cu-cation exchange capacities do not reflect the presence of copper in these phases. Their grain size impedes obtaining phase-linked Cu contents by electron microprobe or automated microanalysis (Qemscan<sup>®</sup> , MLA). Phase bound Cu-contents are expected and requested for predicting Cu-extraction, an answer that cannot be provided by routine analytical proceedings and furthermore many doubts or misconceptions exist (in particular from the engineering point of view) as to the “obligatory” and stoichiometric  presence of Cu in the crystal structure of these clay phases. 

The present contribution aims at providing a mineralogical overview about the presence of Cu in phyllosilicates either as part of the tetrahedral-octahedral framework structure or on internal exchange surfaces, including subject linked efforts to synthesize Cu-clays or modify their structure, as well as the  presence of Cu-phases in above clay size phyllosilicates.  Results of the characterization of Chilean Cu-clays by transmission electron microscopy are presented.  Based on the aforementioned points, ideas for a geometallurgical re-appreciation are put forward. 

#### **COPPER IN PHYLLOSILICATES REVIEWED** 

To begin with, the term clay should be defined. According to the AIPEA (Association Internationale pour l´Йtude des Argiles, www.aipea.org) and the Clay Mineral Society (www.clay.org), clays are natural fine grained materials, which may be plastic and harden upon drying or heating [2]. Upper grain size limits vary according to the field of study: in sedimentology the Udden Wentworth scale limits clays to below 4µm, in clay mineralogy (including nano materials) 2µm and for colloids sizes below 1µm apply [3]. For this presentation reference will also be made to phyllosilicate exceeding the clay size limits, such as biotites or muscovites of igneous origin, which by alterations have been exposed to Cu-rich solutions. However, their structural equivalence to clay size micas merits their inclusion. 

The possibility to adsorb, interchange copper and the possibility to incorporate transition metals in the aluminosilicate framework depends on the basic structural types of phyllosilicates (Table 1). The ionic ratio Si:O=0.29 and Al:O=0.39 mark the tetrahedral and octahedral configuration of the basic building sheets.  Tetrahedral sheets of Si2O5<sup>2-</sup> (Si is frequently substituted by Al, Fe) have Si located at the centre of a tetrahedron formed by corner oxygens. The tetrahedron is linked via basal oxygens into hexagonal grids. The apical oxygens link the tetrahedral sheet to the second building 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

259 

element, the octahedral layer. The basic unit is a hydroxyl octahedron with either a di- or trivalent cation at its centre. These units are linked by sharing two lateral OH groups. In the case of electrical neutrality of an Al4 (OH)12 sheet, Al only occupies two out of three octahedral cavitie

s; for divalent cations (Mg6(OH)12) all centres of the octahedral cavities are occupied [2]. The repetition of tetrahedral-octahedral or tetrahedral-octahedraltetrahedral “sheets” form layers. These layers types (TO, TOT or 1:1, 1:2) are the fundamental discriminating feature of phyllosilicates and are followed by di- or trioctahedral occupancy of the “O” sheet and elemental substitutions within the “sheets” and the interlayer cation to define the phyllosilicate species. 

The presence of Cu in natural large phyllosilicates has been studied from a mineralogical point of view since the late 1950s [4] with copper (2-7%) bearing vermiculites and biotites from Rhodesia where copper was found as interlayer cation, but also biotite inclusions of hematite were documented. This was followed, e.g. in 1972, by studies on the transition element cation substitution in trioctahederal mica structural frameworks [5] and their effect on the crystallographic a, b, and c parameters.  With the availability of electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy, the presence of copper in phyllosilicates permitted in situ imaging and analysis, an opportunity taken by Ilton and Veblen [6] and several follow up publications [7 and 8], describing inclusions of native copper and oxide copper ores in the interlayer space of biotites from porphyry copper deposits and experimentally proving their origin due to weathering and percolation of Cu rich solutions rather than due to hydrothermal events.  For the smaller illite, the same native Cu inclusions and weathering origin have been confirmed by Ahn et al. [9] working on slate from Pinal County, Arizona, USA.  The uptake of Cu by natural muscovite and biotite from slightly acid solutions has been studied by Farquhar et al. [10], studying the removal of elements of environmental concern by minerals in terms penetration into the mineral structure. 

Amongst smectites, the only natural variety described incorporationg Cu into the crystal structure is Yakhontovite ((Ca,Na)0.5(Cu,Fe,Mg)2(Si4O10)(OH)43H2O) described by Postinikova et al. in 1986, as cited in Jambor and Puziewicz  [11] and is classified as a tricotahedral smectite from the  Pridorochnoye sulphite – cassiterite deposit in the Komsomolsk Region, Russia.  The same mineral has been described once by Brimhall et al. [12]  from the initial open cast of the Radomiro Tomic deposit, Chile; although doubts about its presence remain, as the authors did not use infrared spectroscopy to confirm the trioctahedricity of the smectite phase.  Further rare Cu-silicates (zeolite structure o phyllosilicate?) are: Ajoite (K,Na)Cu7Al Si9O24(OH)63H2O; Kurumsakite - (Zn,Ni,Cu)8Al8V2Si5O3527H2O. Phases are well described by Raman spectroscopy, but a crystalographic definition based on XRD is still pending [13 and 14], although a zeolite structure would be more likely. tral pH, whereas the “regular” octahedral site cation Mg hydrolyses at low pH and is slower to form laminar structures than the transition metals.  Starting materials are varied ranging from reagents and glass, to mineral phases, such as kaolinite, zeolite, etc. 

Copper fixed by cation exchange in the interlayer space of e.g. montmorillonite, as organic molecule or copper pillared clay (PILC), the latter cation exchange followed by drying and tempering is used in catalysis, e.g. Achma et al.,[21], the cleaning of waste waters, e.g. Caudo et al. [22] and antimicrobacterian uses, e.g. Malachova et al.,[23]. This modification of the interlayer space tailors microporosity, increases surface area and often results in a greater thermal stability than observed for zeolites, but does not correspond to a process expected in natural minerals, where only Cu as exchangeable cation is found in the interlayer space. 

#### **OBSERVATION OF “COPPER CLAYS”** 

Over the past decade, the working group of this presentation has received a wide range of so called “copper clay” samples from Chilean copper deposits.  Initial characterizations were carried out by a combination of optical microscopy and X-ray diffraction, including preparations of the <2µm fraction.  This permits an adequate textural characterization, mineralogical identification is limited to the limits of resolution of the microscope and the ability to retain possible expansible or water soluble phases up to the final thin section during sample preparation.  This does not result in the identification of specific copper bearing clays.  However, the presence blue-green copper phases like atacamite or chrysocolla suggests that these may also be found on a submicroscopic scale.  To improve special resolution on a micrometer scale, electron microprobe and Qemscan<sup>®</sup> microchemical characterization has been done, again resulting in a mixture a clay mineral phases (illites, smectites, kaolinite) with either now visible copper phases such as atacamite or simply detecting the presence of Cu associated to theses phyllosilicate microaggregates.  Based on the observations of Ilton and Veblen [7,8], transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was the following step of characterization. 

A caveat is necessary for TEM observations with respect to optical and “regular” electron microscopy techniques.  Sample preparation of potentially expansible and other

hydrated mineral phases is complex; it implies prolonged impregnation with Spurr<sup>®</sup> resin, without any guarantee of obtaining a final microtome cut sample slice.  Even when selecting samples of the size of a needle tip, samples observed by TEM will only be a tiny part of the initial sample cut at random from the resin block.  There are no means of getting a final visual inspection of the sample suitability. 



Figure 1 – Typical TEM image of phyllosilicate sheets intertwined with chrysocolla (“bubb

However, once satisfactorily mounted the following repetitive observations could be made.  Distinct matrix clays (kaolinite, illite) were found to be intercalated with either atacamite or chrysocolla on a submicrometric scale (Figure 1).  The observations mimic those on an optical microscope and electron microscope scale.  The difficulty of stabilizing hydrated phases like chrysocolla or atacamite under the intense electron beam of a TEM aids the identification of these nanometric intergrowths, by the bubbly texture of these minerals compared to the stable phyllosilicates.  As is the case with automated electron microchemical analyses, elements like Cl permit to identify atacamite. Chryscolla should be viewed additionally in diffraction mode, where the phase is amorphous.

#### **DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS** 

Based on literature published spanning at least half a century of mineralogical reporting and research with ever improving methods of characterization a pragmatic approach should be adopted with respect to finding discrete new copper phyllosilicate species on a scale and regular occurrence as the “copper clays” mapped in alteration zones associated with Andean porphyry copper deposits. The demonstrated difficulties of synthesis of phyllosilicates which incorporate copper in the octahedral sheet are clearly mimicked in nature by the extreme rarity of natural counterparts, such as yakhontovite. Given the rarity definitive crystallographic characterizations are often missing. Therefore ultrafine phase mixtures as reported in this contribution should be considered a first and not a last option. 

This will imply changing the approach to the characterization of these clay microaggregates, focusing on their textural arrangement within the rock together with the intrinsic physicochemical characteristics.  Amongst these, the average clay-aggregate size and its physical stability generated during an extraction process are to be considered, together with the type of phyllosilicate hosting the nano-scale oxide copper phases.   It will not be possible to inform stoichiometric compositions for these Cu-clay microaggregates. 

TEM characterizations carried on a regular basis are slow and should be replaced in routine operation by a combination of optical microscopy, XRD and, depending on the alteration, IR spectroscopy.  A further option is to combine optical microscopy with automated microchemical analysis, the latter though requiring a good adjustment of the mineral reference database (“SIP”) to subtle variations in phyllosilicate compositions which may result in longer counting times compared to naturally larger sized minerals and with less variable composition.

#### **THE EVOLUTION OF MILL RELINING TECHNOLOGY** 

_149 Hursley Rd, Glenvale, Toowoomba, Queensland, Australia. Wiston.Rocher@rmeGlobal.com_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Over the past fifty years, technology has advanced quicker than in any other time and this has impacted greatly on people’s lives, on the equipment and at work. 

The small grinding mills had an entry in the mill feed end for the spout feeder that didn't allow the entry of a person. The discharge of many of them had grates and the only way for people, liners and tools to get into them was via the manhole. The liners were installed manually with brute force, using tools like chain blocks, rope and chains, extending mills shutdown for many hours and increasing the risk of accidents. 

The increased size of mills and the high prices for metals means equipment designers and mining companies need to work constantly to surpass their mechanised technology, the quality of the materials and their components, increasing their capacity, by making them faster, more accurate and safer. In addition, the operators are working more strategically. The result has been a significant decrease of relining time and an increase in operator's safety.

o, Chile_ 

268 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Concentrator Plan downtime is produced by several reasons, such as unscheduled mechanical, electrical, operational or control system shutdowns. However, the most important reason is the scheduled reline, which represents 80% of wasted time. 

It is important to address this topic applying technology, equipment and work systems that help to achieve better performance. Mining companies, Equipment manufacturers and Reline companies constantly work to increase Mill utilisation. 

This presentation shows the latest Mill relining results, reviews the latest 50 years of Mill relining history, including the systems utilised and the effort made to develop the world class Mill relining technology and organisational systems adopted by companies today. 

#### **DEVELOPMENT** 

#### **The 60’s** 

At that time, grinding mills of small size, between 8 and 10 feet in diameter, made people and liner’s movement very uncomfortable. It was required to empty the mil, discharge the balls, and to load them back once the reline was finished. 

With Bar Mills, it was not practical to take the bars out without having the conditions needed to do this job. It was very uncomfortable to stay permanently bent. However, there are some plants that still empty their mills today to do this job. In the 60’s it was a very hard work to enter and install heavy metallic liners in these conditions, without the aid of equipment and tool designed for this purpose. 

In the same decade, Bars and Ball Mills with a larger diameter, 13’ y 14’, and the first Mill Liner Handler - Lift In/Lift Out appeared. Although they were handcrafted models, installed with an overhead crane, they helped to do this job reducing time, effort and accidents and allowed the utilisation of heavier liners. 

In this decade, rubber liners also appeared. For some plants, they were really successful. However, both steel and rubber liners still remain due to differences in their mineral characteristics, conditions and operation, prices, and composition. 

The utilisation of manual hammers was the only Bolt removal system for many years. 

#### **The 70’s** 

In the 70’s, grinding mills continue to grow slowly in size and mill relining systems did not have great progress. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

269 

Although, SAG and Full AG grinding are very old, the mills utilised at that time had the same characteristics as Ball mills. In the late 70’s, SAG mills adopted the characteristics that they have today, with higher diameter than longitude. 

The emergence of SAG mil with feed trunnion of higher diameter allowed performing the reline trough the feed end, and the utilisation of Mill Liner Handlers with better technology and capacity. Feed chutes, with 20 and 40 capacities, supported over wheels, also appeared.  These chutes were removed using systems with winches and chargers, but this removal method took too much time and represented a high risk for acciden

ts. 

#### **The 80’s** 

In the 80’s, SAG mills of up to 34’ with chutes of around 40 tons appeared. The removal systems used at that time were not too different from the systems mentioned before. Liners’ weight and dimensions increased considerably. 

#### **The 90’s** 

In that decade, SAG mills reached 36’ of diameter using ‘wrap around’ motors while Ball mills reached 21’ feet of diameter. Both of them required powered feed chutes. 

The increase of the diameter of the feed trunnion produced the creation of Mill relining machines of 6 and 7 axis. These machines use a grapple to place liners, which grew in size from 1800 kg to 3500 kg, and new technology that improves relining time. For example, THUNDERBOLT hammers appeared in the market to remove bolts liners in less time, while improving people safety significantly. 

#### **The 2000’s** 

In the 2000’s, SAG mills grew in size up to 38’ and then up to 40’ diameter, with heavier feed chutes, 80 and 100 tons respectively. This produced the creation of Powered Feed Chute Transporters, with 4 wheels first and multi wheels (up to 10) later, to reduce floor load by wheel. 

In some plants, liners reached up to 6000 kg. 

In the current decade, the projects of some plants are considering SAG mills of 42’, with an estimated chute weight of 110 ton, increasing the challenge for the equipment designed to make this job and also for the systems to be applied. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

270 

#### **CURRENT SITUACION** 

#### **HPGR** 

In recent years, High pressure grinding rolls equipment has appeared in the market, which is utilised in Crushing plants for the tertiary stage, and for pebble crushing in SAG plants. 

Bigger and heavier Rolls need to be removed to reline them. One of the manufacturers of this equipment designs them to be removed vertically, using overhead cranes. Other manufacturer designs them to be removed horizontally. For the second case, there is a Maintenance car for the HPGR that removes the rolls, loads them in itself, and transports them to the maintenance place. 

#### **Bolt Removal** 

The use of manual hammers and sledgehammers for bolt removal was widespread for many years. From the 90’s, THUNDERBOLT Hammers appeared in the market in different models. They have been successful in all the plants where they have been used worldwide because they reduce bolt removal time significantly and increase worker’s safety. 

These hammers have many suspension systems: Mobile Jib, Fixed Jib, Monorail and Elevating Platforms. 

#### **Elevating Platforms** 

Elevating platforms, both inside and outside the mill, allow changing more liner rows per Mill position. 

#### **Worn liner removal** 

This is one of the most time consuming operations and maybe represents the highest risk for accidents. 

Liners were removed by human strength for a long time. Lifting them from the floor balls or mill charge is very difficult and, these conditions, exposes operators to accide

nts greatly. 

Today, there are tools called O-ZONE Worn Liner Lifting Tools composed by a ring with two chains and hooks at their ends. The tool is called “scissors” due to their similar shape. This is introduced in the holes of the worn liner, without the need for manual lifting. In their lower end, the scissors takes the bolt from its head. In the opposite end, the holes at both sides of the scissor are aligned to introduce the hooks and lift the liner with the Mill Relining Machine to place it in the liner car and to take it out of the mill. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

271 

In some occasions, the liner drops in the mill charge with a bolt still engage in it. This precludes the use of scissors in this hole. In this case, the scissors need to be replaced in that point for a special piece called “grip”. 

This operation not only reduces the risk of accidents but also reduces the average removal time in about a minute per liner. This is a significant reduction of time if we consider all the liners that must be changed. 

#### **Mill Relining Machine** 

The Machines with the highest technology that are used today are: 

#### <u>Vertimill Relining Machine</u> 

They are manufactured as Fixed, Lift In/Lift Out and Mobile, with grapples of up to 6 axis. With them, there is no need to remove the main axis from the mil as the reline takes place inside it. 

Given the enormous liner weight, these machines have 10,000 Kg rated capacity. 

#### <u>Mill Liner Handler – Millmast</u> 

In small mills, from 8’ to 20’ diameter, that do not have enough space outside to move a Mill Liner Handler, the Millmast is a good solution. The Millmast is manufactured with 400 Kg rated capacity. 

The equipment is assembled inside the mill. The post is hydraulically set between the mill charge and “roof” and operates with a hydraulic telescopic arm. This equipment means a great hep for the operators, significantly reducing time and the risk of accidents. 

#### <u>3 axis Machines</u> 

In small mills, that have enough space outside to move a Mill Liner Handler, three axis equipment can be used, with rated capacity of up to 1500 Kg and with technology of high level in its design, in its parts and manufacturing materials. 

#### <u>7 axis Machines</u> 

In Ball mills, even those with larger diameter and longitude, this technique has advanced significantly, creating the 7 axis Mill relining machine. Its grapple has movements similar to the human hand. Operated from the control system, it can take liners without the need of a person to engage them. 

The high technology utilised in designing the beam and the high quality of steel used in their manufacture, has enabled Mill Relining Machines great length and capacity.

272 

These machines do not use support at the front end of the beam inside the mil due to previous bad experiences in many plants worldwide. Some companies experienced large losses of money w

hen completely destroyed their mills because they forgot to lift their support. Without the machine, the work inside the mill needed to be finished manually. 

The speed of the operation and the precision of liners’ placement have enabled a significantly reduction in mill relining time. 

#### <u>8 axis Machines</u> 

As SAG mills became bigger, the surface of its liners also increased. They had a higher surface compared with the liners of Ball mills. Due to the increased of the increase of liner surface, a great technological effort was made, the 8 axis grapple for the Mill Relining Machine. The 8<sup>th</sup> axis helps to place liners in the discharge end of the mill mainly and has a 7250 kg capacity. 

#### <u>Twin Mill Relining Machine</u> 

Both the dimension limit of the feed trunnion entre and the increase of liners size produced the creation of the Twin machine. The Twin machine consists in two complete totally independent machines, own with bases units, powerpack, independent beams, liner cars, and independent arms, and grapples. Both machines can be used simultaneously, reaching their best performance with coordination. 

It has been shown in the practice that a Twin machine can half the time spent relining the mill cylinder with a single RME Mill Relining Machine. For large discharge end liners, both liner cars are operated as they were just one. 

All this technology has allowed Plants to reduce the time they spent relining mills up to a quarter.

#### **LABOUR ORGANISATION** 

No doubt, the advancement of technology has been a great help to reach the achieved levels. However, crew organisation is also an important part of relining mills. The study of this work, performed by involved equipment and people, is and must be very detailed. 

This work does not start when the mill shutdown for reline, but when the previous shutdown finishes.  After the reline is finished, the crew that has participated, including the responsible for the maintenance of the equipment, meets to analys

e problems experienced and the solution provided to make improvements at every opportunity. 

The work must be planned to detail, including the equipment, tools, steps in each stage, groups of people to move new and worn liners, load and unload of liners into the Mill Relining Machine cars, groups than operate inside the mill, and each team leader. 

Each team leader is responsible for their group not to delay the total process. If their notice a problem, they need to communicate to the General leader to get help and resolve it. 

It is very important to listen to the Plant personnel who are responsible for the organisation. #### **ABSTRACT** 

The SAG mill is the primary workhorse in the majority of comminution circuits throughout the world. With continuingly declining head grades, the need for higher throughput circuits has become prevalent—particularly in Latin America and parts of Asia. This paper describes the recent design knowledge and practical experience gained in both the areas of pulp lifters and integrated trommel screen design. 

The evolution of this work started with the replacement of the OEM discharge mill linings that were generally made of Cr-Mo steel alloy castings. The use of an alternative composite material—comprised of steel/rubber/ceramic—provides a suitable solution with several additional benefits. 

The importance of system efficiency in terms of pulp removal is also described together with the need for enhanced slurry distribution onto the trommel screen. The use of modern tools such as SPH/CFD and DEM models, optimization of process parameters

and slurry evacuation parameters ensures the best slurry draining and pulp evacuation are achieved. Practical data relating to the influence on circuit operating times and availability are also described. As part of this analysis, the trommel screen was also assessed in terms of screen panel design and configuration. Furthermore, correct slurry distribution and usage of available screen area are also described in this paper. 276 #### **INTRODUCTION** Taking a holistic look at the application, process conditions and design in general, as well as applying the modern design tools and advanced material compositions and selection in order to re-design the “discharge assembly,” have made it possible to replace the original liners by a modern solution. This is shown in the optimized shape and form, as well as by using alternative composite materials such as ceramics and rubber. The redesigned solution not only improves the liner performance, relative to its reduction in weight, number of components or sub-assemblies, but also increases the wear life and lowers the total replacement cost, or the operating cost. The new design features are also more robust and allow for effective operation under a wider range of operating conditions without risk of overloading the SAG mill. The key in successful design is the use of modern design tools, which have been properly validated and calibrated for the duty. By using well calibrated tools, the process models become more robust and efficient, and optimized design configurations can be drafted. In this way it is possible to predict and optimize achievable operational parameters and results which can justify the involved changes and investments. #### **GRATE DISCHARGE ASSEMBLY AND FUNCTIONALITY** The discharge system in this paper is defined as the grate discharge assembly, which classifies and transports the slurry and sized pebble fraction out from the mill. An integral component of the mill discharge system is the trommel screen. The trommel screen is used to further process the SAG mill discharge into a slurry flow (screen undersize) and pebble fraction (coarse critical size fraction). With detailed analysis of the process conditions and an understanding of the specific wear mechanism(s) on the pulp lifters, an alternative design selection can be made possible. The integrated SAG discharge assembly—including discharge grates, pulp lifters and a subsequent trommel screen—are key components within the mill and overall grinding circuit. 295 The drive to improve operational efficiency via improving component life and trommel screen performance is vitally important to the successful operation of this part of the circuit. #### **PREVENTING COPPER LOSS PRODUCTION AND FLOW PROBLEMS BY MEASURING THE MATERIALS FLOW PROPERTIES** 

O. Angulo and F. Cabrejos _Jenike and Johanson Chile S.A. Av. Libertad 798 Of. 501 Viсa del Mar, Chile jenike-chile@entelchile.net_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Hundreds of millions of tons of copper-containing products in particulate forms (such as ROM, crushed, agglomerated or leached ore, concentrate, or tailings), having different characteristics (like particle size distribution, shape and density, moisture content, chemical, mineralogical and lithological composition), are daily handled, stored and conveyed in the world through different equipment at the different stages of the copper minerallurgical processes.  In these processes, operators commonly face problems such as loss of production, flow blockages in the equipment, segregation, equipment wear, uncontrolled discharge and occasionally unexpected plant shutdowns.  Due to the huge investments involved in world class projects, the mining industry is particularly sensitive to them. 

The purpose of this paper is to provide a cost effective solution to flow problems in the mining industry, by highlighting a well proven and scientific method used to ensure controlled and reliable flow of bulk solids, based on Jenike’s flow of solids technology and laboratory testing [1].  Knowledge of the material flow properties allows designing new installations or modifying existing defective equipment, and preventing production stoppages due to the formation of chute pluggages, cohesive arches and/or “ratholes” in silos, which are the most common causes of flow problems in the copper mining industry. 

297 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Approximately 16 million tons of copper were produced from mines in 2011 [2]. Behind this massive annual production, there are series of minerallurgical and/or metallurgical processes that require storing and handling the large tonnages of ore extracted in order to produce the refined copper requested by the market. 

Copper containing products in particulate forms, with different properties and characteristics are daily handled, stored and conveyed in different equipment (like bins, silos, hoppers, stockpiles, ore passes, chutes, feeders, rotary valves, belt conveyors, screw feeders, bucket elevators, pneumatic conveyors, etc.) because of their versatility and great adaptation to the process requirements.  The equipment listed have been used for decades, however companies processing copper are still facing common flow problems such as blockages, segregation, equipment wear, uncontrolled discharge and decrease of the storage and production capacity. 

#### **B

ACKGROUND** The mentioned flow problems can be prevented and/or solved by characterising and measuring the flow properties of the particulate product to be processed, in order to correctly design the equipment that will handle it [3-5]. Particulate products usually have different properties and characteristics (such as particle size distribution, shape and density, moisture content, chemical, mineralogical and lithological composition, additive content, like surfactants or flocculants, etc.) that alter their bulk flow behaviour, so an adequately suitable equipment design is necessary for each material depending on its origin, composition, properties and work conditions. The technology highlighted in this paper, for measuring the flow properties of bulk solids (including copper-containing materials), has been available for almost 50 years and up to today has shown to be the only well proven and scientific approach for the design of equipment handling bulk solids [1]. The use of this technology in the mining industry has increased in the last two decades due to the rising need of improving efficiency. Flow problems are mostly caused by phenomena related to the material flow properties, processes conditions and equipment dimensioning. The common causes of these problems could be identified as the formation of “ratholes” and/or arches above outlets, and the development of an inconvenient flow pattern in the equipment [3-5]. Ratholing (see Figure 1a) o ccurs when material discharge takes place only in a flow channel located above the outlet. If the material being handled is cohesive, the material outside of this channel will not flow into it, creating stagnant or dead zones in the equipment; once the central flow channel has emptied, all flow stops. This “rathole” may be stable (permanent dead zones) or unstable depending on the flow properties of the material, a nd in special conditions flooding may occur due to a sudden fall down of the stagnant material. Arching (see Figure 1b) occurs when an arch-shaped obstruction forms above the hopper outlet and stops flow. It can be an interlocking arch, where large 298 particles mechanically interlock to form an obstruction, or a cohesive arch. A cohesive arch occurs when particles bond together due to their cohesion strength produced by moisture content, fines concentration, particle shape, temperature, etc. (a) (b)
Figure 1 – Flow problems: a) “rathole”; b) cohesive arch (Re-printed from www.jenike.com) There are three flow patterns that can be developed in silos and hoppers when handling bulk solids: funnel, mass and expanded flow (see Figure 2). Funnel flow occurs when the hopper is not sufficiently steep and smooth to force material to slide along the walls by gravity means or when the outlet is not fully effective. Conversely, mass flow occurs when a hopper is sufficien

tly steep and smooth to force the material to slide along the walls by gravity effects.  In this pattern, the material is discharged uniformly, first in first out, and there is no stagnant material on the walls.  The combination of the two previous patterns is called expanded flow, where mass flow is developed beneath of a funnel flow silo. 







Figure 2 – Flow patterns:  a) funnel flow; b) mass flow; c) expanded flow Reproduced from www.jenike.com 

Approximately 50 years ago, Andrew Jenike [1] proposed a flow of solids theory to properly design bins and hoppers handling bulk solids.  This theory is based on the flow properties of the material handled, which should be determined in a laboratory 

299 

under the expected operating conditions to be encountered in the process.  Thus, a range of conditions should be taking into account when measuring the flowability of the materials, including   moisture content, pressure, storage time at rest, temperature, etc. 

#### **FLOW PROPERTIES OF THE BULK SOLIDS** 

The most important flow properties to be measured, to ensure a correct equipment design, are described below [1,3-5]. 

#### **Cohesive Strength** 

From the bulk solids handling point of view, this is the main flow property of the solids.  Jenike’s methodology [1] allows to measure the flow behaviour of the material, calculating the angle of internal friction, and drawing the flow function (cohesive strength vs. consolidation pressure).  Based on these results, it is possible to determine the critical dimensions to be used for equipment design in order to avoid arching and “ratholing” formation during discharge.  The cohesive strength of the materials depends on several factors like:  consolidation pressure determined by the dimensions of the equipment (height of the pile or bin geometry), percentage of fine particles, particle density and shape, moisture content, storage time at rest and under pressure, additives, particle voidage, temperature and chemical nature, etc.  For example, in applications where air assisted or fluidized discharge of fine copper concentrate is required, its cohesive strength is considerably diminished to the point that the material flows like a “liquid”.  In an opposite case, a wet crushed copper ore in a tall stockpile can gain cohesive strength due to the high consolidation pressures involved, and the formation of “ratholes” or cohesive arches during the discharge are likely to be experienced if an inadequate equipment design is materialized. 

The cohesive strength of a material for a given situation can be determined using its flow function, which shows the unconfined failure strength as function of the major principal consolidation stress [1].  In general words, it shows the strength of the material that would prevent failure (flow) after a compression force has been applied to the material to initiate the flow.  This cohesive strength must be lower than the stress produced by the combination of gravity and

bin geometry in order to obtain flow. If the stress is lower than the strength, a no-flow situation like arching or ratholing is obtained. 

This concept can be explained using an analogy with the uniaxial compression test [6], where a sample of the material is confined in a cylinder (with frictionless walls) and subject to a vertical pre-consolidation force; then the cylinder is removed and a vertical compression force is applied until the material fails or collapses.  This procedure is repeated for different compression forces forming a data base of the failure conditions. Unfortunately, in the uniaxial compression test is difficult to measure the stresses in the failure plane and to undertake the test with frictionless walls.  Therefore, Jenike [1] proposed an alternative method using a uniaxial shear test (see Figure 3) and the Mohr stress circle to determine the range failure conditions that comprise the flow function of 

300 

the material.  This method has been accepted by the American Society for Testing Materials and nowadays is known as the ASTM D-6128 standard [7].  Unlike other existing methods to measure the flowability of the materials, this method measures average stresses in the measuring plane, has good reproducibility, takes into account the compression of the materials and the time consolidation effect. 

An example of a generic flow function, at two different moisture content levels, is shown schematically in Figure 4, where the cohesive strength, FC, is plotted as a function of the consolidation pressure, σ1.  Here, the flow behaviour is affected by the increment of the moisture content in the material.  Besides, the figure shows the different zones that allow to classify the flow behaviour of the materials as proposed by Jenike [1].  Materials may behave differently in industrial applications depending on the consolidation pressure acting, the range of moisture content, the flow conditions (instantaneous flow or flow reinitiated after X hours of storage time at rest under pressure), among other factors. 



Figure 3 – Jenike uniaxial shear tester (Reproduced from ASTM D-6128 [7]) 



Figure 4 – Generic flow function plot example at two working conditions 

301 

#### **Wall Friction** 

Another important flow property is the wall friction.  The measurement of this parameter allows to determine the equipment dimensions necessary to ensure reliable discharge by developing a mass flow pattern.  For example, knowing the friction properties of the material against the walls is possible to determine the minimum angle of a hopper to force the material to slide over the walls by gravity means; therefore preventing the formation of stagnant material and blockages of the equipment.  This measurement also permits the calculation of the loads on the walls and the design of feeders.  Jenike [1] proposed a wall shear test procedure (see Figure 5) by modifying its uniaxial shear test method.  The test determines the material shear force,

FS, against the equipment wall sample surface for a range of normal forces, FN, applied to the sample. The slope of the resulting curve of plotting the shear stress, τ, as function of the normal stress, σ, determines the coefficient of friction, µ (Equation 1), consequently the angle of wall friction, ϕ , can be defined. 





Figure 5 – Set up to measure wall friction with Jenike shear tester (Reproduced from ASTM D-6128 [7]) 





Figure 6 –Generic wall friction results example at two flow conditions 

As a reference, wall friction angle values typically vary between 10<sup>o</sup> and 40<sup>o</sup> , depending on the wall surface roughness, flow conditions, material characteristics, temperature, etc.  Figure 6 shows a generic wall friction results example of a material at 

302 

two flow conditions (instantaneous and to reinitiate the flow after X hours of storage time at rest and under pressure), showing the increment of this property to reinitiate the flow after storage time at rest and under pressure. 

#### **Compressibility** 

In the majority of industrial applications handling bulk solids, the material’s bulk density varies as a function of the consolidation pressure acting on it.  The bulk density is defined as the weight of material per unit of volume occupied, including the air and the moisture trapped between particles.  Example of the density variation is the crushed copper ore storage in a tall stockpile, where the bulk density increases with the height of the pile (consolidation pressure). 

According to the ASTM D-6683 [8], the compressibility of the bulk solids can be measured by confining a material sample in a cylinder and registering the bulk density changes as a normal force is applied (see Figure 7).  The relation between the bulk density, γ (Equation 2), and the consolidation pressure, σ1, is reflected as a straight line in a log-log graph; where the compressibility grade is represented by the coefficient β, and the constants γo and σo are empiric. 





Figure 7 – Compressibility test (Reproduced from ASTM D 6683 [8]) 

The bulk density varies with several factors like:  moisture content, particle size and shape, temperature, particle elasticity, etc.  This flow property is used to calculate the storage capacity in a bin/silo/hopper/stockpile, in the calculations of the minimum outlet dimensions to prevent flow problems, bin loads and the capacity of conveying equipment such as feeders, belt conveyors, screw feeders, bucket elevators, etc. 

#### **Permeability** 

Permeability of bulk solids is the ability of the material to allow flow of air between particles and to become aerated and/or fluidized.  This property depends on the characteristics of the material (like particle size and shape, moisture content and temperature) and the degree of compaction of the material.  Generally, dry fine and dust 

303 



materials present a high resistance to allow air passing through particles which may challenge control of the d

ischarge flow rate. 

This property can be defined with Darcy´s law [3-4] and the permeability factor, K (Equation 3), is determined in a fluidized column (see Figure 8) where the drop pressure per height (ΔP/H) necessary to aerate and/or fluidize the material is measured as a function of the air velocity, U (Equation 4).  The coefficients α, γo and Ko, in Equation 3, are empiric.  The relation between the permeability factor, K, as function of the bulk density, γ, is reflected in a straight line in a log-log graph. 



Figure 8 – Fluidized column for permeability test 

Generally, fine materials (like dusts from electrostatic precipitators or fine dry copper concentrates) tend to present a limited flow discharge rate and the measurement of the compressibility and permeability properties allow to determine if the deaerated material presents a critical flow discharge rate by gravity for a combination of effective height (consolidation pressure) and bin outlet size.  To overcome a critical flow discharge rate problem the bin outlet size can be increased or the material may be aerated and/or fluidized. 

#### **Wear** 

Wear can be present in industrial equipment due to abrasive (see Figure 9) and/or impact mechanisms, especially when handling hard and abrasive materials like copper ores, and can become a costly problem [4]. 

This property can be affected by the hardness of the particles, particles size and shape, moisture content, particle velocity and pressure against the wall, temperature and corrosion [3,9].  It can be measured by sliding or impact test and the results allow to determine the most suitable wall lining material for specific applications, such wall hoppers and feeders [9]. 

304 



Figure 9 – Abrasive wall wear example in a hopper 

#### **Segregation** 

Bulk solids with wide particle size distribution tend to separate or segregate when handling and discharging in industrial processes [10].  The most common segregation mechanism is sifting (see Figure 10); where fine particles tend to concentrate under the discharge outlet, while the coarser particles tend to roll aside around the pile.  In certain applications segregation can be present when fine particles remain aerated at the top of the silo, while coarse particles deaerate quickly and settle at the bottom.  There are other mechanisms depending on the application; nevertheless all of them can cause waste of products and/or raw materials, increased maintenance, low equipment efficiency, deficient quality of the products and higher capital costs.  This phenomenon can be affected by particle size, shape and distribution, moisture content, cohesiveness, flow pattern developed in the handling equipment, vibrations, magnetic and electrostatic effects, etc. 



Figure 10 – Sifting segregation example in a 2D slice demonstrator model (Reproduced from Cabrejos and del Campo [10]) 

In the mining industry, the major concentration of the fine particles in outlets can cause among others:

formation of cohesive arches (in silos) and “ratholes” (in 305 stockpiles), increment of the energy consumption in mills (because of the fluctuations of the particle size distribution), poor copper recovery from agglomerated ore in the leaching process (due to the low permeation of the pregnant solution). These issues can be minimized or prevented by changing the process, modifying the material, or adequately dimensioning the equipment (according to the flow properties of the materials) in order to develop a mass flow pattern [10]. #### **Angle of Chute** The measurement of the minimum inclination to maintain the flow of the materials after impact, onto a flat wall surface, allows to correctly designs transfer chutes between belts in the mining industry. This angle is called “angle of chute” and is function of the impact pressure and the wall roughness; it can be determined with the chute test (see Figure 11). Figure 11 – Operation and generic results of the chute test #### **Angle of Repose and Drawdown** The angle of repose is the inclination of the heap formed by the material when is piled over a flat surface, whereas the angle of drawdown is the inclination of the stagnant material left in a stockpile or flat bottom silo after its discharge (see Figure 12). These angles don’t provide information about the flowability of the materials; however they are important to calculate the storage capacity in bins, silos, hopper and stockpiles. Bulk solids have the ability to withstand shear stresses in repose, which explains the angle of repose formation. The measurement of the angle of repose is normally wrongly associated to the flowability of the material and it is a device/operator dependant test with poor repeatability [6]. Angle of repose values normally vary between 35o and 40o (measured from the horizontal), whereas the drawdown angle depends on the cohesive strength and can vary between 35o (for easy flowing materials) and up to 90o (for cohesive materials forming ratholes). Figure 12 shows pictures taken in drawdown tests, with a 2D slice demonstrative model, for crushed ore and agglomerate copper ore at different moisture contents. According to the flowability classification in Figure 4, the material in photos (a) and (b) is easy flowing, while the material in photos (c) and (d) is cohesive; in the last two 306 pictures, it can be seen the tendency of the cohesive material to form “ratholes and cohesive arches respectively. Note: Due to the small consolidating pressures involved, the aim of this test is only to illustrate the discharge behaviour of the materials rather than getting a definitive measurement of these angles for design purposes. ## **CONCLUSIONS** 

This paper presents the main flow properties of the bulk solids that affect the storage and handling of products in industrial mining equipment. Besides it describes a scientific well proven approach (available from late 60´s) to measure these properties in a laboratory; in order to allow the design of storage equipment (like bins, silos, hoppers, stockpiles, ore passes, chutes, feeders, rotary valves, belt conveyors, screw feeders, bucket elevators, pneumatic conveyors, etc.), with well determined live capacities and reliable and controlled discharge flow rates. 

The measurement and result interpretation of the material flow properties can provide the correct design of the equipment to avoid flow problems, which if unsolved could lead to decrease the production capacities, and/or high maintenance and production costs, caused by flow blockages, segregation, uncontrolled discharge, equipment wear, inoperative equipment, production delays, etc.  Equipment design is unique for each 

307 

material handling application and operating conditions, because each material behaves differently depending on its properties, characteristics, composition and nature. 

The measurement of cohesiveness and frictional properties provides the equipment storage design parameters, whereas properties like compressibility and permeability help to predict the discharge rates.  Other properties like wear, segregation, angle of repose and drawdown and angle of chute, can provide important insight for reliable handling of bulk solids in the mining industrial operations.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The use of slurry impoundments have traditionally been the primary method of disposal of waste slurry resulting from the recovery of metals and minerals. However, current difficulties in obtaining permits to build new impoundments for grassroots plants, or as the existing ones near the end of their projected life, have made it necessary to explore other alternatives for tailings disposal. Fresh water resources are becoming more precious, and environmental pressures are increasing leading to the elimination of slurry tailings impoundments. 

It is becoming more prudent to consider filtration and dry stacking as a reasonable and sustainable alternative. There are several obstacles to filtration as a way to treat these tailings. Many tailings slurries are difficult to filter and higher plant throughputs have in the past made filtration operations both costly to buy and to operate. 

But as with the equipment used to mine and move the harder lower grade ores, equipment to process the resulting tailings slurries have increased in size, efficiency, and capacity to meet the demand, as well as to reduce the number of people needed to operate them. This paper discusses the technical and financial considerations, OPEX and CAPEX, that influence equipment selection and optimization of the filtration system to produce a satisfactory, transportable and stackable tailings product. Multiple tailings samples have been investigated incorporating lab and pilot scale testing. The impact of different minerologies and grain size will be discussed.

#### <u>Closure and Reclamation Costs</u> 

A typical mine closure plan includes the rehabilitation of the TSF, which requires capping, covering, revegetation, and monitoring of the TSF to ensure it is safe and nonpolluting. Discharging higher solids content tailings reduces the volume of tailings that must be deposited as well as allowing steeper beach angles; the size of the TSF is reduced as the density of the tailings increases. For filtered tailings, progressive reclamation of the TSF can begin while still in operation, which can further reduce closure costs. If a bond has been required to obtain the TSF permit, it may be possible to draw upon the bond as the TSF is progressively reclaimed. This can add another revenue stream to the mine. 

#### **Filtration** 

There are many filtration options for dewatering tailings prior to disposal. The three major categories of filtration equipment employed are vacuum filters, belt presses and filter presses. Each type of filter has unique advantages and disadvantages. In every case, it is always recommended that the filter feed slurry be thickened prior to filtration. Thickening of the filter feed will substantially reduce capital and operating costs of the filtration operation. 

#### <u>Vacuum Filters</u> 

Vacuum filters have been used for tailings dewatering since the 1970’s. This type of filter is continuous in its operation, which leads to a less complicated material handling interface. This filter produces a non saturated filter cake, meaning that the void spaces inside the filter cake are not saturated with filtrate and contain some air. The driving force for filtration is generated by vacuum source, meaning the difference between atmospheric pressure and absolute 0 pressure is the maximum driving force available for filtration. At sea level a vacuum filter can only achieve 0.8 bar driving force and at high altitude, such as in the Atacama Desert less than 0.4 bar of pressure differential can be generated. As the driving force for filtration is reduced the performance of the filter is reduced. Vacuum filters are not usually recommended for use above 2,500 meters above sea level.

Figure 2 – Horizontal Belt Vacuum Filter 

Vacuum filters have many different configurations with disc and horizontal belt, shown in Figure 2, being the most common in minerals applications. Disc filters are commonly used for smaller tonnage underground paste backfill operations. For large tonnage surface tailings disposal horizontal belt filters are the most common type of vacuum filter used, shown in Figure 2. The largest horizontal belt filter tailings disposal site in operation is the La Coipa mine in Chile which operates nominally at 20,000 tons per day and has operated since 1990. 

The feed to a horizontal belt filter can either be pumped or gravity fed directly onto the top of the fi

lter cloth. In either case, care must be taken that the incoming feed energy is dissipated and that the slurry is evenly distributed across the entire width of the filter, which can be as wide as 6.5 meters. The filter cloth is transported down the length of the filter by a rubber drainage belt. While the feed slurry is being distributed onto the filter, the vacuum is applied to the slurry to form the filter cake. After the cake is formed additional filtration time is allowed to pull air through the filter cake further dewatering it before the filter cloth reaches the end of the filter. The filtrate from the cake is collected and transported away from the filter. As the filter cloth reaches the end of the filter the cake is discharged. The filter cloth is washed continuously to maintain its porosity.

#### <u>Belt Presses</u> 

Belt filter presses, shown in Figure 3, have been used extensively for small tonnage tailings dewatering since the 1980’s. This type of pressure filter, originally developed for the sewage industry, also has the advantage of being a continuous operation. The disadvantage of a belt press is that it is limited in size and therefore only suitable for small tonnage operations. Belt filter presses produce a higher moisture, saturated, filter cake and require pre-treatment of the tailings slurry with expensive flocculating agents. The typical maximum driving forces are around 0.8 bar which are produced by tensioning a filter cloth around rolls. Higher pressures can be achieved using nip rolls at the end of the filter. This driving force is similar to a vacuum filter, but unlike a vacuum filter no air is drawn through the cake, meaning it always produces a saturated filter cake, and the 0.8 bar driving force is not impacted by changes in altitude. Machines are supplied in widths of up to 3 meters, with capacities of between 5 and 15 TPH of dry solids per meter of width producing a cake with a moisture content between 30-35 wt%. 



Figure 3 – Belt Filter Press 

The belt filter press feed, which is pumped from the feed tank to the belt press, contains the solids which have been flocculated in the feed line between the feed tank and the filter, and are starting to agglomerate. The associated water is being displaced and separated. The pre-treated slurry then reports to the feed distribution box, where it is distributed across the full width of the machine. The first part of the filter is a gravity drainage zone, where the separated water can freely drain through a moving porous filter 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

cloth. At the end of the gravity drainage section, the deposit of fine solids and residual water is then sandwiched between the original porous filter cloth and a second cloth. The sandwich of solids between the two clothes then passes through a series of decreasing diameter rollers, where the cake is formed and dewatered by compression. The t

wo filter cloths are eventually separated and the dewatered product is discharged continuously as a stackable cake. The two filter cloths are separately washed by high pressure water to remove any entrained solids, prior to re-engaging with the raw feed slurry. Filtrate from the press and used spray water are collected in a sump and re-cycled to the tailings thickener. 

The number of “squeeze” roller pairs and the pressure applied to these rolls will determine the degree of dewatering achieved and is usually determined by test-work. [3] The saturated filter cake that is discharged can be sticky in nature. These sticky cakes can plug transfer chutes and stick to the conveyors causing material handling issues. The saturated filter cakes will also have poor geotechnical properties. 

#### <u>Filter Press</u> 

The advantage of a filter press, see Figure 4, is that it can achieve much higher driving forces compared to a vacuum filter or a belt press. Most pressure filters today will reach a driving force of 15 bar or greater. The disadvantage of a filter press is the batch type process which it uses. The batch discharge of filter cakes can lead to complications in the design of the downstream material handling equipment in installation with multiple filters. The feed to the filter press is pumped from a buffer tank, which has sufficient capacity to allow a constant flow from the tailings thickener, during the batch filtration process. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

315 



Figure 4 – Filter Press 

The pumping of the feed slurry under pressure, into the chambers/cloths, provides the force to build a cake within the chamber. As the cakes form, the pressure to produce a properly compacted cake rises steadily. Most filter presses on tailings applications operate with up to a 15 bar driving force. This driving force can easily be reached using just the feed pumps to the filter. Optionally, filter press can be filled with a lower pressure feed pump and the terminal pressure inside the filter press chambers can be reached by the use of inflatable membranes. Membranes should only be used if the filter cake is compressible. However, hard rock tailings cakes are not compressible and inflatable membranes are, therefore, not required. After the cake is formed high pressure air, in the range of 7 to 10 bar, can be blown through the cake to further reduce its moisture content and produce a non-saturated cake. 

At the end of the filtration cycle the filter press closing mechanism is opened and the plates are discharged by an automatic plate shifting mechanism. Depending on the type of plate shifting mechanism the plates can be opened in a manner ranging from individually to all the plates in one operation. Due to the size and number of plates used in modern filter presses this opening and discharge cycle can take from 1 minute up to 30 Minutes. Filtrate from the press is collected by a “bomb bay door” style under-pan, which retracts before the

dewatered cake is discharged. Filtrate reports to a sump and is returned to the plant tailings thickener. To maintain fully automatic operation it is recommended that the filter plates are shaken and washed every cycle to maintain cloth _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 316 porosity and remove any residual cake, which could cause closing obstructions. In most modern installations, prior to discharging the cake, the “sticky” core of unfiltered feed from the center feed ports is removed by an influx of compressed air. This assists in reducing cake moisture, and contributes to keeping the units in good operational condition. The cycle time is the entire time required to produce one batch of filter cake and ready the filter for another batch. The filtration cycle times on hard rock flotation tailings vary considerably as feed characteristics vary and the amount of cake blowing time required to meet geotechnical requirements vary, but they usually range between 6 and 20 minutes. Automatic filter presses, such as the FLS automatic filter press (AFP), minimize the cycle times and maximize production rates. In all filters of this type the cake is formed by the capture of solids on filter cloths which encapsulate the filter chambers. The press is closed by means of hydraulic cylinders and the multiple plates, which when closed, form the chambers that the filter cake is captured in. Chamber thicknesses are generally from 32mm to 50mm. Plate dimensions have a filtration area of up to 8 m2 per plate, in stacks of up to 200 Chambers. The plates are supported by either a single or dual overhead beams, or sidebars. The moisture of the discharged filter press cake is in the range of 10 to 25 wt% and can be either saturated or unsaturated depending on the filter design and geotechnical requirements. Depending on the mineralogy and particle size distribution, the discharged cakes can be sticky in nature or crumbly. The nature of the discharged cake will significantly impact the operation of the downstream material handling equipment. #### – <u>Plate Design No Membranes Required</u> 

If the cake formed in the filtration chamber is not uniform, from top to bottom and from side to side, in terms of solids compaction and particle size distribution the cake produced will be sloppy and wet. Furthermore, if compressed air is used in an attempt to dewater a poorly formed cake the air flow will not be uniform across the cake again producing a sloppy wet cake. A non uniform cake also does not transfer the filtration loads evenly through the filter plate stack. This can cause breakage of the filter plates and the filter plates can be expensive to replace. Inflating membranes on the plate can compensate for forming a non homogeneous cake by at least ensuring a consolidated cake is formed. 

Feed port location can have significant impact on cake homogeneity in applications where solids densities a

re high, like in hard rock tailings. For hard rock tailings it is important that the chamber is fed in such a way as to promote the formation of the cake in layers over the entire filtration surface simultaneously. This will ensure that particles are evenly distributed and compacted. To accomplish this usually means that the chamber needs to be fed at a fairly high rate in order to create sufficient turbulence to prevent stratification of particles. 

Feeding a filter chamber from an elevated position can promote a cake which is non-uniformly formed and compacted with stratified particles creating a nonhomogeneous filter cake.

Operating costs for a filtered tailings facility are typically broken down between the filter building and the material handling system. For the filter building operating cost input parameters are manpower costs, electrical costs, and maintenance costs. As long as the cloth wash water is reclaimed and reused, water costs are negligible for a filtered tailings facility. Assuming an average manpower cost of $25 per hour, an electrical cost of $0.10/KWhr, an FLSmidth AFP filtered tailings facility will have a total operating cost between $0.30/ton and $0.35/ton of solids. This can also be expressed in terms of costs per m<sup>3</sup> of water recovered. If the feed solids to the filter plant are 55 wt% solids, this range expressed in m<sup>3</sup> of water is $0.55/m<sup>3</sup> and $0.60/m<sup>3</sup> . This compares very favorably with typical water costs in Chile of between $3/ m<sup>3</sup> and $5/ m<sup>3</sup> .

#### **CONCLUSION** 

As high grade ore bodies are mined and depleted, low ore grades are mined and increase the amoun

t of water required to process the ore and the amount tailings that must be stored. There are many drivers towards dry tailings storage; among them are the lack and cost of water and land, reclamation responsibilities, environmental legislation, permitting, and wet tailings legacy liability. The wet tailings impoundments also suffer from high evaporation rates. The industry sees that the dry tailings process will increase with new operations especially those situated in desert environments and areas where land available for tailings storage is a constraining factor and the cost of water is high. Filter presses are usually chosen for filtering tailings and can recover up to 90 – 95% of the recoverable process water required modern concentrator. Filtered tailings generally need a smaller footprint for storage area. 

As with the equipment used to mine and move the harder lower grade ores, equipment to process the resulting tailings slurries have increased in size, efficiency, and capacity to meet the demand, as well as to reduce the number of people needed to operate them. Pressure filters with active filtration areas of over 2000 m<sup>2</sup> per filter which can process up to 20,000 tons per day of hard rock tailings and produce an 85 wt% solid cake are now available. Average capital costs range between $7 and $8 million dollars per filter system, including accessory equipment. Including installation costs, the range is $14 to $16 million dollars per filter system which competitive with the cost of installing a tailings dam. Operating costs for this same filtration system can be as low as $ 0.30/ton and $0.35/ton on a solids basis or $0.55/m3 and 0.60/m3 of water recovered. These costs compare very favorably with typical water costs in Chile of between $3/ m<sup>3</sup> and $5/ m<sup>3</sup> .

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The concern regarding grinding media consumption rates is as old as the invention of the tumbling mill. Over the years many materials and grinding media shapes have been tested. Through all this, steel grinding balls have proved to be the most effective media for comminution in tumbling mills. There have been several approaches to be able to the wear

of the ball charge in any given mill, all of them based on limited empirical evidence. The mining industry still utilizes the Bond Abrasion test that was developed in the 1960´s. As shown later in this publication, this approach shows error greater than 60%. 

More recently, in 2007, Radziszewski from Mc Gill University has proposed a different total grinding media wear model; this model is based on decoupling the effects of the abrasion, corrosion and impact wear mechanisms. Also in 2007, Benavente, at the time with Moly-Cop Peru, presented an empirical model relating both ore properties and operational conditions that would affect the wear performance of the grinding media. For the database referred in this article, Benavente’s model shows an average error of ± 12% which represents a higher degree of improvement in comparison with previous approaches. 

The current paper presents recent research conducted by Moly-Cop Peru to further improve the capability of the empirical model originally developed by Benavente to estimate grinding media wear rates. The work performed included extensive determinations of the Bond Abrasion Index for different types of ores, collected at industrial grinding applications where the corresponding operational information was made available. The results of the research enabled us to build a more robust and confident model for estimating the grinding media wear rate. The average error of this new model is in the order of ± 9% which is a significant improvement over the models previously described.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Reclaim tunnels are large structures of reinforced concrete located under mineral stockpiles whose purpose is protecting pieces of equipment used for distributing such mineral to other downstream processes; reclaim tunnels are characterized by: 

- Permanent soil-structure interaction. 

- Capacity to withstand high static loads associated to mineral stockpiles. 

- High transverse rigidity in any direction given by its box-like transverse shape consisting of a foundation mat, walls, and upper plate with openings. 

- Reduced mechanical design of internal space.

#### **NORMATIVE ASPECTS** 

#### **Design** 

Even though Supreme Decree (SD) N° 60 states that the design of any concrete structure must abide by this decree and by Code ACI 318-08 (see Article N° 1 of the decree), this instruction is in direct contradiction with the provisions under Code ACI 318-08 (USA Code applied together with the above Chilean Norm) in matters related to the structural system associated to the tunnel and its validity of use. The reason is that ACI 318 conditions its application to the design of that structure, as long as it has been assigned a high seismic design behavior or category (item 1.1.6 of that Code). However, this structural system does not fall within the structural systems that must meet a special seismic design (see items and their comments: item 21.2.1.2, Art. N° 3, SDN° 60 and 1.2 of the Norm NCh2369 of 2003, _Earthquake Resistant Design of Industrial Structures and Facilities_ ) nor it requires a certain ductile behavior, considering its characteristics. 

Thus, the above raises some confusion when decisions must be made in relation with the design of reclaim tunnels and, eventually, SD Nº60 and Code ACI 318 must be used instead of the recommendations made under Chapter 21 in both norms. 

#### <u>Loads associated to mineral stockpiling</u> 

The great disparity between load factors when applied to the 2 loads associated to mineral have made it necessary to review normative aspects before a category was assigned to both of them

. The maximum mineral load (𝐶max⁡_𝑀) has a wellestablished limit (using variables such as bulk density, the maximum stockpile height and the angle of repose of stockpiled material, defined by specialists from other disciplines). Since neither the SDN°60 nor the ACI318 or ASCE7 Codes contain precise descriptions to define the concept of that load, a description was found in the NCh 2369 Code that fits the description of that load. That standard contains a partial definition stating that the action whose variation tends to a limit load is defined as permanent ( _D_ ). Given the above, the maximum mineral load should be classified as a permanent load of special application, not as a load associated to bulk material, given the difference in accuracy resulting in the calculation process. Due to its static nature and its frequent, not negligible variations in relation to its means value, the mineral operation load ( _C_ Op __M_ ) is a live load.

#### **CONCLUSIONS & COMMENTARIES** 

- Both of the proposed load states associated to stockpiled mineral (maximum and mineral operation loads) as well as the load distributions suggested for the structural design offer a load level which is consistent with the analysis conducted by academics and experts and with designs working flawlessly to date considering, also, how the stockpile is generated and how it operates. 

- The use of methodologies to obtain the seismic increase of LEP of the tunnel side fill such as: the Mononobe Okabe variant, the Norm NCh 433 and, for rigid walls of the Highway Manual, as long as applicable, are good only for the pre-design phase. For detail engineering, specific applications for the kinematic method project should be used or expressions obtained from FEM (Finite elements modeling) of soil and structure. 

- The way in which the design of these or similar types of works are to be addressed should be explicitly mentioned, at least, in the commentary sections of eventual issues of the NCh 2369 or other norms; otherwise the interpretation is left to the engineer and possible reviewers. 

- The definitions of loads associated to the side fill LEP should be reviewed in future editions of Norms NCh 433, 2369 and 3171 and also ensure these are in line with international Codes more widely used. The above finds justification on two important facts: LEPs not associated to overloads are classified as permanent loads ( _D_ ) in the two first Codes while in other USA Codes any static LEP receives the same classification ( _

H_ ). In the third Code, LEP seismic increases are classified just as static LEPs ( _H_ ) while for USA Codes any load increase caused by a seismic event is categorized as a seismic load ( _E_ ). All the above might create confusion when deciding on load combinations. 

- Promote the use of package bars, a thorough detailing, and the use of 3D assembly sequence schemes to prevent problems in the construction process, both in concrete pouring and insert installation. It should be noted that paragraph 7.6.6.6, Section N°.3 of SD No.60 does not allow the use of package bars in elements where reinforcement bars may enter the plastic range or where it may be subjected to seismic internal forces (push-pull). However, both for loads applied as well as for the consideration of a proper detailing, this restriction would not apply to the reclaim tunnel. 

- Whether or not the above recommendations are followed, the consequences will be reflected in the CAPEX associated to the reclaim tunnel of that specific mining project. These recommendations will benefit: material takeoff (to be assessed due to considerations on punching shear resistance reduction); construction and repair times for occurrence of sections to be concreted (nests).

- Promote the protection of exposed concrete without insert protection with the help of a sand bed since, in the stockpile generation process, the first layers of crushed mineral fall from important heights damaging unprotected concrete surface. 

- Make efforts to equip a reclaim tunnel with load cells in order to verify the expressions associated to mineral loads under the stockpile contained in a number of scale studies and modelings but, basically, to check how that load would behave in a seismic event. In this case, the use of a sand bed becomes more important to protect the load cells.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

In an effort to recover additional copper and gold at KGHM International’s Robinson Mine located near Ruth, Nevada, an in-plant study was undertaken to quantify potential flotation recoveries from the concentrator’s final tailings stream. Tests were conducted by passing a small continuous sample of final tailings though a single 1.5 m<sup>3</sup> demonstration flotation machine. Two phases of testing were conducted on differing ore types. Results indicated that up to 30% of the contained copper was recoverable along with significant quantities of gold. Based on these results, the existing flotation circuit was expanded by installing four (4) 160 m<sup>3</sup> FLSmidth _XCELL_ ™ flotation machines to treat the final tailings stream. This paper reviews the results obtained from the in-plant testing with the single 1.5 m<sup>3</sup> flotation cell and provides a comparison to the subsequent operational performance of multiple 160 m<sup>3</sup> flotation machines.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The Robinson Mine and concentra

tor are located near Ely, Nevada about 400 kilometers north of Las Vegas, Nevada, USA. Multiple ores bodies have been historically mined in the Robinson Mineral District.  The ore bodies are typically highly faulted with varying degrees of alteration. Currently, the Robinson Operation is mining porphyry-skarn deposits with leach cap, supergene, and hypogene mineralizations, Figure 1. The Robinson ores are quite complex posing considerable metallurgical challenges. Copper is the primary value along with byproduct gold and molybdenum. Copper-gold concentrates produced at Robinson are transported by truck from the mine site about 210 km to East Wendover, Utah. The concentrate is then railed to west coast port facilities for sea transport. 



Figure 1.  KGHM International's Robinson Mine—Ruth Pit 

Run of mine ore is transported to a single 54 inch (1.37 m) primary crusher via 220 tonne haul trucks. The ore ball mill bond work index ranges from 8.5 to 12.5 kWhr/tonne.  Stockpiled, crushed ore is fed to a 32’ x 15’ (9.8 m x 4.6 m) SAG mill at a rate of about 44,000 metric tons per day.  The SAG mill discharge is further ground with two 20’ x 31’ (6.1 m x 9.4 m) ball mills operated in closed circuit producing flotation feeds with a 106 micron P65.  Prior to the investigation described in this paper, the flotation circuit consisted of twenty, 85 m3 roughers, single stage cleaning with six 3.0 m dia. columns, six, 42 m3 mechanical cleaner-scavengers, and a four-stage moly circuit. A photo of the stockpile and concentrator is provided in Figure 2.

In an effort to increase recovery, the Robinson Mine investigated the feasibility of treating the concentrator’s final tailings with large scavenger flotation cells.
