Because of FLSmidth’s proximity to the plant, the promising new _XCELL_ ™ flotation technology and the ready availability of a 1.5 m<sup>3</sup> _XCELL_ ™ flotation machine for pilot testing, FLSmidth was invited to exclusively participate in the study. 

The FLSmidth _XCELL_ ™ flotation machine used in this study is a relatively new technology.  It is a forced-air machine characterized by a unique low profile rotor and a compact caged stator. Unlike traditional forced-air flotation machines, both the rotor and stator are located in the center of the cell.  In addition to the mid rotor and stator position, the flotation mechanism features a velocity cone, a draft tube, a vortex breaker, and a froth crowder.  The flotation tank has full depth mixing baffles, external launders, and radial launders when appropriate, see Figure 3. This unique patented design provides for relatively high slurry velocities which are very effective at lifting coarse particles into the stator volume or contact region where bubble-particle contact primarily occurs. Th

e specific energy within the contact region (14 kW/m<sup>3</sup> ) is among the highest in the mechanical flotation cell industry.  This high contact region specific energy promotes turbulence which increases the probability of fine particle-bubble attachment. 

The genius of the _XCELL_ ™ design is that the unique energy distribution and exceptional hydrodynamic characteristics are produced efficiently with overall energy consumption being some of the very lowest in the mechanical flotation cell industry. The combined specific energy for the _XCELL_ ™ flotation mechanism plus energy to operate the required process air blower is typically 0.7 kW/m<sup>3</sup> .

#### **FEASIBILITY TESTING** 

The objective of the test program was to quantify how much copper and gold could be recovered from Robinson’s final tailings stream. A plant-wide material balance based on average 2007 metallurgical performance shows considerable copper values in the concentrator final tailings stream, as shown in Figure 4.

In an effort to determine how much of the contained copper in the final tailings was recoverable, Robinson installed the FLSmidth demonstration _XCELL™_ flotation unit in the lower level of the concentrator, shown in Figure 5. The in-plant test program was comprised of two test campaigns that were conducted simultaneously—Baseline Testing and a Design of Experiments (DOE) campaign, Montgomery [1]. Both test campaigns were conducted by pumping a sample stream of final tailings as feed to the demonstration flotation machine at feed rates ranging from 20 to 39 m<sup>3</sup> /hr. #### **SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS** 

The 1.5 m3 pilot and 160 m3 _XCELL_ ™ flotation machines effectively recovered copper and gold from the Robinson final tailings. 

Average results from baseline and DOE test campaigns were in good agreement and showed that about 30% of the contained copper was recoverable and concentrates of 12–15% copper could be produced. 

The DOE test campaign produced a highly reliable Copper Tailings Grade Model. This model predicted a 27% average copper recovery at the test campaign feed conditions. Based on this average recovery, about 5.5 million kg of additional copper production was projected to be recoverable from treating the final tailings stream. 

After installation and commissioning of the _XCELL_ ™ plant, actual operational data validated the performance of the predictive model and pilot cell testing. The fullscale flotation plant achieved a 27.1% recovery over a three-year period. The added recovery has increased copper production by 5.95 million kg annually and gold by a significant but undisclosed amount.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Several hydrometallurgical processes for high and moderate pressure leaching of copper sulfides have been developed in the past years, such as the Total Pressure Oxidation, Sepon, Platsol, Mt. Gordon, AAC/UBC, Dynatec, CESL, Activox and MT-DEW-SX processes. Nowadays, several are under industrial scale application, or well tested at pilot scale level. 

The basics and current status of these processes is briefly reviewed, with special consideration on their applicability to the leaching of different copper ores, depending on its sulfide mineralogy and occurrence of impurities such as arsenic and the presence of other valuable metals. A comparison of the general conditions in the autoclave leaching for each process is presented, and a decision tree is proposed for a simple choice of the best technology for a given application from a process point of view, before proceeding to perform feasibility study.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The intensive exploitation of copper deposits has produced a sustainable depletion of high grade copper resources, leading the industry to research and develop new process and techniques for economic profit of low grade minerals. 

Heap leaching has not been able to economically process primary sulfides as chalcopyrite, despite the long years of research and process development. Leaching in chloride media has shown advantages to leach secondary sulfides, but it has not been successful to process primary sulfides yet. Also special attention has to be put to corrosion aspects when chloride media is used. 

Biohydrometallurgical process also has presented low recoveries from primary copper sulfides, particularly chalcopyrite, even extended heap leach cycles are used. Other atmospheric technologies like Galvanox and Geocoat have not been successful neither technically nor economically to leach low-grade primary sulfide copper ores. 

The increasing environmental restrictions for smelting, and the growing difficulties in power generation make necessary an alternative process-route to smelter for copper sulfide concentrates. Particularly critic is the case of arsenic (As) bearing copper concentrates. The smelting process forms hazardous arsenic oxide dusts and fumes that are difficult to manage and stabilize for safe disposal in the sulfuric acid plant. Arsenic is also distributed to the matte, and consequently to final anodes, thus difficulting the production of high quality cathodes in the electro refinery. Typically, mining companies incur in penalties for selling concentrates with As contents above 0.2%, and the smelter rejection limits are close to 0.5%. 

The pressure leaching of copper concentrates in autoclave seems to be an option and some plants have been constructed and are successfully operating. This paper summariz

es the basics on autoclave leaching chemistry, and the current status of the main processes developed for pressure leaching of copper sulfides. A decisional diagram is given to define the best option for a certain concentrate as function of its copper sulfide composition, occurrence of impurities, presence of other valuable metals, and the chances for profit/neutralize high acid production. 

#### **AUTOCLAVE LEACHING CHEMISTRY** 

High pressure leaching of concentrates is performed in autoclaves pressurized by oxygen. These units permit to operate at temperatures over 100ºC, enhancing the leaching kinetics of the minerals. Chemical reactions are similar to those occurring at atmospheric leaching, but some considerations must be done [1] 

Taking chalcopyrite as example, leaching reaction at atmospheric pressure is 

4𝐶𝑢𝐹𝑒𝑆2 + 13𝑂2 + 2𝐻2𝑆𝑂4 →4𝐶𝑢𝑆𝑂4 + 4𝐹𝑒𝑆𝑂4 + 2𝑆<sup>0</sup> + 2𝐻2𝑂 (1) 

Under pressure, high oxygen concentration and temperature produces a fast ferrous sulfate oxidation to ferric sulfate, and at temperatures over 120ºC, ferric sulfate starts to precipitate mainly as hematite, according to 

𝐹𝑒2(SO4)3 + 3H2O →Fe2O3 + 3H2SO4 (2) 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

372 

High temperature may produce complete sulfide oxidation, according to 

4𝐶𝑢𝐹𝑒𝑆2 + 17O2 + 4H2O →4CuSO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 4H2SO4 (3) 

At temperatures above the sulfur melting point (119ºC), and below 180200ºC, a considerable portion of sulfide is converted to molten elemental sulfur, according to 

4𝐶𝑢𝐹𝑒𝑆2 + 5O2 + 4H2SO4 →4CuSO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8S<sup>0</sup> + 4H2O (4) 

When temperature is increased near 200ºC, almost all sulfur is oxidized according to Eq (3). 

It is important to note that oxygen consumption in Eq (4) is only 30% of the oxygen consumed according to Eq (3), and that Eq (4) is an acid consuming reaction, while Eq (3) is an acid producer reaction. This drives the acid balance in the autoclave, depending on pressure and temperature conditions. 

Operating the autoclave with molten sulfur is difficult because it tends to spread over the sulfide mineral surfaces, forming “prills” that blocks the reactive surfaces. Also prill formation can interfere with the material transport throughout the vessel and its discharge out [1]. 

Sulfur viscosity increases dramatically with temperatures above 160ºC, reaching a maximum value at 185-188 ºC [1]. This practical constraint makes difficult to operate in the range 160-190ºC, and leads to define as medium pressuretemperature process those close to 160ºC, and high pressure-temperature process those around 200ºC. 

The autoclave equipment commonly operates in a range of 10-15% solids load, which means a flow of raffinate solution or fresh water must be fed to keep the water balance. Lower solid percent is limited by the mineralogy of the concentrate, given that enough energy is needed for the autogenous operation in the autoclave. 

#### **As precipitation** 

The smelting of As-bearing concentrates produces arsenic

trioxide (As2O3) in the flue gas which has to be treated before released to atmosphere. Hydrometallurgical processing produces acid solutions with As in the form of arsenates (AsO4<sup>3-</sup> ), which can be stabilized as scorodite (FeAsO4·2H2O, Equation 5), a highly crystalline compound, which is the most stable As form and presents good thickening and filtration properties, thus permitting a safe tailing disposal. 



Scorodite is naturally formed in As-containing solutions with ferric content, and is very stable when is formed at temperatures above 120°C and pressures over 10 atm. Chloride content in solution has minor effect in scorodite formation, which can reach about 99% As yield in the autoclave. This converts autoclave leaching in a valuable option for As-bearing concentrates, where As stabilization is performed together with copper extraction.

#### **Precious metals (PM) dissolution** 

Dissolution of precious metals (PM), namely Au, Ag or Platinum group metals (PGM), is scarce in sulfate media. Au and Ag are practically insoluble in absence of a proper complexing agent, such as thiocyanate (SCN<sup>-</sup> ), thiourea (SC(NH2)2) or chloride in acidic media, while PGM are present in refractory ores which frequently requires very aggressive conditions, or increased residence time in autoclave to dissolve and release these elements into solution [2,3]. 

#### **HIGH PRESSURE PROCESS** 

#### **Total pressure oxidation process** 

"Total pressure oxidation process" (TPO) comprises those processes in which sulfur oxidation is completely performed at high pressure and temperature, close to 30 atm and 225ºC, to oxidize all sulfide minerals to sulfates and sulfuric acid [3]. 

Complete oxidation of sulfide minerals involves high cost due to the high oxygen consumption (Equation 4), and consequently, a high acid production occurs. This option has to be considered when acid is required in other part of the processchain, such as the secondary heap leaching, that may reduce the acid contents to the level required by conventional SX. If this extra acid is not used, then an extra cost for acid neutralization must be added. The precipitates resulting from neutralization, together with the hematite, jarosite or scorodite, can be recovered with the non dissolved mineral fraction, by S/L separations, and further processed if PM are present in the concentrate, which are expected to remain in the residue [2,3]. 

TPO facilities have operated since 1950’s in the US for processing of concentrates of cobalt, nickel and copper, so this is not a new development [4] The Phelps Dodge Bagdad pilot plant in Arizona, operates in 2003 producing about 16,000 t/year of Cu from chalcopyrite concentrates, ground at P80 about 40 µm [5], with an autoclave discharge of 30 g/L copper, with 50 g/L de free acid and 1.8 g/L Fe. The large excess of acid is sent to a stockpile leach [2,3,6].

Nevertheless, the fact that up to date it has not been applied in a pilot-plant status, and that the aggressive conditions applied involves high capital and operation costs, makes the choice of PLATSOL technology a high risk decision. 

In case of As-free concentrates, for secondary sulfides Mt. Gordon is a cheap process because its low aggressive autoclave conditions, but if the concentrate has a High ANC, an autoclave process for higher acid generation, like Sepon or PLATSOL, is required. 

For primary sulfides without As or PGM; TOP, CESL or MT-DEW-SX processes can be considered. If the concentrate has a high ANC, or there is an acid requirement by a side-project, TOP can be applied. Instead, if acid generation is a problem, CESL or MT-DEW-SX can be chosen. 

MT-DEW-SX, is a process without chloride addition, with very strict milling requirements (p80 7 µm), and an acid production in autoclave which permits the use of Direct EW. Nevertheless, the acid production is not as high as for TOP.  Instead, CESL is a chloride leaching process (which permits the use of seawater), that operates at a higher particle size in autoclave (p80 37 µm), with a low acid production, and a conventional SX/EW. 

For a concentrate with As content, TOP, CESL or MT-DEW-SX can precipitate As as stable Scorodite in the autoclave. In case of precious metals occurrence like Au or Ag, they could be easily extracted from the autoclave solid residue by a leaching with complexing agents. 

But in case of PGM content in the concentrate, it can be recovered by leaching from any residue only if As is not present. If the concentrate contains As and PGM , the PLATSOL process is required. 

#### **CONCLUSION** 

The most profitable pressurized leaching technology will depend on the concentrate mineralogy, and the requirements of parallel process for acid consumption. 

For concentrates with high arsenic content, autoclave leaching is an opportunity to perform in the same vessel the leaching process, and the As stabilization process, reducing treatment cost.

#### **GRINDING CHEMISTRY – THE EFFECTS OF GRINDING ENVIRONMENT ON THE FLOTATION RESPONSE OF COPPER ORES** 

C.J. Greet and J. Kinal _Magotteaux Australia Pty Ltd PO Box 54 Mansfield Park SA 5012 Australia christopher.greet@magotteaux.com_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Numerous studies completed by academia and at industrial scale have consistently demonstrated that grinding with an electrochemically inert grinding media has significant benefits when processing copper ores.  This paper provides a summary of pulp chemical and laboratory flotation response data for a variety of copper ores classified by geological type prepared using forged steel and high chrome grinding media.  The results intend to show that the mineralogical character of the ore has a profound impact on the pulp chemistry and this affects the flotation behaviour of the sulphide minerals.  Further, the choice of high chrome grinding media, to better control the chemical environment during grinding, is driven by the mineralogy of the system under consideration. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

385 

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

The key to a successful separation in mineral processing is the preparation of particles with adequate liberation under the correct pulp chemical conditions. 

While the importance of liberation on flotation separations is generally understood and well documented in the literature [1-4], the importance of pulp chemistry is more nebulous, particularly with regard to the impact of grinding media.   Extensive work examining the electrochemical interactions between grinding media and sulphide minerals has been completed (for example, [5-9]).  Broadly, these studies indicate that most sulphide minerals are nobler than the grinding media used during comminution, therefore a galvanic couple between the media and the sulphide mineral(s) exists, which increases the corrosion rate of the grinding media.  The corrosion products of the grinding media, iron oxyhydroxide species, invariably precipitate on to the surfaces of the sulphide minerals thereby affecting their floatability [10]. 

Cullinan’s work [11] and the efforts of Peng [12] provide strong evidence that the iron contamination on the surfaces of minerals ground with forged steel emanate from the grinding media.  Further, the corrosion products from the galvanic couple between the forged steel grinding media and the sulphide minerals within the ore drive the pulp chemistry of the system. 

The degree, to which the mineralogy contributes to variations in the grinding chemistry, and how this affects flotation, requires quantification.  This paper will examine the influence mineralogy, as described by geological ore type, has on grinding chemistry and laboratory flotation behaviour.  The discussion will be restricted to copper sulphide ores. 

#### *

*GEOLOGICAL ORE TYPES FOR COPPER** 

There are four major geological ore types for copper: 

- **Porphyry copper deposits** are those ore bodies that are intimately associated with intermediate to acid plutonic intrusives, and all are characterised by intense and extensive hydrothermal alteration of the host rock.  The sulphide minerals occur in the host rock as either a disseminated mineralisation or within quartz veinlets in micro-fractures 

Porphyry ore bodies typically contain between 0.4 and 1 percent copper with smaller amounts of other metals such as molybdenum, silver and gold.  The pyrite content of these ores is generally less than 5 percent. 

These style of deposits occur around the Pacific Rim, some notable examples are: Ok Tedi (in Papua New Guinea), Highland Valley Copper (in Canada), Cananea (in 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

386 

Mexico), Chuquicamata (in Chile).  The highest concentration of porphyry copper deposits in the world occurs in Chile. 

- **<mark>Sedimentary exhalative (SedEx) deposits</mark>** <mark>are those ore bodies formed by the release of metal-bearing hydrothermal fluids into a water reservoir (usually the ocean), resulting in the precipitation of stratiform sulphide mineral bands.  These deposits are common lead-zinc ore, but also make up an economically significant source of copper.  The most famous SedEx copper deposits occur in the Zambian copperbelt.</mark> 

- **Iron oxide copper gold (IOCG) deposits** are formed in iron oxide dominated assemblages, and contain high concentrations of copper (0.2 to 5 percent), gold (0.1 to 3 grams per tonne) and uranium minerals.  Their high grade and relatively simple mineralogical textures make these deposits comparatively easy to process, and therefore highly profitable.  Typical examples of IOCG deposits are:  Olympic Dam (in Australia) and La Candelaria (in Chile). 

- **Volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposits** are predominantly layered accumulations of sulfide minerals that precipitate from hydrothermal fluids on or below the seafloor in a wide range of ancient and modern geological settings.  They occur within environments dominated by volcanic or volcanic-derived (e.g., volcano-sedimentary) rocks.  They represent a significant source of the world's copper, lead, zinc, gold and silver.  Examples of VMS deposits are:  New Brunswick (in Canada), Sominco (in Portugal), Aguas Tenidas (in Spain). 

#### **METHODOLOGY** 

In the past, many laboratory studies have not used plant-operating conditions during testing. This has led to a suspicion of laboratory results.  To avoid this complication a new tool, the Magotteaux Mill®, has been developed [13]. 

The Magotteaux Mill  (Figure 1) allows the researcher to generate a product in the laboratory that has nominally the same physical properties (particle size distribution) and pulp chemical properties (Eh, pH, dissolved oxygen, oxygen demand and EDTA extractable iron) as an equivalent sample taken

from the plant.  This is achieved by grinding an appropriate sample to achieve the particle size distribution of the flotation feed, and manipulating the pulp chemistry, by purging the system with an inert gas, so that it matches the plant grinding mill discharge. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

387 

The experimental strategy adopted to achieve the desired outcomes is completed in three phases: 



Figure 1 - Schematic representation of the Magotteaux Mill<sup>®</sup> 

_Phase 1 - Plant data collection:_ The collection of plant data is vital to the success of the test program, for this data forms the basis of the calibration process by defining the target parameters.  This initial step involves: 

- The completion of a pulp chemical and EDTA survey of the grinding and adjoining flotation circuit; 

- Determination of the oxygen demand at strategic points within the circuit; 

- The completion of a metallurgical survey; 

- The collection of conditioned flotation feed for laboratory testing; and 

- The collection of a bulk sample of the grinding circuit feed for further testing. 

It is important to note that the metallurgical survey must include both a down-thebank survey of the flotation stage immediately following grinding, and a block survey of the plant to determine overall metallurgical performance. 

_Phase 2 – Magotteaux Mill_<sup>_®_</sup> _calibration:_ The data collected in Phase 1 essentially describes the circuit under consideration, and provides targets for the Magotteaux Mill® calibration.  The calibration process uses the same grinding media as the operating plant. The objective of the calibration process is to produce a laboratory mill discharge which has 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

388 

the same particle size distribution as the conditioned flotation feed, and the pulp chemistry of the plant grinding mill discharge.  To achieve this match involves careful manipulation of the dissolved oxygen, Eh and grinding time, such that all the measured parameters line up when grinding the bulk sample collected during the metallurgical survey.  This task is not trivial. 

Once the Magotteaux Mill® is calibrated, oxygen demand and flotation tests are completed on the ground ore.  These data are compared with the results of tests conducted on the conditioned flotation feed.  If they are the same, a match is achieved. 

_Phase 3 – Media testing:_ With the Magotteaux Mill® calibrated, alternative grinding media are substituted into the mill for testing.  The procedure determined during the calibration process for the current grinding media is then applied while grinding the bulk sample employing the alternative grinding media.  In this way, it is possible to measure changes in pulp chemistry and flotation response.  The changes observed are attributed to the variations in grinding media composition, as the only intentional parameter being changed in the test is the grinding media. 

When the flotation res

ults of tests completed on the bulk sample prepared in the Magotteaux Mill® using the current grinding media are correlated with the metallurgical survey of the plant, it is possible to determine the scale-up between the laboratory and the plant. Knowing this relationship (scale-up), and the laboratory flotation response of the bulk sample when ground with high chrome grinding media, a prediction of the plant performance can be made if the alternative grinding media were to be used. Thus, this approach provides a robust laboratory methodology that firstly provides a link between the laboratory and the plant using the existing grinding media and secondly investigates changes to the pulp chemistry and metallurgical outcome when high chrome grinding media is substituted into the grinding circuit. Further, it provides a means of estimating plant performance should the best high chrome grinding media be installed in the plant. If used correctly, this strategy will provide an excellent screening procedure that will yield valuable information about the “best” grinding media for the operation. Firstly, this data suggests for all alloys tested that the copper recovery decreases as the pyrite content increased. The second and probably the more important point, is that the high chrome alloys produced markedly different copper recoveries depending on the alloy and the pyrite content. That is, for low pyrite ores (i.e. porphyry copper deposits) the low chrome alloy produced superior maximum copper recoveries to forged steel and the two higher chrome _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 394 content alloys. As the pyrite content of the ore increased the metallurgical performance of the low chrome alloy deteriorated to below that of forged steel. The reasons for this behaviour are related to this alloys poor corrosion resistance. The vast majority of the chrome in this alloy is present as chromium carbides that give this media excellent abrasion resistance but poor corrosion resistance. #### **CONCLUSIONS** 

One of the most significant differences between the various geological ore types is the pyrite content, which has a major influence on the mineralogical character of the ore. Using the Magotteaux Mill<sup>®</sup> is was possible to show that when grinding with forged steel 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

395 

grinding media as the pyrite content increased the Eh of the system becomes more reducing, suggesting that the grinding environment became more corrosive with increasing pyrite feed grades.  By changing from forged steel to a more chemically inert grinding media the pulp chemistry of the ball mill discharge for all geological ore types tested shifted to: 

- More oxidising Eh values; 

- Higher dissolved oxygen level in the pulp; 

- Lower oxygen demands; and 

- Lower EDTA extractable iron values. 

These changes in the pulp chemistry produced increased copper recoveries. 

It is apparent that the application of one high chrome alloy to all situations (i.e. a one size fits all policy) will undoubtedly lead to disaster.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Pneumatic flotation term is generally accepted to apply on froth flotation where bubbles generation and bubbles-particles attachment takes place outside of the separating vessel and separation of tailing from concentrate occur in the vessel, which is totally different with conventional mechanical, column, Simonis (1) and another cells. 

The external aeration is usually achieved by special venturi system specialized fine bubbles generation technology, The Imhoflot V Cell and G Cell pneumatic flotation uses this external self-sucking aeration unit both kind of cells  have been designed by Dr Rainer Imhof and introduced by IDM from 1992 in Chile and South America (2, 3). 

Imhoflot pneumatic flotation tries to reach perfection by generating a range of bubble sizes in the aerator. The aerator is self-aspirating using a high shear ceramic multi-jet venturi system operating in a range of 2.0 - 3.0 bar pressure, providing this way enough energy to the small mass particles liberated. Bubble sizes generated start with ultra-fine bubbles at around 10μm but also generating a range of bubbles sizes distribution, which has interaction with particles under pressure condition, this form, in the interaction particles-bubbles section, some minimum coalescence of bubbles takes place. The high shear aerator reactor is designed to maximize the attachment of bubbles to all hydrophobic particles mainly there. To achieve more recovery, the tails of the separating vessel must be introduced again to an aerator in a second chance, third or subsequent stages, until the desired recovery is achieved. 

Successful applications for Imhoflot flotation technology,  models of G Cell and V Cell, are applied for: Copper sulphide and oxide using sea water were applied CMM, Chile), Reverse flotation of silica and silicate from magnetite concentrate(CMP, Chile), reverse flotation of carbonate from Willemite concentrate (VM, Brazil), as cleaner for Sphalerite (VM, Brazil),  as  pre rougher producing end concentrate and sending the tailings to scavenger and after to end tai

ling, changing circuit configuration dramatically  for copper, full process using sea water (LL, Chile), first cleaner-end concentrate for Molybdenite (LP, Chile), rougher and cleaner for copper–gold (CMT, Chile), low grade Copper Slag using sea water (LM, Chile). (3) 

Promised new application in progress occurs for fresh tailing copper and copper slag.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Processes of continuous copper matte converting and fire refining, developed by Universidad de Chile and ENAMI, permit for projection and analysis of feasibility of the totally continuous process of copper concentrate smelting up to anodes of fire refined copper. 

Concentrate smelting in Teniente Converter, flash smelter or other type of smelting units is continuous or strictly speaking semi-continuous due to periodic tapping out of copper matte and slag. Mitsubishi process in smelting concentrate and matte converting is fully continuous. However, produced blister copper is refined in a classical batch process.                  Kennecott-Outokumpu process of melting and converting are continuous, but between is copper matte solidification, crushing and milling as noncontinuous processes. 

Continuously tapped out copper matte is directed to packed bed continuous converter, producing over-oxidized blister (8000 ppm [O]), directed to continuous packed bed refining furnace, where is reduced and casted continuously in twin type of anode casting wheels. The slag from the smelting furnace is tapped out continuously into electric furnace for slag cleaning and tapped out as waste slag into a ladle or granulation installation. The slag from converting furnace with high copper content is recycled into smelting unit or a slag cleaning furnace in a solid or liquid form. 

The projection of the “dream”, totally continuous process, points out the potential advantages of the processes of continuous converting and refining being under development. 

The results of laboratory and industrial scale tests, together with mass and heat balances, permit to initiate the discussion and feasibility analysis of totally continuous copper smelters in their pyrometallurgical part. 

There are no-continuous copper fire refining process worldwide. Wuth et  al. [1-2] developed interesting process in pilot scale, but the process did not find further development. 

Separate class of processes are direct to copper smelting, such as WORCRA and Noranda which were stopped, and Glogow and Olympic Dam in the flash smelter, which operate successfully. The processes produce blister in one unit ready for classical, batch fire refining. However, up to 1/3 of copper from a concentrate goes to a slag and has to be recovered in an electric furnace with further processing of metallic alloy. 

All smelting processes

produces a slag containing from 1.5 to 15.0 % Cu and needs slag cleaning operation, such reduction and settling in an electric furnace, Chilean HLE or flotation. The most popular process in an electric furnace can be batch, semicontinuous or continuous. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

418 

Continuous copper smelting, converting and fire refining has been metallurgist´s dream for long time. It has been partly achieved by direct copper smelting processes, such as WORCRA, Noranda Mitsubishi and Outokumpu direct copper flash smelting, but only  Mitsubishi and direct copper flash smelting (GLOGOW and OLYMPIC DAM) are in operation. 

The aim of this paper is the analysis of possibilities and feasibility of totally continuous copper smelter from concentrate to anodes, directed to the electrorefining. The base are successful projects of continuous copper matte converting and blister copper fire refining, developed at University of Chile and tested in the laboratory scale and further developed with ENAMI in the Hernan Videla Lira Smelter (Paipote) with support of engineering companies, such as last leading company BUILTEK S.A. proposed new process that consists in three series reactors with continuous gravitational flow of copper matte, blister copper and continuous casting of anodes. 

#### **CONTINUOUS CONVERTING** 

Continuous converting has been developed at University of Chile with cooperation with ENAMI, Pyrotech and currently Builtek. The process of copper matte converting in a packed, ceramic bed is totally original. The process principles, fundamental research, pilot-demonstrate tests and the design of pilot industrial scale, has been presented in papers [3]. 

Shortly, the process of continuous converting, in two possible options, is presented in Figure 1 and 2. The classical, two steps of copper matte converting  i) iron blowing and ii) copper blowing are carried out in two identical reactors with ceramic packed bed. The copper matte flows continuously from smelting furnace to the first reactor, where is dispersed and flows down through the packed bed porosity. The air (or slightly enriched air in oxygen) is blown through tuyeres into the packed bed. Countercurrent flow of the copper matte and the air results in reactions of iron sulphide oxidation to magnetite and wustite. Added mix of fluxes: silica, limestone and clay on the packed bed surface, melts and flows down in the bed porosity, contacting wustite and reacting with magnetite The converting slag FeO-SiO2-CaO-Al2O3-Fe3O4 is formed and flow down, creating a layer on the surface of white metal. Partly oxidized copper sulphide and the part of impurities oxides dissolve in the slag. Volatile compounds of impurities are leaving the furnace with the off-gas. White metal is tapped continuously out through an inclined hole, playing a role of siphon. Converting slag is tapped out continuously by side tapping block with a hole. 

The degree of matte oxidation, corresponds to th

e classical first stage of converting. White metal flows continuously into the second reactor, where copper sulphide is oxidized to metallic copper by injected air through the tuyeres. The small amount of refining slag generated during the process, depends on the degree of copper _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 419 oxidation. Classical bister 4000 ppm O and 400 ppm S can be produced and directed to fire refining. The gases from both reactors are collected, cooled by air dilution or convectional cooling installation, and sent to an electrostatic precipitator, and then from the precipitator to the sulphuric acid plant. On stage continuous converting, presented in Figure 2, is controlled for high degree of blister oxidation (7000 – 9000 ppm O and 20 – 40 ppm S), ready for reduction in fire refining and casting of anodes. The process of blister copper refining in a packed bed is totally original. The process principles, fundamental research, pilot-demonstrate tests and the designed and results of the tests of pilot industrial scale, has been presented in papers [4 –5]. The continuous, two stages (two furnaces), process is shown in Figure 3. The first reactor is filled with ceramic packed bed, where gravitationally flown blister copper flows down in the bed porosity in countercurrent to the oxygen containing gases, injected by tuyeres. In addition with the air, some relatively small amount of natural gas or liquid gas is injected in order to cover heat losses and control the copper temperature. ister flow, the tuyeres are converted into burner, in order to maintain the temperature When the content of arsenic and antimony in the blister are elevated, fluxes can be add. Refining slag is tapped continuously through a side block and oxidized copper flows. Oxidized copper flows through a siphon and launder to the second reactor, filled with packed bed of charcoal, or low sulphur coke. Injected air reacts with carbon of charcoal, producing carbon monoxide, which reduces oxygen in the copper. Reaction gases leaving packed bed are rich in carbon monoxide, so the burner over the bed is what make post-combustion effective. The furnaces are closed, and the hoods over tapping holes with suction should dramatically decrease the fugitive emissions. Periodic tapping out of copper matte and slag make the process semi-continuous. Mitsubishi process with continuous matte and slag evacuation and continuous matte converting presents full continuity. Presented processes of continuous matte converting and fire refining in the packed bed reactors allow for the design of fully continuous copper smelter. Conceptual design is shown in Figure 5. Teniente Converter (TC) melt dry copper concentrate, injected through tuyeres. The series of tuyeres inject the air enriched in oxygen (32-35% O2) into copper matte. Silica flux is added through gurr-gun. High grade copper matte (70-75% Cu) is tapped out continuously though a tapping block and launder into continuous converting furnace (CCF). The smelting slag is continuously tapped out through a tapping block and launder in the electric furnace. The slag is reduced and cleaned in an electric furnace and tapped out continuously to the launder or the installation of water granulation, and transported to the waste yard. The relatively small amount of copper matte from electric furnace can be recycled liquid to TC or solidified, crushed and added with fluxes to TC or continuous converting furnace (CCF). Copper matte stream entering the converting furnace is dispersed on the packed bed. Mix of fluxes melts and with copper matte infiltrates the porosity of the packed bed. The following reactions form blister copper and converting slag: 3 [FeS]matte + 5 {O2}blast = (Fe3O4)solid + 3{SO2}gas (Fe3O4)solid+ (CaO)solid+ (SiO2)solid = (CaO.Fe2O3)slag + (Fe2SiO4)slag The over-oxidation of blister copper in the converting furnace, corresponds to the first stage of blister oxidation in an anode furnace (8000 ppm O, 40 ppm S). _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 427 It results in local saturation of copper in oxygen and precipitation of Cu2O, which is transferred into slag. Thus, the impurities (S, Fe, As, Sb, Pb, Zn) go partly to the slag, gas and small amount, acceptable for electrorefining is in the copper together with precious metals and nickel. Finally, the copper content in the converting slag is high. Off-gases from smelting furnace (TC, flash smelter etc.) rich in SO2 can be join with off-gases of converting furnace, cleaned and send to sulphuric acid plant. #### **DISCUSSION** The totally continuous copper smelter is feasible. Gravitational flow of the copper matte, copper blister and slag requires the positioning of every furnace at proper level. The most challenging is the elevation of a smelting furna

ce. Figure 6, shows a flow sheet of continuous copper smelter with approximated major parameters. The converting furnace is very compact, O.D=2.5 m and H=2.7 m. Fire refining reactor is smaller O.D=1.8 m, H=2.2 m. The converting and fire refining reactors are so simple and cheap in investment, that two parallel lines from smelting furnace to casting wheel can be built, one in operation and the second in standby. It will ensure continuity of the production. Where the installation of twin casting wheels will be impossible the refined copper can be directed to the holding furnace and anode casting will be classically periodic. Continuous stream of gases from smelting furnace and converting furnace will stabilize the SO2 content and results in higher sulphur capture. Minimization of the transportation of liquid materials as well as hoods and suction of the gases from tapping holes and launders should strongly decrease fugitive emission. The high intensity of the converting process and refining process, affect the decrease of unitary heat losses, increasing the energy efficiency of the smelter. Minimization of the operations with tapping holes (only electric furnace matte tapping hole) results in the decrease of the labor and safety of operators. The totally continuous smelter “in line” is easy for automation and precise control of key parameters in every stage of the process. Continuous converting and fire refining furnaces have very small amount of a liquid phase inside. It means that the furnace respond very fast for the changes of control parameters. It is easy control the degree of oxidation and temperature in converting furnace as well as in fire refining furnace. Potentially various scrap can be melted in converting furnace, such as anode scrap, electronic scrap, after preparation of the size of scrap grains. #### **IMPLEMENTATION OF NUMERICAL MODELING FOR EFFICIENCY INCREASE IN FIRING OF ROTARY ANODE FURNACE** 

E. Kolczyk, Z. Miczkowski and G. Krawiec _Institute of Non-Ferrous Metals Sowińskiego 5 44-100 Gliwice, Poland Ewa.Kolczyk@imn.gliwice.pl_ 

#### **ABSTRACT** 

The paper presents analysis of variants of rotary anode furnace firing for minimization of fuel consumption by application of a burner and tuyeres. A mathematical model of heat exchange in the rotary anode furnace was developed. The model was used for determination of average copper charge temperature and uniformity of thermal field in the anode furnace which was fired by traditional method and with application of tuyeres. Based on the performed calculations and analyses it was established that the   rotary anode furnace fired with application of a burner only requires higher volume of the fuel to provide appropriate temperature of the bath. Implementation of the submerged tuyeres beside the gas burner in the firing of the anode furnace, provides possibilities to reduce fuel consumption and improves uniformity of thermal field in the bath. The highest firing efficiency was produced with application of the burner and tuyeres supplied with gas in the amount of 100 + 50 + 50 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h, where the average temperature of liquid copper of 1219°C with standard deviation of 18.2°C was reached.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Rotary anode furnaces are used in fire refining of blister copper and casting of copper anodes. No solid charge is melted in the furnaces and they are fired with a single gas-oxygen-air burner. 

A rotary anode furnace is constructed in a form of a steel drum with two layers of lining (Fig. 1). The analyzed unit had a nominal

capacity of 250 -270 Mg of liquid copper. Every furnace is equipped with a system for afterburning of process gases which are then mixed and sent for sulfur and dust removal. Copper fire refining process consists of the following technological stages: - furnace charging, - oxidation, - removal of arsenic with mixture of soda and lime, - draining off slag, - reduction, - casting of anodes. The basic component of rotary furnace charge, is liquid blister copper from flash furnace and liquid converter copper from fining of CuPbFe alloy, or liquid converter copper from fining of copper matte. In the final stage of fire refining liquid copper of temperature 1150-1220°C which contains about 0.001 wt % of S and 0.15 wt % of O2. The copper is cast into anodes which contain 99.40 wt % Cu; 0.17 wt % Pb; 0.12 wt % As. The anodes are sent to tank house for electrorefining [1-3]. BURNER

The numerical model was developed with PHOENICS software [4]. The model of rotary anode furnace consisted of the following components:

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Based on the performed calculations and analyses the following conclusions can be drawn: 

- The rotary anode furnace which is fired with gas burner only, after taking under consideration heat loss, requires 300 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h of natural gas to provide the necessary bath temperature. 

- Application of submerged tuyeres beside the gas burner in firing of the anode furnace results in reduction of fuel consumption. Higher average bath temperature (1219°C) was reached when in the burner and the tuyeres 100 + 50 + 50 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h, respectively, of natural gas was used for firing than in the firing with the burner only at the rate of 300 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h (1197°C). 

- Firing of the furnace with application of the tuyeres improves also uniformity of thermal field in the bath. The standard deviation from the average bath temperature was 18.2°C in firing with the tuyeres while in firing with the burner only it was 26.3°C. 

- Comparison of firing with application of the burner and the tuyeres at the same total volume of the consumed fuel (200 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h) but at different ratios of the streams supplied to the burner and the tuyeres shows that in the analyzed ranges the efficiency of heat utilization is higher when higher amount of gas is delivered through the tuyeres. The average bath temperature for the gas streams 100 + 50 + 50 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h was 1219°C and for 150 + 25 + 25 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h it was 1205°C. 

- The highest firing efficiency, from among the analyzed variants, was reached when the burner and the tuyeres were used and supplied with gas in the amounts of 100 + 50 + 50 Nm<sup>3</sup> /h, respectively. Average liquid copper temperature of 1219°C with standard deviation of 18.2°C was reached.

#### **MAXIMIZING POWER GENERATION FROM METALLURGICAL SULPHURIC ACID PLANTS**

#### **ABSTRACT** 

Modern metallurgical processes operating with oxygen enriched air, such as the Outotec Flash

Smelter and Flash Converter, generate very concentrated SO2 off-gas which in combination with Outotec sulphuric acid plant technology allows the production of high pressure steam to be used for power generation. Outotec combines well proven technology of sulphur burning plants for this purpose with metallurgical plants. 

The application of Outotec’s proven LUREC<sup>TM</sup> process enables processing of SO2 gas of up to 25 vol.-%. This process maximizes the energy recovery from the SO2 oxidation at a suitable high temperature level which can be turned into high pressure steam. 

The application of the Outotec HEROS<sup>TM</sup> heat recovery system enables the generation of low pressure steam from the absorption energy released at the intermediate absorption step. Additionally, energy is also recovered in the acid coolers for boiler feedwater pre-heating. 

The concept of integration of high and low pressure steam in combination with the pressurized operation of the boiler feedwater deaerator, thus heating up the boiler feed water to temperatures around 160…170°C, enables indirect transfer of low pressure steam (for deaerator operation) into more valuable high pressure steam, which improves the degree of heat recovery. This is the characteristic of Outotec’s HIPROS<sup>TM</sup> process. 

The thus increased generation of high pressure steam will in turn enable the generation of more electricity when compared to a standard traditional sulphuric acid process.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

In the past, energy recovery in metallurgical sulphuric acid plants did play a minor role in plant design.  Most of the few existing energy recovery applications in metallurgical acid plants use a low level heat integration where e.g. hot air is utilized or hot water is produced.  This paper describes the potential of power production for modern metallurgical acid plants based on combinations of existing technologies. 

The first section describes process routes to achieve high power generation and the necessary preconditions.  The second section demonstrates the effect of different levels of heat integration in a straight forward case study.  The last section focuses on the commercial impact of the different solutions and discusses some practical issues. 

#### **PROCESS DESCRIPTION** 

The basis for power production in metallurgical acid plants is a strong and preferably continuous gas source to obtain a high SO2 concentration with sufficient oxygen at the inlet of the SO2 converter. A high SO2 concentration corresponds to a high surplus of useable energy in regard to the (physical) autothermal limit of the plant. This concentration difference is a direct measure of the amount of energy recovery physically possible from the given process gas. 

The maximum SO2 concentration in conventional acid plants is limited by the maximum operating temperature of the catalyst as shown in Figure 1.  In principle also convent

ional plants allow some energy integration, but in practice the heat is often removed in SO3 coolers by cooling against air. In fact, at low SO2 concentrations around 6.5%-vol., no excess heat is available for other use. This is called the autothermal point. With increasing SO2 concentrations the amount of excess energy increases significantly and must be removed from the system. But power production in conventional plants is only useful if the plant has an existing steam infrastructure. For a stand-alone power generation the SO2 concentration must preferably be above 12%-vol. SO2– the higher the better. This energy is used for the production of valuable high pressure steam. To avoid exceeding the maximum catalyst operating temperature in bed 1 while further increasing the SO2 concentration a simple chemical principle can be used: The chemical equilibrium in bed 1 is shifted towards higher SO2 concentration by adding SO3 to the gas entering the first bed from the upstream metallurgical plant as shown in figure 1. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago,Chile_ 449 100

##### **INTRODUCTION** 

Information systems are becoming more and more intertwined with the operational processes they support. As a result, multitudes of events are recorded by today’s information systems. Nevertheless, organizations have problems extracting value from these data [1]. 

Most of the data stored is unstructured and it is not easy to deal with such large quantities of data. One of the main challenges of organizations is to extract information and value from data stored in their information systems. 

Process measurements mainly aim at improving operational performance, keeping parameters in a certain range at each step. An almost continuous stream of detailed data does not help in gaining a broad look at the whole process. #### **PATTERN REPORT** 

Once we have the set of records (a knowledge base) we can perform some analyses based on data mining tools. The Pattern Report is based on k Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) Classification. The task is to find entities close to the parameters set by the user. The k-nearest-neighbor classifier is based on the distance between the test sample and the specified training samples. 

In practice the user sets the parameter values (up to 8), then decides on the level of deviation (acceptable distance). In fact the user sets two levels of deviation, average and maximal. The algorithm classifies records and “chooses” the meeting criteria. 

The output result can be analyzed in two ways: 

- Predictor – the algorithm chose the nearest cases and calculated variables’ averages. We can assume with some level of confidence that the unknown variables should come close to those calculated. 

- Classifier – the chosen cases can be treated as a cluster and help to build classification rules to optimize the process.

#### **INTRODUCTION**

High power rectifier system includes rectifier transformer, rectifier, rectifier control panel, and power factor improving capacitors and filter etc. The traditional rectifier system layout is shown as the Figure 1, in traditional layout, the equipments require conditional environment, located indoor generally, need locate the rectifier control panel in the room with are-conditioner. 

Outdoor integrat

ed green energy-saving high power rectifier system for copper smelter which combine all the equipments except the rectifier transformer, oil water cooler, power factor improving capacitor and filter into the complete sealed outdoor rectifier container, shown as Figure 2. #### **ABSTRACT** 

Copper heap leaching operations are challenging both from monitoring and operational perspectives. A common denominator for both challenges is definitely the presence of an enormous heap leach pad representing an active and highly heterogeneous in-process copper inventory. Not only this in-process copper inventory has to be assessed for process monitoring and optimization purposes but also its economic value needs to be reported to various stakeholders on a regular basis. Due to random and possible systematic measurement errors, favorable or unfavorable adjustments of in-process inventories often have to be made. While most stakeholders understand very well the intrinsic volatility of metal prices,

there is much less empathy for negative adjustments to metal inventories (write-offs). The analysis herein shows that severe metal accounting as well as operational challenges could arise when the design of the heap and of the solutions management system do not comply with state of the art metal accounting principles such as those proposed by the AMIRA P754 Code of Practice. This paper shows that such challenges can be coped with when best practices are considered from the heap layout design phase and maintained throughout the full operating lifecycle.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Copper heap leaching operations offer challenges both from monitoring and operational perspectives [1] . A common denominator for both challenges is definitely the presence of an enormous heap leach pad representing an active and highly heterogeneous in-process copper inventory. Not only this in-process copper inventory must be assessed for process monitoring and optimization purposes but also its economic value needs to be reported to various stakeholders on a regular basis. 

However, accurately determining the in-process copper inventory of a heap leach unit is challenging in industrial practice. Audits have shown that available indirect or direct measurements often carry large inaccuracies. Sooner or later, ignoring these measurement errors lead to unexpected incoherencies in reported copper balances. In such situations, coherent copper balances are then achieved through subjective and sometimes significant adjustments of in-process inventory levels. While such metal accounting methods applied by mineral processing engineers used to be rarely challenged, they are now being increasingly scrutinized by various stakeholders. This accrued scrutiny is obviously no stranger to the corporate governance tightening that happened through the years in response to outrageous accounting scandals. While most stakeholders understand the intrinsic volatility associated with metal prices, there is much less empathy for negative adjustments (write-offs) of in-process copper inventories, especially when they are found to be caused by poor metal accounting practices [2]. 

This paper analyses metal accounting in copper heap leach operations mainly through the estimation and reporting of copper balances. After briefly describing the layout of a typical heap leaching operation, three key principles of metal accounting, according to the AMIRA P754 Code of Practice [3], are highlighted. The challenge of determining the depleting copper inventory of active leaching heaps is then emphasized and estimation methods are presented. 

#### **COPPER HEAP LEACH OPERATIONS** 

Copper heap leaching is an extractive metallurgy process mostly applied to recover copper from low-grade ores. It is amongst the simplest processes often involving no more material preparation than crushing and agglomeration. The processed ore is then stockpiled on a specifica

lly-designed pad shown in Figure 1 upon which a sulfuric acid solution is sprinkled for several weeks or months. The pregnant leach solution (PLS) is then collected at the bottom of the pad (or at the uppermost liner level in case of multiple lift designs). The PLS solution is then processed by solvent extraction (SX) and electrowinning (EW) for producing copper cathodes . The design shown in Figure 1 also includes the option of closed-loop leaching through the use of an intermediate leach solution (ILS) pond. With this design, should the leach solution strength be too low for the SX-EW plant to process it efficiently, the leach solution can be recirculated back to the heap until an acceptable copper concentration is reached. _Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 487 Figure 1 – Boundaries of a complete metal balance for a typical heap leaching operation Another important differentiator among various heap leaching flowsheet designs is the heap construction and management strategy (see Figure 2). While it happens that single-layered (or single lift) heaps are constructed, most often, heaps are constructed in successive vertical and/or lateral layers that may or may not be isolated from one another through geomembrane lining [4]. Expanding heaps are typically divided into zones (often referred to as ‘cells’) that correspond to specific portions of the heap that were constructed during a contiguous period in time. Such cells are used for heap micromanagement and, as such, each given cell can have its own irrigation scheme. Single lift Multiple cells

Figure 3 – Primary metal accounting model for heap leaching operations #### In-Process Inventory The P754 Code of practice clearly states that these in-process inventories should be determined through physical stock-takes. In other words, inventories must be determined through actual measurements of the material quantity and quality within each holding unit. For a typical heap leaching operation, this means that copper inventory should be regularly measured in each leaching heap, solution pond, SX-EW process units and storage tanks as well as in the copper cathodes storage area. In almost all of these holding units, copper inventory m

easurements can made without major technical difficulties. The exceptions are the leaching heaps. 

Stock-taking a leaching heap demands that representative samples [5] are collected from it and analyzed for copper content. However, because leaching heaps typically are extremely heterogeneous (both in space and time), representative sampling can only be achieved through multiple samples taken at different locations and depths

490 

within the pile. As drilling is often required for collecting under-surface samples, stock-taking a leaching heap always is a significant endeavour. 

The Code recognizes that sampling costs may preclude mining companies from performing physical stock-takes at the end of each metal accounting period (typically, monthly). However, the Code states that physical stock-takes should be performed within each holding unit at least once a year. 

#### <u>Data Validation and Redundancy</u> 

The principle of Data Validation and Redundancy listed in Table 1 essentially stipulates that the reported metal balance should be determined through statistical data reconciliation [6] and not through a ‘by-difference’ method. A metal balance is said to be determined ‘by-difference’ when all but one (the unknown) streams feeding and leaving a process unit are characterized through mass (or volume) measurements and chemical analyses of representative samples. The characteristics of the unknown stream are simply calculated by difference. Although simple to obtain using any common spreadsheet, the results of ‘by-difference’ metal balancing can hardly be validated knowing that all the involved measured values carry random and possible systematic measurement errors. Indeed, this method is hindering the estimation of random errors thus preventing the computation and reporting of confidence intervals for metal balance figures. Furthermore, the lack of analytical redundancy [7] of this method precludes any bias detection. 

A statistical reconciliation can be performed when all the streams feeding and leaving a process unit are independently characterized. This well-known technique [6] makes it possible to determine the accuracy of the metal balance figures and therefore, to validate the reported metal balances (including in-process metal inventories). By systematically monitoring over time the corrections made on measured values, measurement biases can also be detected and actions be taken to eliminate them. 

#### **PRACTICAL METAL ACCOUNTING FOR HEAP LEACHING** 

The primary copper balance discussed in the previous section (Figure 3) is in fact the summary of a more detailed copper balance that needs to be reported at the end of each metal accounting period (typically, monthly). Such detailed copper balance can be obtained by taking an appropriately simplified process flowsheet such as the one illustrated in Figure 1. Each of the six active nodes therein carries a copper inventory that needs to b

e taken into account when significant. Of course, the metal balance could be further detailed by including the copper flows within the SX-EW plant (between the extraction, stripping and electrolysis sections of the plant) if required. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

491 

A first condition for this detailed copper balance to comply with the P754 Code of Practice, is that it must be determined through statistical reconciliation. Therefore, redundancy must be generated by measuring copper flow in each stream and copper inventory within each node. As pointed out already, most of these measurements are technically feasible. The greatest challenge is determining the in-process copper inventory within the leaching heaps. 

#### **Copper Inventory Within Single Leaching Heaps** 

From a theoretical standpoint, the most attractive method for determining a heap copper inventory is to apply the Direct Method of measurement [8]. This method basically consists in measuring the volume of the whole heap (using optimal instruments) and drilling multiple holes in it for collecting representative samples. Although volume determination can be made regularly, drilling program can be very demanding (both in terms of human and economic resources) and therefore, impractical to repeat on a monthly basis. For complying with the P754 Code of Practice, however, systematic drilling and sampling of the heaps should be performed at least once a year. 

In spite of the Direct Method challenges, monthly production reports, including accurate metal balances along with in-process inventories, must be issued. An alternative method must then be adopted for assessing copper inventory within the heap between the low-frequency surveys (i.e. between the applications of the Direct Method). 

The first alternative method is referred to as the Indirect Method [8]. The method is called ‘indirect’ because it does not require any physical measurements (weighing, drilling, sampling, surveying, etc.) of the stockpile. The closing inventory I _C_ of the stockpile is rather calculated through a simple material balance 



where IO is the opening copper inventory within the stockpile while F and E are the amount of copper fed to and extracted from the heap during the accounting period. 

Although attractive from a cost minimization perspective, the indirect method carries significant flaws. 

1. Because in-process inventory is determined from the copper fed to the heap (new ore and copper carried by the recycled acidic solution) and extracted, it has not been be determined independently from them. Since there will never be incoherence between flow and inventory measurements, it will not be possible to pick up and estimate the random errors and possible biases that are attached to the flow measurements around the heap. For statistical reconciliation to respectively estimate and detect these errors, inventory and flow measurements must be taken independently from one another. 

_P

roceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

492 

2. Because of the errors associated with the metal flow measurements (mass flowrates, volumetric flowrates, samples, chemical analyses, etc.), the inaccuracy of copper within-the-heap inventory calculated increases monotonously with time [8] . Depending on the quality of the instrumentation and of the solution sampling procedure, the cumulated estimation variance associated with the copper inventory can rapidly become significant. 

Another method is the _Predictive_ method that makes use of a mathematical model capable of predicting the depletion of copper within the heap with time. The model [9] would use the flowrate and chemical composition of acidic solution sprinkled on top of the heap as an input but within-the-heap copper inventory and copper extracted from the heap would be predicted by the model. Since the copper extraction and in-process inventory will be predicted independently from the measured copper extraction, redundancy is created and it becomes possible to apply statistical reconciliation techniques to obtain a coherent metal balance around the heap. This gained redundancy comes however with the need to characterize numerous model parameters. 

Whether the _Indirect_ or the _Predictive_ method is used, both the feed and discharge solution streams of the heap must be systematically and rigorously monitored for flow rate and chemical composition. Basic solution monitoring must be available. 

#### **Copper Inventory Within Expanding Heaps (with Multiple Cells)** 

Single heap copper accounting methods can be applied to layouts where each heap is equipped with a dedicated solution monitoring system for feed and discharge streams. They can also be applied to horizontally and/or vertically expanding heaps (see Figure 4) provided that the solutions feeding and discharging from of each cell (zone of the heap with a specific leaching age and status) can be monitored independently. Figure 4 is the schematic of an expanding heap with distributed solution monitoring (the symbols represent flow meters and solution sampling points). 



Figure 4 – Expanding heap with a distributed solution monitoring system. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

493 

Distributed solution monitoring may not always be conducted or technically feasible. In many cases, only basic solution monitoring, where overall feed and discharge flows are monitored, is carried out routinely (Figure 5).  In those cases, the methods suggested for single heap copper accounting can still be applied but the benefits that they provide will be slightly different. 

As for the single heap case, the Direct method is the most accurate but the most labour-intensive. The P754 Code of Practice states that it should be conducted at least once a year. It will require stock-takes (involving drilling, sampling and chemical analysis) of every active or under construction cell. The key benefit will be a cell-by-cell breakdown of co

pper inventory within the whole expanding heap. 



Figure 5 – Expanding heap with a basic solution monitoring system 

The Indirect method is the cheapest and, as with single heaps, it carries significant drawbacks. In addition to those already stated, this method is only capable of assessing the copper inventory within the whole heap. No cell-by-cell inventory breakdown will be obtained. From an operation optimization standpoint, this is often inadequate. 

As it may compensate for the shortcomings of the Indirect method, the Predictive method is particularly interesting. By assigning a specifically calibrated leaching model to each cell of the expanding heap, a cell-by-cell breakdown of copper inventory can be obtained. The cell-by-cell predictions of solution discharge can then be reconciled with the actual measurement of the combined discharge to further increase the accuracy of the cell-by-cell estimates. The main challenge of the Predictive method (in addition to calibrating the model adequately), is to determine the distribution of the feed solution flow between the different active cells which, ideally, should always be measured. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

494 

#### **CONCLUSIONS** 

High-quality metal accounting can clearly be conducted at copper heap leaching operations. The application of the rigorous AMIRA P754 principles of metal accounting makes it possible to obtain detailed copper balances based on reliable figures for in-process copper inventories. The determination of the depleting copper inventory of leaching heaps, often perceived as the greatest challenge, can be overcome through the application of different methods. Most of them rely on flow rate measurements and chemical compositions of solution feeding and being extracted from heaps. Consequently, all they require is a well laid-out and instrumented solution distribution system as well as systematic solution sampling and analysis procedures. All of these are accessible technologies. 

Although the most cumbersome of all, the Direct method is the only method that allows the validation of in-process copper inventory within the heaps. This explains why a key AMIRA P754 principle states that in-process inventories must be stock-taken at least once a year.

#### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper describes how to make advanced control choices when difficult processes need improvement. How does one determine the best approach? The decision-making process involves choosing between a rules-based approach and a modelbased approach as well as weighing benefits and drawbacks, complexity and simplicity, investment and results. This paper will present briefly each solution and define terminology for the most common solutions:  basic control (single-loop control), advanced regulatory control, model predictive control, and expert systems such as fuzzy logic controllers and neural networks. The article then proposes a decision tree for selecting the most appropriate approach. The decision tree includes a list of questions, a series of tests to validate models, and a series of questions for interviewing operators. Potential solutions and approaches will be organized in a simple schematic by hierarchy. Examples for each solution will be presented and discussed. A table will compare usage, development, commissioning, maintenance and lifecycle costs for each approach. Finally, conclusions and suggestions will summarize the methodology.

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

Advanced process control (APC) is a popular topic. How can one decide whether advanced control should be added to an existing system? Advanced control is used to improve performance, stabilize production, handle constraints, protect equipment and manage grade changes. 

Most plants use feedback controllers, usually PID (proportional, integral, derivative) controllers. It is common to develop special control schemes to handle more complex processes. 

In classic PID process control, a

controller brings a single value close to a set point using a single manipulated variable. On the other hand, APC brings several values close to optimal targets simultaneously using several manipulated variables. 

APC's four main strategies are advanced regulatory control, model predictive control (MPC), fuzzy logic and neural networks. 

Simple solutions are always preferred. Complexity will be increased if performances (production, quality, etc.) are below par. Profitability analyses should be conducted to validate project viability. Needs—not trends—should dictate choices! 

Before increasing complexity, it is important to define needs, goals, technical support, budget, etc. All these approaches entail strengths and weaknesses. Building a project based on technology rather than needs spells trouble. 

This paper will focus on how to select the appropriate approach. 

#### **HOW TO SELECT THE APPROPRIATE APPROACH DECISION TREE:  IS ADVANCED CONTROL NECESSARY?** 

The first step is to determine whether we need more than just PID control. 

The following questions must be answered: 

- Are the performances adequate? 

   - Performance expectations should be discussed and prioritized. 

- Have the loops been optimized? 

   - All loops should be optimized. 

   - All equipment should be verified. 

   - All control strategies should be reviewed. 

- Do the control systems handle disturbances? Do the control loops interact? (Brittain and Dubй, 2011) [1] 

- Does an operator perform better than the control system? 

499 

#### **MODEL-BASED OR RULES-BASED SYSTEMS** 

APC can be divided into two categories:  model-based and rules-based. Model-based control is essentially advanced regulatory control and model predictive control, while rules-based control is mainly fuzzy logic control. Other techniques exist, such as genetic algorithm and neural networks. 

Model-based approaches are usually the first choice. If models cannot be identified, or if there is a wide variation in models, then rules-based systems are considered. In rules-based approaches, the best operator’s knowledge is used to manipulate set points on control loops. In other words, the process models the best operator (McMillan, 2011) [2]. 

#### **ADVANCED PROCESS CONTROL APPROACHES ADVANCED REGULATORY CONTROL** 

To achieve better performance, cascade control, feedforward and constraint control are commonly used. This approach is referred to as advanced regulatory control and is widely used because it is well understood and the plant’s personnel can maintain these solutions. The control scheme is based on mass and energy balance (Brittain and Dubй, 2011) [1]. 

#### **MODEL PREDICTIVE CONTROL (MPC)** 

If process performances require more sophisticated control approaches, model predictive control (MPC) is usually the first choice. MPC is best used for processes with strong coupling among variables, competing optimization goals and limited process constraints. 

MPC is an advanced metho

d of process control that has been used in the petrochemical industry since the 1980s. Model predictive controllers predict future behaviour based on dynamic models of the process, most often linear empirical models obtained through system identification. MPC is widely used in chemical and petrochemical plants where process reactions, energy balance and mass balance are well known. Not only are theoretical relationships known, but the actual process behaviour resembles theory. Although good models can be calculated, in practice tests are performed on the process and models are developed based on those tests (McMillan, 2011) [2]. 500 Linear or non-linear models can be handled by MPC but it is usually easier to consider non-linear processes as a series of linear models and to switch models based on process conditions. MPC is a multivariable control algorithm that uses an internal dynamic model of the process, and then predicts the best next moves on manipulated variables; the decisions are based on history, models and an optimization cost function. #### **ABSTRACT** 

With reference to greenfield plant projects, using process simulators similar to the designed plant Human Machine Interface (HMI) or Distributed Control System (DCS) has become common practice. These simulators represent a “virtual plant” based on process modeling of the circuit chemistry and thermodynamics, and on the physical nature of the plant, including equipment, valves, piping, etc. The virtual plant allows trainees to troubleshoot problems, optimize process variables, react to alarms, etc., all based on the process simulation model. 

Performance Associates’ experience is that this complex simulator training is valuable, but only after more in-depth training on the process and control logic. To truly optimize a process plant, prior to simulator training, the control room operators must have detailed knowledge of the following: 

- Process objective of each process system, comprising a group of unit operations. 

- Process objective of each unit operation. 

- Process chemistry and the variables affecting it. 

- Important characteristics of each unit operation, the variables affecting it, and the impact on downstream unit operations. 

- Plant control loops, interlocks, and alarms. 

- Safety issues related to the process and control schemes. 

- Operating procedures for start-u

p and shutdown under various scenarios, as well as important operator tasks. 

Additionally, trainees must be intimately familiar with the applicable fundamental scientific concepts, such as pressure, temperature, heat exchangers, electricity, PID control logic, combustion, etc. With this fundamental and plant-specific foundation, the process simulator can be fully exploited for training. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_

#### **INTRODUCTION** 

It is common practice in the metallurgical process industry to develop a process simulator for training plant operators prior to plant start-up. These simulators generally have a DCS interface similar to the DCS interface the operator will see and use in the actual plant. Process graphics, controller face plates, and motor start-stop controls are all positioned as they are on the actual DCS. A mathematical model of the process provides the necessary information to the DCS front end so the simulator will act as it does in the actual process. 

Performance Associates International, Inc., specializes in developing plant start-up training programs for new metallurgical process plants. Therefore, we are familiar with the approach taken by various mining companies to prepare operators for start-up. In this capacity, we have observed that some companies use the simulator as the primary training tool for their operators. While the simulator is a valuable tool, we have found that simulator training is more effective after more basic fundamental and plant-specific training has been conducted. 

#### **TRAINING PYRAMID** 

Performance Associates visualizes process training in the form of a pyramid consisting of basic, intermediate, and advanced levels. Refer to Figure 1. 



Figure 1– The training pyramid 

_Proceedings of Copper 2013 Santiago, Chile_ 

509 

#### **Basic Training** 

The theoretical foundation for training is the basic level of the pyramid— the introductions and fundamentals. This training includes applicable scientific principles, such as pressure and pressure measurement, temperature and heat exchangers, acids and bases, solutions and solution concentration, slurries and slurry density, etc. It also includes the basics of process unit operations, such as crushing and conveying, grinding, pumping, size classification, flotation, dewatering, sampling, furnaces, boilers, offgas, etc. The training on each process unit operation includes topics covering the objective, applicable scientific principle of operation, equipment components and general design, and key characteristics and variables. The basic training provides the foundation for the intermediate or plant-specific training. Ideally, the basic training is computer-based training (CBT) where trainees can interact with the training material via a computer; CBT facilitates the use of animations and videos with voice-over narration to support the theoretical material.
